Procedures may include faster approval processes, fewer signatures, different authority levels. The Emergency Procedures are activated for a specific period of time.

component_responses.notes: BDRCS uses Navision for financial functions at NHQ level. For project-based activities, Tally, a small-scale accounting software is used and Information from Tally is entered into Navision.   BDRCS has Administration and Finance as different departments. Within NHQ, BDRCS has 8 finance officers spread out over different projects.  BDRCS does not have an EOC SOP and during an emergency, one finance officer is assigned to support operations. To support the finance officers 12 BDRCS staff have been trained in general financial procedures but training content does not cover emergency financial support. Exceptions have been created for Population Movement Operation (PMO)/ Myanmar Refugee Response Operation (MRRO) to expedite financial procedures. BDRCS has financial rules and regulations to facilitate transparency issues, which are managed by financial committee. To prevent fraud and corruption, BDRCS has systems and procedures at different levels for control and oversight. These include levels/hierarchy to initiate file for approval. Finance department reviews and pre-and post-audit. Finance team also has an ability to monitor any project site for verification. Relevant finance staff are familiar with agreements made with suppliers and PNS. BDRCS Finance Department is normally involved when other departments make agreements with suppliers and PNS, and the Finance Director is a member of the procurement committee.

component_details.title: Information and Communication Technology (ICT)
component_details.description: Refers to technologies that provide access to information through telecommunications. This includes the Internet, wireless networks, mobile phones, radios and other communication mediums.

component_responses.notes: Key BDRCS staff are equipped with mobile phones and SIM cards and staff receive reimbursement for mobile charges only for emergency response or project purposes. Key BDRCS personnel have contact lists on their personal devices and phone numbers are also available on the BDRCS website. BDRCS sends notifications to various staff and branches via email or group scanned letter.  Currently BDRCS has draft SOP for NDRT and NDWRT for notification. WhatsApp groups are established for response communications with teams and official notification sharing is also done through Facebook. BDRCS has internet capability when operating in the field through hotspots and communicate with response teams through established WhatsApp groups. In an emergency BDRCS HQ uses the CPP network (using VHF/HF) to communicate with branches. It is noted that BDRCS has no communication options for other responses. BDRCS lack several types of equipment and functions expected to be found in a well performing NS e.g. vehicles equipped with radios, satellite phones, portable regularly tested and functioning generators, frequencies for emergency radio transmission.

component_details.title: Resource Mobilisation
component_details.description: A documented strategy for raising domestic funds from the government, private sector, general public and other in-country actors to support the national society’s response. This would include allocation of responsibilities, practical mechanisms for accepting funds and for being accountable on funds.

component_responses.notes: Key BDRCS staff are familiar with Resource Mobilisation (RM) options but its Resource Mobilisation (RM) efforts are limited to PNS and some corporate support. BDRCS has an agreement with Grameen Phone and also receives donations from different banks and use the MOB table to track donations. Support received from PNSs are utilised for certain BDRCS project based and limited disaster preparedness activities. and online platform accepting donations 24/7. An up to date Pre-disaster agreement does not exist.  BDRCS RM strategy, developed in 2005, requires revision and branches do not have RM plans. BDRCS has an established Emergency Fund and accesses this before requesting external support. BDRCS have RM focal point, Director of Fundraising and RM is also part of emergency responses. In-kind donations are accepted on an ad hoc basis as BDRCS does not have a written, formal list of acceptable in-kind donations.

BDRCS Logistics Department staff do not all have clear Job Descriptions, and both BDRCS volunteers working in emergencies, and staff require more training in logistics. Key BDRCS staff are familiar with IFRC logistics services through Movement coordination meetings, and working jointly with IFRC logistics staff. BDRCS has considered elements of an analysis of optimal supply chain options but has not completed/conducted such analysis. BDRCS follows SPHERE standards, that addresses sectoral risks (e.g. pre-position stocks like shelter kits, tarpaulins, blankets, water kit, jerrycans) in at risk communities, and takes into account gender, age and disability. Pre-positioned stock are mostly stored in 2 of the 5 BDRCS warehouses, and strategically located.//BDRCS acknowledges that humanitarian actors are exempted from import duties tax as per Statutory Regulatory Order, issued by the National Board of Revenue. BDRCS applied and was granted import duties tax exemption. Occasionally BDRCS coordinates with key in-country stakeholders regarding their stock and equipment. Branches know the process for requesting relief items from NHQ and have access to their own emergency funds. No written guidelines for accepting or rejecting in-kind donations and BDRS is not fully familiar regarding the respective element in the IFRC Principles and Rules. In practice, BDRCS aims to follow SPHERE and IFRC standards where applicable.  BDRCS is also working on IDRL to further ease the import of goods.  //The number of BDRCS procurement staff is insufficient and require more training. BDRCS standing order covers both emergency and non-emergency procurement procedures, but it needs to be revised to include relevant items of procurement. Government procedures are followed when not covered in BDRCS Standing Order. BDRCs has an annually updated list of suppliers (and can blacklist suppliers if they breach agreement), but there is uncertainty whether they are in full compliance with IFRC Code of Conduct. BDRCS does not have pre- agreements with suppliers for immediate access or service delivery but agreement with Bangladesh Post Office and Bkash exist for electronic money transfer. //BDRCS does not have a fleet manual. BDRCS keeps a logbook of the use of their fleet for maintenance, insurance and registration purposes. Although BDRCS fleet is not sufficient for their response, they contract vehicles out during emergencies. All BDRCS vehicles have First Aid kits, while seatbelts and fire extinguishers are not standard items in all. There is no BDRCS policy on ‘no weapons in vehicles’ however the NS follows this in practise. BDRCS uses registered vehicle workshops for the fleet maintenance. BDRCS does not have procedures for recording and reporting accidents and insurance claims.  Information will be reported to HQ where a file will be initiated and appropriate action taken. In general, fleet and transportation procedures and trainings are limited, and do not for example cover aspects of non-standard driving hours or trainings beyond First Aid. BDRCS drivers are not regularly tested but have correct licence for vehicles driven. BDRCS does not have formal procedures to guide the hours for drivers.//BDRCS does not have a warehouse and stock manual and uses forms and templates found in Standing Order. Staff but not volunteers are trained on procedures and it is noted that there is a need for more trained staff and volunteers. BDRCS has storage space in flood and cyclone prone areas but in previous operations there was a need to rent additional space. If needed BDRCS also has the option of utilising government spaces. BDRCS has 5 warehouses in strategic locations with the majority of stock in 2 locations. The remaining 3 warehouses has limited prepositioned stock and is managed by Unit Branches. It is noted that with severe damage in Dhaka, other branches would not be able to help.

component_details.title: DRM Strategy
component_details.description: An outline of the overall goal that the NS seeks to achieve in its disaster and crisis response operations. The goal considers: context analysis, ongoing/regular all-hazards risk assessments: it may define the target proportion of affected population that will be reached, and a definition of the areas/sectors where a NS will usually respond during an emergency.

component_responses.notes: BDRCS has a DRM Strategy that reflects its mandate and includes analysis of country context, operational objectives and indicators. The DRM Strategy that is available on the NS’s website was last reviewed in 2014 and will need revision in 2019/2020. The Strategy is disseminated and well known by the relevant members of the BDRCS, but the participants felt that there is a need for greater sensitisation of the Strategy at governance level. The Strategy has been published and disseminated to branches and RCY leaders are aware of its goals. The current Strategy has references to technical sectors and support services.

component_details.title: DRM Policy
component_details.description: Reflects the NS mission, RCRC principles and mandate. It acknowledges other relevant NS policies, and aligns with the government policy (where applicable), incorporating the general rules that the NS will obey in order to achieve something (i.e mandate, strategy, etc.)

component_responses.notes: Currently BDRCS does not have a DRM Policy, however it is noted that there are elements in the existing DRM Strategy which are normally found in a DRM Policy. According to some participants, BDRCS intends to develop a DRM policy in 2020, but they acknowledge the DRM Strategy may be sufficient for the time being.

component_details.title: DRM Laws, Advocacy and Dissemination
component_details.description: Designed to support the NS in improving legal preparedness for disasters and crisis and to promote the use of the IDRL Guidelines in order to reduce human vulnerability.

component_responses.notes: With the support of IFRC BDRCS developed an IDRL HD Plan in March 2019. In 2017, supported by external consultation with ONOCHA, relevant areas for improvement in national legislation was identified and advocated for with the government. BDRCS does not have trained staff or current focal points for IDRL and IHL. In practice Disaster Response Director acts as the focal point as he has experience in IDRL and IHL. IDRL issues are not assessed separately when reviewing response operations.

component_details.title: Quality and accountability
component_details.description: Describes the essential elements of principled, accountable, and high-quality humanitarian action. The RCRC Movement provides support to the most vulnerable people in line with the Sphere and CHS standards, Code of Conduct for the RCRC Movement and NGOS in Disaster Relief and the Code for Good Partnership of the RCRC Movement, Gender & Diversity, inclusion and protection, BPI/ Do no harm, context-sensitive analysis, violence prevention, accountability to affected population and disability considerations, Community engagement and accountability (CEA).

component_responses.notes: Community engagement and accountability, including feedback mechanisms, are essential elements that have been incorporated into BDRCS programming throughout. BDRCS is about to finalise its revised draft Complaint Response Mechanism guidelines. CEA focal points exist at NHQ and selected branches. BDRCS uses IFRC CEA toolkit and templates. PMO has dedicated IFRC and BDRCS CEA staff. BDRCS has a child protection policy and is working on a Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) policy to be finalised in 2020. No ‘broader’ protection policy exists to cover other protection services. BDRCS adheres to SPHERE Standards in its assessments, planning and action, and staff and volunteers participate in trainings on SPHERE standards. BDRCS does not have formal plans and procedures to actively minimise harmful economic, social and environmental impacts of assistance, but considers these from the ‘do no harm’ perspective and in practise, examples exist from PMO and longer-term projects/programs. Examples of BDRCS’s implementation of Minimum Standards for Protection, Gender and Inclusion (PGI) in emergencies includes lactating mothers, disabilities, the elderly and separate facilities for men and women in cyclone shelters.

component_details.title: RC auxiliary role, Mandate and Law
component_details.description: A constitutional reference to the role of the NS in responding to disasters and crises, which may be legislated or included/ recognized in the National Response System.

component_responses.notes: The role of the BDRCS as a regulated auxiliary organization of the government with branches spread all over the country and complimenting the governmental efforts during disaster is defined in the President’s Order. A new law adopted by the Parliament would give strong legal base, and the 7FP will be clearly articulated in the law. A new law would offer more details and clarification on roles and responsibilities. The auxiliary role is already defined in the existing 12 mandates. In general, mandates are reflected in strategies, policies and procedures for the services with some exceptions (e.g. ambulance services). Relevant staff are aware of the mandates, while volunteers in general have less awareness and understanding. BDRCS does not work in the promotion of IHL with public authorities and currently does not have an IHL focal point.  With respect to Humanitarian Diplomacy BDRCS has done limited advocacy work with public authorities.

component_details.title: Hazard, Context and Risk Analysis, Monitoring and Early Warning
component_details.description: Describes how the NS monitors and maps past, present and potential hazards, disasters and crises (e.g. hazard, vulnerability assessments, gathering information from communities and government authorities) and systematically evaluates the damage that could be caused by a potential disaster/crisis, the frequency, severity of the impact, and the alert the relevant areas to scale the preparedness actions to reduce population vulnerability.

component_responses.notes: BDRCS has a hazard risk monitoring system for cyclones, floods, cold waves and monsoon, and collects both primary and secondary data. Analysis capacities are limited, and currently supported by partners. BDRCS is aware of the gaps to acceptance, security and access, and specific actions are taken to secure support during cash distributions. BDRCS has established EWEA/FbF mechanism, including developed Early Action Protocols (Cyclone and Flood), for which improvements are needed/on-going. Updated risk analyses from BDRCS and Government (including forecast based information) are shared with high risk and programme/project branches. Communities contribute to risk analyses through community risk assessment processes (VCA/EVCA). Limited analyses regarding issues that divide communities during response are conducted, but it is noted that elements of the BPI (Better Programming Initiative)/Do No Harm approach is considered and part of BDRCS longer term CBDRR/Resilience programmes. In their VCA reports BDRCS disaggregates data by gender, age and disability. For cross-border activities there are no systems in place to share information.

component_details.title: Scenario planning
component_details.description: A set of practical operation plans that closely mirror the generic disaster or crisis response plan but are tailored to a specific hazard type (e.g. earthquake, dengue epidemic, floods, cyclone) and a specific scenario (i.e. number of people affected, their locations and other important factors).

component_responses.notes: BDRCS has contingency plans (CPs) for floods and cyclones but these do not contain triggers for activation. It is noted that BDRCS has triggers as part of the early action protocols for forecast-based action. The scenarios are based on analysis of hazards and vulnerabilities from multi-sector perspective, however, they have not been updated since 2011. A revision is planned for 2020. In general, the focus of the CPs have been on coastal areas as well as project/program areas and scenarios or response plans have not been developed for specific/each high-risk areas of the country. There has not been a focus on cross-border scenario planning and coordination, while some mechanisms for communication have been established with neighbouring national societies.

component_details.title: Risk management
component_details.description: A mapping of the potential risks in every area, along with its related mitigation measures. Including financial, reputational, organizational risks etc.

component_responses.notes: BDRCS has internal audit function that covers financial risks, with some guidance for monitoring.  There are no roles assigned for other organizational risks and they are not monitored or managed systematically. Stakeholder analyses and roundtable meetings are conducted to increase acceptance and to reduce operational risks, but engagement strategies are not developed. BDRCS has systems and procedures to prevent fraud and corruption in place, including Accountability Plan of Action, Code of Conduct and a draft Fraud and Corruption Policy. Reputational and integrity risk management has not been included as a standing item on the agenda of the BDRCS governance board, rather on an ad hoc basis. BDRCS does not have a crisis management unit/function, for critical incidents an ad hoc committee is established.

component_details.title: Preparedness plans and budgets
component_details.description: Plans identifying organisational resources, determining roles and responsibilities, and developing policies, procedures and activities in order to reach a level of preparedness to be able to respond effectively to a disaster or crisis. Budgets ensure that the necessary financial support is secured to allow capacities to be built and readiness maintained.

component_responses.notes: BDRCS has no nominated focal point for disaster preparedness and when needed this function is by default performed by the DRM Director. Currently there is no consolidated mapping of BDRCS organisational gaps as it relates to organisation preparedness work. It is noted that BDRCS going through the PER process, will aid in identifying these gaps. Gaps when identified are done so informally and without any structure and there are limited resources to take remedial action for any gaps identified.  There has been limited focus on structured process for preparedness planning and budgeting, beyond project-based processes. In practice BDRCS aim to allocate budget for preparedness strengthening, from projects but without formal written policy and procedures for this allocation. There is no ‘overarching’ preparedness plan in place, but it is noted that BDRCS revise plans after projects and operations are completed.

component_details.title: Business continuity
component_details.description: A strategy to counter any potential or anticipated obstacles to effective functioning of the NS, with an eye to ensuring that personnel and assets are protected and able to function in the event of a disaster/crisis.

component_responses.notes: The BDRCS do not have a Business Continuity Plan as of today. As part of asset protection, it was noted that BDRCS just recently established a digital platform that is cloud-based, but not functioning yet (need to enter documents/data).

component_details.title: Emergency Response Procedures (SOPs)
component_details.description: Written guidelines that describe duties and rights of personnel, command structures, coordination with other organizations, and reporting requirements, etc. Includes detailed organogram, decision-making flow chart, and defined roles and responsibilities.

component_responses.notes: BDRCS has no up-to-date SOPs for all its specific areas of intervention.  Draft NDRT SOPs and CBI SOPs (2019) exist, that have been partially disseminated and are good examples of SOPs showing procedures, roles and responsibilities (no organogram included though). In addition, the CBI SOPs incorporate all phases of response as well as a decision-making flowchart. As ‘overarching’ Emergency Response SOPs do not exist, there are no examples of procedures for scaling up or down the alert levels or examples of ‘overarching’ Emergency Response SOPs for branches.

component_details.title: Response and recovery planning
component_details.description: A documented set of procedures for the disaster/crisis response and recovery process. Including use of local capacities, transition to recovery, type of activities and serivices provided during response and recovery activities and exit strategies, procedures for DREF & EA, and templates for planning, budgeting and accessing funds.

component_responses.notes: BDRCS does not have a multi-sectoral response plan, although templates (which consider PGI aspects) for specific areas of response to inform response planning exist. Plans adhere to Fundamental Principles and are developed by the BDRCS with inputs from communities, branches, and IFRC. BDRCS is less familiar with Principles and Rules and does not have DRM Policy in place. BDRCS has not advanced with development of Proforma EPOAs yet. In practise recent BDRCS emergency operations plans of action have included focus on secondary risks and revises plans of action based on changing context including when there is a transition from relief to recovery. For transition from relief to recovery phase, BDRCS requires funding support from its partners. BDRCS has a network of network of community-based volunteers who functions as the base for longer term work with communities.  BDRCS’s needs assessments considers work of other actors to avoid duplication and identify gaps. Lessons learned exercises contribute to the response and recovery planning. BDRCS has a donation webpage, however the reach is limited.

component_details.title: Pre-disaster meetings and agreements
component_details.description: A commitment to arrange meetings and agreements with Movement stakeholders and external actors to identify, plan for and address gaps for any upcoming disaster season (e.g. monsoon, floods or cyclones, or for any generic disaster/crisis event (e.g Epidemic, pandemic, confilict situations). Pre-disaster agreements should set out each partner's role in the event of a disaster/crisis.

component_responses.notes: Pre-disaster meetings currently do not take place on an annual basis and the last meeting was in 2016. BDRCS key staff are familiar with pre-disaster agreement of 2012 however the agreement has not been updated since. The CPP is an example of an agreement that BDRCS has with the public authorities and for FBF there are also agreements with UNOCHA, WFP and Strat fund. Currently BDRCS does not map Movement partners capacity and there are no Movement Coordination Agreements. BDRCS are currently working on IDRL and sensitising current ministries. BDRCS currently do not have any agreements with key suppliers but are expecting to have this in place by the end of 2019. For CBI agreements with money transfer providers are formalised and there is an agreed mechanism for activation. Currently BDRCS has no formal agreements with Social Protection systems in place they are however in discussions with Bangladesh Election commission and the social welfare department to get access to data.

BDRCS relies on WFP for food security data and analysis. BDRCS does not have technical staff trained for food assistance, while relevant CBI technical and food distribution capacity exists and forms part of BDRCS responses. Specific food security objectives and indicators are not included in DRM Strategy. BDRCS does not have its own policy and relies on Bangladesh Standard Testing Institute (BSTI), a government institution, to do food testing. BDRCS has an agriculturalist within the DRM team. BDRCS participates irregularly in Food Security cluster. BDRCS does not have a plan or SOPs to scale-up procurement and distribution of food. BDRCS follow Standing Order for procurement (which can enable quicker procurement of resources). During peacetime procedures for procurement is 300,000 Takawith need to go for press-tender (i.e. published). In all emergencies BDRCS can procure for up to 1.5 Million Taka without publishing.

Search and rescue is part of the BDRCS DRM Strategy but Search and rescue is not mentioned in BDRCS contingency plans (CP) for cyclones and floods. It is noted that there is no earthquake CP (where Search and Rescue would normally be used frequently)  Karthick

BDRCS ensures active participation to reflect community needs and from assessment to distribution, communities are involved with mechanisms for communities to provide feedback (i.e. hotline, feed-back boxes). Awareness raising and public education is primarily happening in project-based areas. BDRCS occasionally does national campaigns (e.g. dengue awareness leaflet). Regarding public education, BDRCS goes to schools and colleges to provide training on DRR, First Aid, and Search and Rescue and street dramas are used as a means of awareness building. Early warning early action systems are in place in CPP areas and in project/program areas. In areas where BDRCS is less active, local branch networks notification of potential threats are not fully functional. In project areas BDRCS has Community Disaster Response Teams (CDRT), Unit DRT and National Disaster Response Teams. BDRCS has Contingency Plans (CP) for (e.g. waterlogging, floods, cyclones at community level; earthquake CP in Dhaka) primarily in project areas. BDRCS Community members and the responders need more sensitization of the concept of PGI (e.g. lactating mothers, the elderly and people with disabilities).

component_details.title: Mapping of NS capacities
component_details.description: A list of the NS capacities including HR (staff, response teams and volunteers) and equipment that are available for disaster/crisis response. Teams could include branch and national response teams. This should be defined by technical speciality where relevant.

component_responses.notes: BDRCS has assigned focal points, trained staff and volunteers for different technical/thematic areas (e.g. PGI, WASH, Health, PHAST, PASSA). It is noted that BDRCS does not currently have a Shelter focal point. During disaster responses, BDRCS would assign an individual as the shelter focal point. No database exists for response materials and equipment, some of this information can be found on different excel sheets making it difficult to identify gaps. BDRCS has sufficient Human Resources (HR) for small and medium scale disaster responses, but for large scale disasters there would be a need for more Human Resources including skilled volunteers.   BDRCS has a list of volunteers in excel format, however the capacity is not mapped against the different levels of responses. Mechanisms are in place for requesting and sharing resources between and amongst BDRCS NHQ and branch networks.

BDRCS, in collaboration with Government Health Department has identified multi-sectoral response needs for different epidemics (e.g. anthrax, bird flu, dengue), but does not have scenarios for multi-country outbreaks. BDRCS closely works with the WHO and is a member of the health cluster. Although BDRCS has no proper tool for collecting health data it does collect information from the communities, such as infectious disease outbreaks, primarily through Maternity and Child Health Centres.  On the spot information is provided to communities on potential risks but due to limited staff numbers there is no sufficient mechanism to consolidate and share information about preventative actions.  Only informal procedures for management and response to rumours exist, normally handled through the branches. BDRCS does not have protocols in place for staff and volunteers to deal with infection prevention and epidemic control. BDRCS has a responsibility in dead body management, which consists of provision of body bags and carrying bodies. Not all responders are equipped with PPE when deployed for response. The role of BDRCS in epidemics is not defined in any policy or strategy currently.

component_details.title: Early Action Mechanisms
component_details.description: Designed to translate warnings into anticipatory actions to help reduce the impact of specific disaster or crisis events. They focus on consolidating available forecasting information and putting procedures in place to ensure that a NS can act ahead of any disaster/crisis. Forecast-based financing is included within the scope of this area.

component_responses.notes: BDRCS has long-standing focus on EWEA systems due to the CPP program, which has been strengthened through the inclusion of the FbF approach/mechanism, which also forms part of the Government Standing Order on Disasters (SOD). BDRCS has two Early Action Protocols in place for cyclones and floods, including agreed roles for their activation and implementation. BDRCS is working on formalising agreements with relevant government agencies. BDRCS is also developing a software for automated alert systems. BDRCS has established multiple channels for dissemination of alerts (e.g. Email, SMS, WhatsApp, Facebook Messenger, phone calls). Human Resources (HR) and procedures are in place for sending alerts and starting early actions, however, the system and HR capacities for early action needs to be improved. In CPP areas and project/program areas branches have functioning local networks to inform communities of potential threats, but in areas where BDRCS is less active and there are no programmes/projects, branch networks notifications are not as fully functional.

component_details.title: Cash Based Intervention (CBI)
component_details.description: An effective and flexible way, including all forms of cash and voucher-based assistance, to support people affected by emergencies, maintaining their dignity and choice, while fostering local economies. Cash should also be mainstreamed into other sectors (including Relief, shelter, livelihoods) and services (Logistics, Finance, etc.)

component_responses.notes: To get to five (High performance) more sensitization needed  CTP/CBI preparedness plan forms part of BDRCS Strategic Plan and BDRCS is well resourced for scale-up of CTP/CBI. CTP/CBI is in the annual budget incl. target number of beneficiaries to be reached. BDRCS keeps records of the four levels of CTP/CBI training, which can be converted into a database. BDRCS uses standardised cash analysis, including market analysis, of IFRC CTP/CBI Toolkit.  In addition, BDRCS has adopted and approved CiE tool as part of the CTP/CBI Toolkit. BDRCS is part of national cash working group. RCRC cash working group supports with mapping of other actors and coordination. BDRCS has a Cash SOP, including clear roles and responsibilities adopted in 2019, which needs to be disseminated at branch level. BDRCS has agreements, including activation mechanism, with two service providers (Bangladesh Post Office and Bkash).

component_details.title: Emergency Needs Assessment
component_details.description: Assess the extent and impact of the damage caused by the disaster/crisis and the degree of vulnerability of the affected population. The first step in any emergency response, such an assessment will identify the needs that require external intervention and the gaps to be filled. It is a vital component of the programme-planning process.

component_responses.notes: BDRCS has standardised paper-based and electronic ENA templates used by trained multi-sectoral teams, which inform emergency plans of action. BDRCS systematically disaggregates data according to gender, age, disability, child and female headed. BDRCS ENA includes an analysis of accessibility, availability, quality and use of goods and services, as well as existing capacities and gaps whilst considering other actors present. BDRCS ENA does not analyse secondary risks, specific needs/concerns of vulnerable people/coping mechanisms/early and self-recovery.

component_details.title: Affected population selection
component_details.description: Identification and selection of target Affected population for interventions, using a pre-defined set of criteria based on need and vulnerability. This includes consideration of specific vulnerabilities such as disability, age and gender.

component_details.title: Emergency Operations Centre (EOC)
component_details.description: A central command and control facility responsible for carrying out disaster/crisis management functions at a strategic level in an emergency situation. The common functions are to collect and analyze data; facilitate decision making that protects life and livelihoods; and disseminate those decisions to all concerned agencies and individuals. Generally located at the headquarter level of an organization.

component_responses.notes: BDRCS has a Response Coordination Centre and not a formal EOC from where it responds to disasters. This room has insufficient space and is in need of modernisation and plans exist to construct a new HQ facility with functional EOC. BDRCS Response Coordination Centre, when activated displays information, including daily sitreps during responses and these are regularly updated and decisions are made based on information collected from the field. When activated, the BDRCS Response Coordination Centre is operational 24/7 and shifts are kept to an 8-hour rotation. BDRCS’s Disaster Response Director is formally appointed as Response Coordination room focal point. Based on the NS’s strong experience in responding to frequent disasters ad hoc procedures exists for the activation of the Response Coordination Centre but this is not defined in a formal EOC SOP.  Clarity on the authority levels between strategic and managerial exists for specific events (e.g. flood and cyclone) as reflected in the contingency plan but the practice is to form a team defining roles and responsibilities on an ad hoc basis.  The BDRCS Response Coordination Centre has water, generators and back-up communications. BDRCS has a legal access to radio frequency as part of the CPP joint program with government (both VHF and High Frequency), but noted this is limited to only cyclone prone areas, but it was noted that it should be able to use it  in other areas when needed. There is no alternative location if the Response Coordination Centre is not accessible. BDRCS has an electronic directory of staff contact details and each department has access to a hardcopy.

component_details.title: Information Management (IM)
component_details.description: Ability to manage information including requesting, receiving, analyzing and disseminating as per its procedures and partner requirements (IFRC and public authorities in particular). There should be a clear digital/paper trail that documents what, when and how the NS has acted and provides key information for the development of Emergency Plan of Actions. Includes IM between levels, between departments and Situational Reports, mapping, visualisation of data, GO platform (IFRC).

component_responses.notes: BDRCS has developed some systems for mobile data collection (e.g. beneficiary selection, emergency needs assessment) with staff familiar with templates. Awareness and use of data collection system is more developed in branches which benefit from partner projects/support and which are frequently exposed to disasters. The cloud based digital platform is in its initial phase and not yet functional. BDRCS has no dedicated person responsible for Information Management but the recruitment of individuals skilled in this field is planned. NS have basic equipment and capacity to compile, visualise and share information at HQ level but need more equipment (e.g. mobile data collection). Branches have ability to visualise and share information shared by HQ (e.g. through printing). Currently BDRCS has access to updated data on high risk areas through government sources, this includes Information for beneficiary selection (at household-level). All BDRCS decisions are documented through various methods (e.g. meeting minutes, situation reports, “approval note for file”) and all information is preserved by the responsible departments. as a hardcopy. For auditing purposes, files are preserved for a minimum 5 years. BDRCS has standardised sitreps that include information on the situation, the NS and other actors response, challenges, achievements and gaps. BDRCS response plans are adjusted based on sitreps information. BDRCS shares information through the department directors and relevant staff but it is noted that information is not disseminated down to all staff.

component_details.title: Testing and Learning
component_details.description: Drills and Simulations allow the organization to test, identify and learn from the results of these type of exercises and incorporate learning into future preparedness and response planning.

component_responses.notes: BDRCS, including branches, use simulation and drills regularly to test its early action and response plans for cyclones, floods and earthquakes. BDRCS Branches take part in drills twice a year. Lessons learned are regularly collected through simulation/drill debriefing sessions including in project plans. Safer access issues have not been systematically tested through the simulation/drills. There is needed for future trainings/awareness of Safer Access Framework with accompanying simulation exercises. Cross-border simulations do not take place. BDRCS participates in simulations/drills with national authorities (e.g. Fire Services, Civil Defence, Armed Forces Division and Ministry of Disaster Management)

component_details.title: Activation of regional and international support
component_details.description: Procedures for requesting and accepting regional and international support in operations, including triggering coordination mechanisms for funding, materials and human resources deployments.

component_responses.notes: BDRCS is familiar with support available from/through IFRC, procedures and contacts for coordination and for requesting regional and international support, however, BDRCS does not have formal, written procedures/SOP for regulating/guiding a coordinated response. As well as informing IFRC of assistance requests, BDRCS is regularly taking a lead role in drafting Emergency Plans of Action with IFRC. BDRCS uses partnership and project agreements to receive bilateral assistance from partners for smaller/medium scale disasters, while in large scale operations one window approach is followed. BDRCS Director for Disaster Response acts at the default focal point for regional/international responders.

component_details.title: CHEMICAL, BIOLOGICAL, RADIOLOGICAL AND NUCLEAR (CBRN) EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS

component_responses.notes: BDRCS has a focal person assigned for CBRN. There are no SOPs, action plans or defined roles and responsibilities for CBRN.

Livelihood is incorporated into the BDRCS DRM Strategy and is also part of the Strategy 2017-2020. BDRCS does not have livelihoods (or food security) focal point, programming support is provided by IFRC and partners. BDRCS does not have a Livelihood/Food Security focal point but for CBI there are technical human resources with ability to support market analysis. Mapping of main livelihood zones and market systems are mainly supported by project/programs at a microlevel.  Livelihood is incorporated into BDRCS Emergency Needs Assessment and volunteers have been trained in livelihood topics, including related data collection. BCRCS conducts Livelihood Trainings of Trainers. A standard livelihood assessment forms part of multisectoral assessment before any recovery support.

When working with communities around shelter solutions, BDRCS follows the Participatory Approach for Safe Shelter Awareness (PASSA) process, including PASSA trainings for volunteers. In consultation with communities and in collaboration with authorities, BDRCS has developed standard shelter and specific toilet designs.  BDRCS pre-positions shelter kits, tarpaulins and family tents in two main warehouses (one located in high risk area). BDRCS has IFRC guidelines in place for the management of disaster preparedness stock and jointly manages the stock with IFRC. BDRCS has no identified suppliers of shelter items or pre-disaster/framework agreements in place for shelter items.

component_details.title: MANAGEMENT OF DEAD BODIES TO FACILITATE THEIR IDENTIFICATION

component_responses.notes: Relevant BDRCS staff and a specific group of volunteers have been trained in RFL and in coordination with ICRC, provide RFL services based on a Partnership Framework Agreement (PFA).

BDRCS’s mandate for recovery is clearly defined in the Presidents Standard Order on Disaster. BDRCS’s key staff and teams are familiar with detailed multi-sectoral recovery assessments, which consider cross-cutting issues and there are trained multi sectoral teams (WASH Shelter, livelihoods, Health, Relief, Cash, PGI, PSS, Logistics, CEA, CBI, etc.). The transition from relief to recovery is part of the BDRCS’s emergency appeal. BDRCS manages the transition from relief to recovery but it is noted that there is often a need for support and funding from partner national societies. BDRCS coordinates with government authorities regarding available resources and occasionally a joint needs assessment is done to establish capacities and gaps. BDRCS is part of humanitarian coordination task team (HCTT), which meets regularly during disasters. Meetings with public authorities take place at Union and District level but on a needs basis. BDRCS has long-standing agreements with UNHCR which specifically covers MRRO (Myanmar Refugee Relief Operation).

component_details.title: NS-specific areas of intervention
component_details.description: Sector-specific or services provided by the NS in case of emergencies, it is in line with the NS mandate and legislation in country. It includes Community Based DP/DRR, Evacuation, Health in Emergencies, Epidemic and Pandemic, First aid, WASH, Food security and Livelihoods, Search and rRescue, Shelter, Management of dead bodies, RFL, Transition to recovery, and CBRN preparedness.

component_responses.notes: Evacuation is part of BDRCS’ DRM Strategy. As per the government SOD, BDRCS is part of the national mechanism for evacuation for all disasters. BDRCS has specific capacity in flood and cyclone evacuation.

First Aid is part of BDRCS mandate and DRM strategy, and there are first aiders in all branches. First aid is identified in different scenarios e.eg. floods, cyclones and landslides. BDRCS does not have a CDBRR strategy, but in practice all staff and volunteers in the community are first aid trained. The BDRCS Youth Policy identifies skills for providing first aid as a priority area for capacity building of the different groups of the Red Crescent Youth (RCY). Not all responders are equipped with PPE and First Aid material when deployed for response.

BDRCS responses to WASH related needs, included in BDRCS response plans, are supported by the Disaster Response Department. BDRCS has appropriate equipment for water testing and purification (i.e. no need to obtain this equipment from elsewhere). BDRCS has WASH trained NDWRT, an engineer and movement partners with WASH expertise (IFRC, German RC, Swiss RC and Swedish RC), and access to training through the department of public health and engineering. BDRCS coordinates with NGO fora and Government, and forms part of WASH cluster.

BDRCS Projects using CBHFA approach support First Aid trainings and limited refreshers are provided. CBHFA Refreshers should be done every three years but due to funding and planning this is not happening. Volunteer training includes how to report suspected health events. When simulations occur at community level, volunteers may participate, but do not necessarily lead the process from simulation, planning, implementation and evaluation of the exercise. Volunteers provide post exercise feedback as part an evaluation debrief.

component_details.title: Coordination with External Agencies and NGOs
component_details.description: Mechanism that facilitates coordination and collaboration with Non-Governmental Organization (NGO), both local and international NGOs, civil society organizations (CSOs) and United Nations agencies in country.

component_responses.notes: BDRCS has established coordination with external agencies and NGOs. The NS is a member of the Humanitarian Coordination Task Team (HCTT) and during disasters, HCTT meets regularly. BDRCS has long-standing agreements with UNHCR which specifically covers Myanmar Refugee Relief Operation (MRRO) and the NS is represented in different clusters (e.g. WASH, Health, Shelter). BDRCS is aware of the IFRC role as co-chair of the shelter cluster. AT senior level there is a general awareness of UN-led appeal and strategic processes and the NS receives reports from UNOCHA.

component_details.title: Civil Military Relations
component_details.description: Dialogue and interaction with military actors, essential to protect and promote humanitarian principles, avoid competition, minimize inconsistency and, when appropriate, pursue common goals.

component_responses.notes: BDRCS engages in the dissemination of IHL, promotion of FPs and appropriate use of RC emblem to military actors, participates regularly in exercises organized by them and works independently from the military bodies. NS is not familiar with the Movement guidance on military bodies. BDRCS considers potential impact on security of affected population when coordinating with military forces and usually does not use military assets and services, while there are some exceptions.

component_details.title: Coordination with Movement
component_details.description: Mechanisms that facilitate the coordination with ICRC, IFRC, and PNS in-country.

component_responses.notes: BDRCS has limited awareness of the SMCC toolkit but follow some of the SMCC elements. BDRCS does not systematically seek to capture partners resources that could be utilised in times of a disaster or organise regular, formal systematic pre disaster meetings. It is noted that BDRCS has a Pre-Disaster Meeting MoU dated 2012. BDRCS has partnership agreement with IFRC, PFA Partnership Framework Agreement with ICRC and cooperation agreements with PNS. BDRCS has no movement security agreements or Movement Cooperation Agreement (MCA) as per MCA template. Information is shared during Movement Coordination meetings organised on an ad hoc basis and more frequently during operations. BDRCS has no system in place to share information with neighbouring countries. When BDRCS accepts support from partners they have agreements with, a report is provided. With non-BDRCS partners (e.g. Chinese government, Qatar RC), support is documented and NS is able to report, in some cases, the partners provide the financial and reporting template.

component_details.title: Coordination with authorities
component_details.description: Mechanism that facilitates coordination and cooperation with local and national authorities. It is connected to the NS auxiliary role for humanitarian assistance.

component_responses.notes: BDRCS is identified in the government’s Standing Order on Disaster (SOD) and a member of the Disaster Management Committees at different levels of the government. BDRCS has meetings, on a needs basis, with public authorities at Union and District level where the government informs BDRCS on resources at both levels. BDRCS distributes relief items independently using their own emblem and has control over assets, resources and emblem. For the joint CPP government and BDRCS program respective emblems are used. BDRCS has established coordination with public authorities at local and national level on specific services (e.g. Joint Needs Assessment Coordination Team and Humanitarian Coordination Task Team (HCTT). When deploying a health team, BDCRS coordinate with the local civil surgeon, to ascertain where support is needed.

component_details.title: Coordination with local community level responders
component_details.description: Engagement with Community Disaster Response Teams (CDRTs), through training, coordination, and the development of community disaster preparedness and response plans.

component_responses.notes: Community engagement and coordination with community response teams follows established top-down and bottom-up information sharing practises and feedback/complaint mechanisms, which support two-way communication with community responders and members and related decision-making. BDRCS has an established Hotline manned by trained volunteers at NHQ as a feedback/complaints mechanism. BDRCS branches have systems for coordination with community responders. Communication with CDRT is done in writing by Unit Level Officers (ULO), community volunteers, organisers and facilitators. The NS supports community response systems in coastal areas through its CCP systems and with CCP volunteers. In project areas unit/ward/community disaster response teams support community response systems.

component_details.title: Cooperation with private sector
component_details.description: Mechanism that allows cooperation with private sector that often plays a strong role in response, particularly if there is impact on their staff and businesses. There is often a willingness to donate goods and services. Advance agreements help to expedite response actions.

component_responses.notes: At the moment BDRCS has no mechanism for ensuring due diligence when selecting private sector partners but potential partners are assessed. BDRCS’ Child Protection Policy forbids the use of child labour and this is strictly assessed when choosing any private sector partner. BDRCS ensures appropriate use of emblem with partners/partner collaborations and when distributing relief items BDRCS logo must be used. BDRCS does not yet use volunteers from corporate partners.

component_details.title: DRM Strategy
component_details.description: An outline of the overall goal that the NS seeks to achieve in its disaster and crisis response operations. The goal considers: context analysis, ongoing/regular all-hazards risk assessments: it may define the target proportion of affected population that will be reached, and a definition of the areas/sectors where a NS will usually respond during an emergency.

component_responses.notes: requires context-specific update

component_details.title: DRM Policy
component_details.description: Reflects the NS mission, RCRC principles and mandate. It acknowledges other relevant NS policies, and aligns with the government policy (where applicable), incorporating the general rules that the NS will obey in order to achieve something (i.e mandate, strategy, etc.)

component_details.title: DRM Laws, Advocacy and Dissemination
component_details.description: Designed to support the NS in improving legal preparedness for disasters and crisis and to promote the use of the IDRL Guidelines in order to reduce human vulnerability.

component_details.title: Quality and accountability
component_details.description: Describes the essential elements of principled, accountable, and high-quality humanitarian action. The RCRC Movement provides support to the most vulnerable people in line with the Sphere and CHS standards, Code of Conduct for the RCRC Movement and NGOS in Disaster Relief and the Code for Good Partnership of the RCRC Movement, Gender & Diversity, inclusion and protection, BPI/ Do no harm, context-sensitive analysis, violence prevention, accountability to affected population and disability considerations, Community engagement and accountability (CEA).

component_details.title: RC auxiliary role, Mandate and Law
component_details.description: A constitutional reference to the role of the NS in responding to disasters and crises, which may be legislated or included/ recognized in the National Response System.

component_details.title: Hazard, Context and Risk Analysis, Monitoring and Early Warning
component_details.description: Describes how the NS monitors and maps past, present and potential hazards, disasters and crises (e.g. hazard, vulnerability assessments, gathering information from communities and government authorities) and systematically evaluates the damage that could be caused by a potential disaster/crisis, the frequency, severity of the impact, and the alert the relevant areas to scale the preparedness actions to reduce population vulnerability.

component_details.title: Scenario planning
component_details.description: A set of practical operation plans that closely mirror the generic disaster or crisis response plan but are tailored to a specific hazard type (e.g. earthquake, dengue epidemic, floods, cyclone) and a specific scenario (i.e. number of people affected, their locations and other important factors).

component_details.title: Risk management
component_details.description: A mapping of the potential risks in every area, along with its related mitigation measures. Including financial, reputational, organizational risks etc.

component_details.title: Preparedness plans and budgets
component_details.description: Plans identifying organisational resources, determining roles and responsibilities, and developing policies, procedures and activities in order to reach a level of preparedness to be able to respond effectively to a disaster or crisis. Budgets ensure that the necessary financial support is secured to allow capacities to be built and readiness maintained.

component_details.title: Business continuity
component_details.description: A strategy to counter any potential or anticipated obstacles to effective functioning of the NS, with an eye to ensuring that personnel and assets are protected and able to function in the event of a disaster/crisis.

component_details.title: Emergency Response Procedures (SOPs)
component_details.description: Written guidelines that describe duties and rights of personnel, command structures, coordination with other organizations, and reporting requirements, etc. Includes detailed organogram, decision-making flow chart, and defined roles and responsibilities.

component_responses.notes: All staff and volunteers follow the SOPs.

component_details.title: Response and recovery planning
component_details.description: A documented set of procedures for the disaster/crisis response and recovery process. Including use of local capacities, transition to recovery, type of activities and serivices provided during response and recovery activities and exit strategies, procedures for DREF & EA, and templates for planning, budgeting and accessing funds.

component_details.title: Pre-disaster meetings and agreements
component_details.description: A commitment to arrange meetings and agreements with Movement stakeholders and external actors to identify, plan for and address gaps for any upcoming disaster season (e.g. monsoon, floods or cyclones, or for any generic disaster/crisis event (e.g Epidemic, pandemic, confilict situations). Pre-disaster agreements should set out each partner's role in the event of a disaster/crisis.

component_details.title: MANAGEMENT OF DEAD BODIES TO FACILITATE THEIR IDENTIFICATION

component_responses.notes: NS staff and volunteers are  not trained in response interventions for rehabilitation of productive assets (small infrastructures, clearance etc.).

component_details.title: CHEMICAL, BIOLOGICAL, RADIOLOGICAL AND NUCLEAR (CBRN) EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS

component_details.description: Ability to manage information including requesting, receiving, analyzing and disseminating as per its procedures and partner requirements (IFRC and public authorities in particular). There should be a clear digital/paper trail that documents what, when and how the NS has acted and provides key information for the development of Emergency Plan of Actions. Includes IM between levels, between departments and Situational Reports, mapping, visualisation of data, GO platform (IFRC).

component_details.description: Drills and Simulations allow the organization to test, identify and learn from the results of these type of exercises and incorporate learning into future preparedness and response planning.

component_details.description: Procedures for requesting and accepting regional and international support in operations, including triggering coordination mechanisms for funding, materials and human resources deployments.

component_details.title: Coordination with Movement
component_details.description: Mechanisms that facilitate the coordination with ICRC, IFRC, and PNS in-country.

component_details.title: Coordination with authorities
component_details.description: Mechanism that facilitates coordination and cooperation with local and national authorities. It is connected to the NS auxiliary role for humanitarian assistance.

component_details.title: Coordination with External Agencies and NGOs
component_details.description: Mechanism that facilitates coordination and collaboration with Non-Governmental Organization (NGO), both local and international NGOs, civil society organizations (CSOs) and United Nations agencies in country.

component_details.title: Civil Military Relations
component_details.description: Dialogue and interaction with military actors, essential to protect and promote humanitarian principles, avoid competition, minimize inconsistency and, when appropriate, pursue common goals.

component_details.title: Coordination with local community level responders
component_details.description: Engagement with Community Disaster Response Teams (CDRTs), through training, coordination, and the development of community disaster preparedness and response plans.

component_details.title: Cooperation with private sector
component_details.description: Mechanism that allows cooperation with private sector that often plays a strong role in response, particularly if there is impact on their staff and businesses. There is often a willingness to donate goods and services. Advance agreements help to expedite response actions.

component_details.title: Staff and volunteer management
component_details.description: Well-functioning staff and volunteer management systems and practices allow for effective recruitment, supervision, support and encouragement of staff and volunteers.

component_details.title: Communication in emergencies
component_details.description: Incorporates a system of public messaging to enable the NS to share timely, accurate information before, during, and after a disaster or crisis.

component_responses.notes: The NS has a good communications structure but need to enhance Communications in Emergencies (CiE) and recognize the importance and potential risks if CiE protocols are not standardized. This includes identifying and training key spokespersons for the NS as well as ensuring staff and volunteers take care in communicating, even as individuals, in social media.

component_details.title: Resource Mobilisation
component_details.description: A documented strategy for raising domestic funds from the government, private sector, general public and other in-country actors to support the national society’s response. This would include allocation of responsibilities, practical mechanisms for accepting funds and for being accountable on funds.

component_details.title: Safety and security management
component_details.description: Addresses policy and procedures to ensure the safety of staff and volunteers. This include awareness, effective recruitment, training and management processes in place to ensure that personnel are capable of undertaking the roles demanded of them (from NS operational, management and leaders) according to the Stay Safe (IFRC) and Safer Access (ICRC). Based on safer access framework, including concepts of access, perception, identification and acceptance, and protection and violence prevention.

component_details.title: Operations Monitoring, Evaluation, Reporting and Learning
component_details.description: The PMERL is designed to implement a results-based planning, monitoring and evaluation system that provides an evidence base of NS performance, including relevance, efficiency, effectiveness, sustainability and impact. A reliable and trusted organization is accountable, providing transparent and timely information and building systems to strengthen data collection and reporting. It is data-driven, analytical and results-based.

component_details.title: Finance and Admin policy and emergency procedures
component_details.description: Overall budgeting, accounting, treasury, assets, financial reporting and financial services operations. it also includes the efficient delivery , cost effective and timely services to the NS. Pre-approved, auditable, expedited procedures that allow for flexibility during a disaster/crisis. These must meet transparency, oversight and accountability standards. Procedures may include faster approval processes, fewer signatures, different authority levels. The Emergency Procedures are activated for a specific period of time.

component_details.title: Information and Communication Technology (ICT)
component_details.description: Refers to technologies that provide access to information through telecommunications. This includes the Internet, wireless networks, mobile phones, radios and other communication mediums.

component_responses.notes: NS has not SOPs for accepting (or rejecting), storing, disposing and reporting on in-kind medical donations.

component_details.title: RC auxiliary role, Mandate and Law
component_details.description: A constitutional reference to the role of the NS in responding to disasters and crises, which may be legislated or included/ recognized in the National Response System.

component_responses.notes:
Mandat définit dans un statut et adopté par décret. Le nouveau statut doit être transmis au ministère de l’intérieur. 
Le rôle d’auxiliaire de l’état du CRM était relativement connu par les anciennes générations (sécheresse 1970) dans les structures étatiques au niveau central et régional. A présent, les nouvelles générations connaissent moins.
En pratique, les comités sont demandés parfois à faire des choses qui ne relèvent pas du Mandat du CRM ni des principes fondamentaux du Mouvement. 
Le rôle du CRM n’est pas compris par tous les volontaires, qui pour beaucoup, ne sont pas impliqués activement ou ne sentent pas d’appartenance.
La promotion du DIH n’est pas régulière. Se fait dans le cadre des évènements. 

Implications: il n’y a pas de coordination claire et systématique entre comités et autorités locales. Les preneurs de décision à chaque niveau ne comprennent pas le rôle complémentaire du CRM. Les comités sont parfois empêchés de travailler, ou demandés à faire des choses qui ne s’alignent pas aux principes du Mvt et donc mettent à risque la réputation de la SN et les volontaires.

component_details.title: DRM Strategy
component_details.description: An outline of the overall goal that the NS seeks to achieve in its disaster and crisis response operations. The goal considers: context analysis, ongoing/regular all-hazards risk assessments: it may define the target proportion of affected population that will be reached, and a definition of the areas/sectors where a NS will usually respond during an emergency.

component_responses.notes:
Le CRM n’a pas une stratégie de GRC mais le plan stratégique tente de couvrir la partie préparation et réponse. 
Les plans stratégiques ne comprennent cependant pas les indicateurs précis qui peut guider les actions de la SN (et le support des partenaires) en réponse.
La présence d’une stratégie marquerait l’engagement clair des secteurs et services techniques. Elle serait la ligne directrice de tous les plans d’intervention (national – local).
vent guider les actions pratiques de la SN (et du support des partenaires).

Implications: le fait que les objectifs opérationnels n’existent pas et ne couvrent pas la proportion de la population à secourir, la SN ne peut pas avoir de plan de réponse clair ni un plan de préparation qui couvrirait le pré-positionnement ou autres activités, ni même bénéficier d’une action précoce.

component_details.title: DRM Policy
component_details.description: Reflects the NS mission, RCRC principles and mandate. It acknowledges other relevant NS policies, and aligns with the government policy (where applicable), incorporating the general rules that the NS will obey in order to achieve something (i.e mandate, strategy, etc.)

component_responses.notes:
La SN n’a pas de politique de GRC. Elle pourrait utiliser le format créé dernièrement par la FICR, ou adopter le politique de GRC de la FICR.
Bien qu’il n’existe pas de politique GRC, la collaboration entre les départements GRC et santé/wash se fait au niveau central.
Les branches ne sont pas au courant des politiques principales à suivre pour la prise de décision.
Une politique adaptée serait une ligne directrice des plans de réponse.

Implications: le manque de politique pourrait résulter en une incohérence dans les différentes activités du CRM. Une politique adoptée et bien reconnue sert de guider la prise de décision quelque soit le niveau, sans perdre le temps à attendre des consignes centralisées.

component_details.title: DRM Laws, Advocacy and Dissemination
component_details.description: Designed to support the NS in improving legal preparedness for disasters and crisis and to promote the use of the IDRL Guidelines in order to reduce human vulnerability.

component_responses.notes:
La SN ne fait pas un travail particulièrement axé sur le DIH et le IDRL.
En terme de facilitation de l’entrée des secours dans le pays, lorsqu’ils sont au nom du CRM, ils sont exonérés des taxes de la douane mais pas des autres impôts (TVA et une autre taxe), ce qui pose problème à quelques partenaires.
Il serait bénéfique de recevoir la liste de vérification de la FICR et de choisir les points importants à prioriser pour le contexte, en ayant comme objectif de faciliter les opérations.
Une fois le travail sur le DIH et le IDRL enclenché, la SN gagnerait à avoir un point focal par comité pour guider les actions et identifier les besoins. 

Implications: le manque de travail sur le DIH ne met pas la SN dans une position forte de plaidoyer, au cas où un incident survient au cours d’une réponse.

component_details.title: Quality and accountability
component_details.description: Describes the essential elements of principled, accountable, and high-quality humanitarian action. The RCRC Movement provides support to the most vulnerable people in line with the Sphere and CHS standards, Code of Conduct for the RCRC Movement and NGOS in Disaster Relief and the Code for Good Partnership of the RCRC Movement, Gender & Diversity, inclusion and protection, BPI/ Do no harm, context-sensitive analysis, violence prevention, accountability to affected population and disability considerations, Community engagement and accountability (CEA).

component_responses.notes:
La population affectée n’est pas impliquée dans toutes les étapes de l'intervention. Une enquête détaillée pourrait avoir lieu après avoir reçu les listes des autorités, pour une idée plus détaillée sur les besoins. 
Des volontaires sont formés sur l’Engagement Communautaire et la Redevabilité (CEA )mais les comités n'en sont pas au courant. Ils ne gardent pas de record des formations et des formés (le siège non plus).
Pas de mécanisme sûrs pour les réclamations (quelques projets le font), mais ceci n’en réduit pas le besoin: des réclamations se font à présent chez le Hakem ou aux volontaires du CRM, sans pour autant avoir un cadre où l’information est enregistrée et bien gérée (explications, action, etc.).
Une formation sur la protection, le genre et l’inclusion a été faite (2021 sans résultats, et 2023) mais pas de politique adoptée. 
Les branches ne sont pas au courant de normes spécifiques que la SN suit, ni ne prêtent une attention spéciale aux violences liées au genre et aux besoins des personnes handicapées. 
Il n’existe pas une analyse qui assure le « Do no harm » à travers les plans et procédures.
Les bénéficiaires sont choisis par les autorités. Mais à travers les programmes, la SN priorise l’inclusion.

Implications: l’aide risque de ne pas répondre aux besoins, ce qui pourrait pousser les personnes à vendre les aides; des personnes pourraient trouver le choix des bénéficiaires injuste (résidents/migrants); les possibles comportements non-acceptables des volontaires pourraient ne pas être détectés.

component_details.title: Hazard, Context and Risk Analysis, Monitoring and Early Warning
component_details.description: Describes how the NS monitors and maps past, present and potential hazards, disasters and crises (e.g. hazard, vulnerability assessments, gathering information from communities and government authorities) and systematically evaluates the damage that could be caused by a potential disaster/crisis, the frequency, severity of the impact, and the alert the relevant areas to scale the preparedness actions to reduce population vulnerability.

component_responses.notes:
Le siège détient d’une carte contenant les zones à risques. Les branches n’en détiennent pas et donc les volontaires et communautés ne les mettent pas à jour. 
Il n’y a pas de système de surveillance local ni d’alerte précoce.
Pour les systèmes de surveillance, le siège reçoit des informations de la part de ARCO sous demande. Au niveau national, l'Office Nationale Météorologique (ONM) envoie des informations à la SN en cas d'évènement important. Dans la région de La Saba (5 départements), c'est le CRM qui fait la surveillance pour la sécurité alimentaire. Il existe 28 méchanismes de surveillance communautaire et une analyse trimestrielle se fait, de laquelle un bulletin détaillé est dégagé. 
La SN a la capacité de collecter et d'analyser les données reliées à la sécurité alimantaire.
Les risques en termes d’acceptation et de sécurité d’accès ne sont pas analysés. Il y a eu même un groupe de volontaires qui s’est fait attaqué car ils ont été considérés comme rattachés au Gouvernement.
Les listes des autorités sont ventilées par sexe et âge mais pas par handicap et n’incluent pas les conséquences potentielles de la protection.
Le CRM n’a pas de façon officielle de partager avec les regions transfrontalières les informations sur la capacité et les besoins. 2 presidents le font parfois à titre personnel.
Il n’y a pas de système spécifique pour la surveillance des risques épidémiques. 

Implications: Le manque d’analyse et le manque d’inclusion des communautés et des volontaires locaux dans l’évaluation de la vulnérabilité et des capacités (EVC) fait que la réponse ne commence que longtemps après le début de la catastrophe.

component_details.title: Scenario planning
component_details.description: A set of practical operation plans that closely mirror the generic disaster or crisis response plan but are tailored to a specific hazard type (e.g. earthquake, dengue epidemic, floods, cyclone) and a specific scenario (i.e. number of people affected, their locations and other important factors).

component_responses.notes:
Des scénarios de réponse existent au siège pour les inondations et les élections sous des plans de contingence, mais ne sont pas mis à jour et les gens comités ne les connaissent pas. 
Le manque de scénario fait qu’il y a un manque de limite sur ce que les volontaires peuvent faire. Faisant partie de la communauté, ils mettent leur gilet et foncent à l’aide. Mais ceci serait un risque pour l’image du CRM and pourrait créer des conflits avec les autorités qui s’attendent à ce que le CRM informe de toute activité.
Même le siège considère le scénario comme non mis à jour et ne l’utilise pas comme référence. 


Implications: quand une catastrophe survient, les comités ne peuvent pas commencer immédiatement à agir, ils doivent attendre les indications du siège. Mais aussi, vu que les volontaires sont dans la communauté, ils mettent le gilet et agissent sans plan précis. Ceci a un risque sur l’image et l’unité du CRM.

component_details.title: Risk management
component_details.description: A mapping of the potential risks in every area, along with its related mitigation measures. Including financial, reputational, organizational risks etc.

component_responses.notes:
Pas de façon systématique d’identifier, d’évaluer et d’atténuer les risques éventuels pesant sur les opérations ou la réputation, sauf pour la presse. La responsabilité repose chez le SG.
Pas d’analyse de l’acceptation selon les zones, ni stratégie d’implication des personnes. 
Incident: équipe de volontaires qui se sont fait attaqué par des pierres. La cause n’a pas servi de leçon apprise aux autres opérations futures. 
Les programmes et les donations d’urgence de la CRF se font avec des procédures qui évitent les risques de fraude et corruption. Mais pas de systèmes et procédures propre à la SN, pour fraude et corruption, mais aussi pour renforcer l’acceptation, la sécurité et l’accès.
Les listes des autorités sont un problème majeur car elles ne reposent pas sur les besoins.
Pas d’unité/fonction pour gérer crises et incidents mais aussi pas de réunions de conseil de direction pour que la gestion des risques soit un point systématique de l’ordre du jour. 


Implications: Le siège ou les partenaires gèrent tous les stocks. La niveau central ne gère que des fonds bien définis et limités aux programmes, les comités n’en gèrent presque pas. Pour obtenir un pré-positionnement de stock qui faciliterait une réponse rapide, il est nécessaire d’avoir un système de gestion des risques.

component_details.title: Preparedness plans and budgets
component_details.description: Plans identifying organisational resources, determining roles and responsibilities, and developing policies, procedures and activities in order to reach a level of preparedness to be able to respond effectively to a disaster or crisis. Budgets ensure that the necessary financial support is secured to allow capacities to be built and readiness maintained.

component_responses.notes:
Il y a un point focal préparation au siège. 
Les comités n’ont pas une identification claire des lacunes de préparation qui se base sur l’analyse des risques et la stratégie d’intervention. Par conséquent, il n’existe pas de mesures correctives. Quoique, ceci a été fait en 2021 pour les inondations à Nouakchott et le plan de préparation a été mis en oeuvre.
Les déficits de financement pour la préparation et les actions précoces ne sont pas identifiés.
Il n'existe pas de politiques et procédures pour allouer des budgets d’urgence ou de développement pour le renforcement des capacités de préparation.

Implications: la SN se trouve dans l’incapacité de se préparer pour une réponse. Les comités doivent attendre l’impact, les instructions et les fonds pour agir. Par conséquent, l’action précoce est impossible, ainsi que la réduction de l’impact le cas échéant.

component_details.title: Business continuity
component_details.description: A strategy to counter any potential or anticipated obstacles to effective functioning of the NS, with an eye to ensuring that personnel and assets are protected and able to function in the event of a disaster/crisis.

component_responses.notes:
La SN ne dispose pas d’un plan de continuité des activités connu par tous, pour en cas de crise majeure qui pourrait empêcher les personnes d’arriver au siège ou au comité, ou même de communiquer lorsque les lignes sont coupées. 
Il n’existe pas de procédure actualisée et approuvée pour communiquer avec les donateurs afin de réaffecter les fonds à des besoins urgents inattendus ou émergents.

Implications: en cas de risque majeur inattendu, la SN se trouverait dans l’impossibilité d’agir.

component_details.title: Emergency Response Procedures (SOPs)
component_details.description: Written guidelines that describe duties and rights of personnel, command structures, coordination with other organizations, and reporting requirements, etc. Includes detailed organogram, decision-making flow chart, and defined roles and responsibilities.

component_responses.notes:
Il n’existe pas de procédures d’intervention d’urgence qui guident les comités à faire face aux catastrophes. 2 SOPs existent pour la sécurité alimentaire et le CASH. Ils elles sont connues par le personnel du siège mais pas par les comités. 
La SN n'a pas de document pratique qui explique le rôle de chacun aux niveaux stratégiques, opérationnels et de management au siège, dans les branches et les communautés.
La SN gagnerait à avoir un organigramme de réponse d’urgence comprenant les coordonnées des personnes clés. 

Implications: l’existence de procédure, tout comme les plans, permettrait à chaque personne d’agir en temps opportun. Leur absence ne fait qu’ajouter du retard aux actions de réponse du CRM.

component_details.title: Response and recovery planning
component_details.description: A documented set of procedures for the disaster/crisis response and recovery process. Including use of local capacities, transition to recovery, type of activities and serivices provided during response and recovery activities and exit strategies, procedures for DREF & EA, and templates for planning, budgeting and accessing funds.

component_responses.notes:
Il n’existe pas de plan d’intervention ni de relèvement. 
L’expérience montre que, vu que l’action est assez centralisée, lorsque les comités informent le siège de leur besoin, l’aide arrive 1 mois après comme l’aide aux 400 familles de Rosso, ou 2 mois après comme pour le cash et les NFI à Bogue. 
Serait-il plus effectif de prendre ce délai en compte? Et donc de voir quel serait le besoin de ces personnes un mois après l’impact?
Et si on se basait sur les interventions passées pour prévoir les besoins et développer un plan en fonction, fait par le personnel du siège, des branches, et des volontaires puis partagé avec la communauté, la gouvernance, la direction et avec la contribution technique de la FICR et des partenaires?

Implications: pas d’analyse de l’intervention qui prend en compte la capacité du CRM, celles d’autres acteurs, mais aussi le genre, l’âge, le handicap et les complexités de la communauté, et qui prévoit l’action envers la population affectée.
Une bonne dissémination du rôle d’auxiliaire à l’état pourrait permettre au CRM d’avoir un plan approuvé et la possibilité de pré-positionnement de vivre.

component_details.title: Pre-disaster meetings and agreements
component_details.description: A commitment to arrange meetings and agreements with Movement stakeholders and external actors to identify, plan for and address gaps for any upcoming disaster season (e.g. monsoon, floods or cyclones, or for any generic disaster/crisis event (e.g Epidemic, pandemic, confilict situations). Pre-disaster agreements should set out each partner's role in the event of a disaster/crisis.

component_responses.notes:
