•	لدى سياسة إدارة مخاطر الكوارث مبادئ وقيم ارشادية توجه عملية صنع القرارات بشأن نهج وإجراءات الاستجابة ويتم اظهارها في خطط ويتم التقييد بها من قبل الموظفين والمتطوعين

component_details.title: DRM Laws, Advocacy and Dissemination
component_details.description: Designed to support the NS in improving legal preparedness for disasters and crisis and to promote the use of the IDRL Guidelines in order to reduce human vulnerability.

component_responses.notes: •  تمتلك لدى جمعية الهلال الأحمر اليمني خطة وإجراءات عمل للدبلوماسية الإنسانية في برنامج القوانين والقواعد والمبادئ الدولية للاستجابة ومحدد فيها التسهيلات القانونية ذات الصلة (أي المستحقات الخاصة والاعفاءات) مثل المواد التي تم تسليمها للدفاع المدني والتي تم اعفاؤها من الجمارك، ودائما ما تدعو الجمعية الي سن التشريعات التي تتماشى مع القانون النموذجي الخاص تسهيل وتنظيم المساعدات الدولية للإغاثة والانتعاش وتأخذ بالدروس لتحسين وتوجيه عملها الدبلوماسي الإنساني.

component_details.title: Quality and accountability
component_details.description: Describes the essential elements of principled, accountable, and high-quality humanitarian action. The RCRC Movement provides support to the most vulnerable people in line with the Sphere and CHS standards, Code of Conduct for the RCRC Movement and NGOS in Disaster Relief and the Code for Good Partnership of the RCRC Movement, Gender & Diversity, inclusion and protection, BPI/ Do no harm, context-sensitive analysis, violence prevention, accountability to affected population and disability considerations, Community engagement and accountability (CEA).

component_responses.notes:
• تمتلك الجمعية خطة للمشاركة المجتمعية والمسائلة ولديها نماذج معيارية وإجراءات مدرجة فيها وتساهم الخطة والاجراءات في التقليل من تأثير المساعدة الضارة على الصعيد الاجتماعي والاقتصادي والبيئي (مبدا عدم الحاق الضرر) كما تلتزم الجمعية بمعايير أسفير والمعايير الإنسانية الاساسية وتدمجها في الأنشطة اثناء التقييم والتخطيط والاستجابة 
• تم تدريب منسقين في المركز الرئيسي والفروع وتعتمد اليات امنه للمراجعة والشكاوى ومراقبة مخاوف المجتمع وطلباتها فيما يخص المساعدة المقدمة

component_details.description: A constitutional reference to the role of the NS in responding to disasters and crises, which may be legislated or included/ recognized in the National Response System.

The goal considers: context analysis, ongoing/regular all-hazards risk assessments: it may define the target proportion of affected population that will be reached, and a definition of the areas/sectors where a NS will usually respond during an emergency.

It acknowledges other relevant NS policies, and aligns with the government policy (where applicable), incorporating the general rules that the NS will obey in order to achieve something (i.e mandate, strategy, etc.)

The RCRC Movement provides support to the most vulnerable people in line with the Sphere and CHS standards, Code of Conduct for the RCRC Movement and NGOS in Disaster Relief and the Code for Good Partnership of the RCRC Movement, Gender & Diversity, inclusion and protection, BPI/ Do no harm, context-sensitive analysis, violence prevention, accountability to affected population and disability considerations, Community engagement and accountability (CEA).

component_details.title: Business continuity
component_details.description: A strategy to counter any potential or anticipated obstacles to effective functioning of the NS, with an eye to ensuring that personnel and assets are protected and able to function in the event of a disaster/crisis.

component_details.title: Emergency Response Procedures (SOPs)
component_details.description: Written guidelines that describe duties and rights of personnel, command structures, coordination with other organizations, and reporting requirements, etc. Includes detailed organogram, decision-making flow chart, and defined roles and responsibilities.

component_details.title: Response and recovery planning
component_details.description: A documented set of procedures for the disaster/crisis response and recovery process. Including use of local capacities, transition to recovery, type of activities and serivices provided during response and recovery activities and exit strategies, procedures for DREF & EA, and templates for planning, budgeting and accessing funds.

component_details.title: Pre-disaster meetings and agreements
component_details.description: A commitment to arrange meetings and agreements with Movement stakeholders and external actors to identify, plan for and address gaps for any upcoming disaster season (e.g. monsoon, floods or cyclones, or for any generic disaster/crisis event (e.g Epidemic, pandemic, confilict situations). Pre-disaster agreements should set out each partner's role in the event of a disaster/crisis.

component_details.title: Hazard, Context and Risk Analysis, Monitoring and Early Warning
component_details.description: Describes how the NS monitors and maps past, present and potential hazards, disasters and crises (e.g. hazard, vulnerability assessments, gathering information from communities and government authorities) and systematically evaluates the damage that could be caused by a potential disaster/crisis, the frequency, severity of the impact, and the alert the relevant areas to scale the preparedness actions to reduce population vulnerability.

component_details.title: Scenario planning
component_details.description: A set of practical operation plans that closely mirror the generic disaster or crisis response plan but are tailored to a specific hazard type (e.g. earthquake, dengue epidemic, floods, cyclone) and a specific scenario (i.e. number of people affected, their locations and other important factors).

component_details.title: Risk management
component_details.description: A mapping of the potential risks in every area, along with its related mitigation measures. Including financial, reputational, organizational risks etc.

component_details.title: Preparedness plans and budgets
component_details.description: Plans identifying organisational resources, determining roles and responsibilities, and developing policies, procedures and activities in order to reach a level of preparedness to be able to respond effectively to a disaster or crisis. Budgets ensure that the necessary financial support is secured to allow capacities to be built and readiness maintained.

component_details.title: Mapping of NS capacities
component_details.description: A list of the NS capacities including HR (staff, response teams and volunteers) and equipment that are available for disaster/crisis response. Teams could include branch and national response teams. This should be defined by technical speciality where relevant.

component_details.title: Early Action Mechanisms
component_details.description: Designed to translate warnings into anticipatory actions to help reduce the impact of specific disaster or crisis events. They focus on consolidating available forecasting information and putting procedures in place to ensure that a NS can act ahead of any disaster/crisis. Forecast-based financing is included within the scope of this area.

component_details.title: Cash Based Intervention (CBI)
component_details.description: An effective and flexible way, including all forms of cash and voucher-based assistance, to support people affected by emergencies, maintaining their dignity and choice, while fostering local economies. Cash should also be mainstreamed into other sectors (including Relief, shelter, livelihoods) and services (Logistics, Finance, etc.)

component_details.title: Emergency Needs Assessment
component_details.description: Assess the extent and impact of the damage caused by the disaster/crisis and the degree of vulnerability of the affected population. The first step in any emergency response, such an assessment will identify the needs that require external intervention and the gaps to be filled. It is a vital component of the programme-planning process.

component_details.title: Affected population selection
component_details.description: Identification and selection of target Affected population for interventions, using a pre-defined set of criteria based on need and vulnerability. This includes consideration of specific vulnerabilities such as disability, age and gender.

component_details.title: Emergency Operations Centre (EOC)
component_details.description: A central command and control facility responsible for carrying out disaster/crisis management functions at a strategic level in an emergency situation. The common functions are to collect and analyze data; facilitate decision making that protects life and livelihoods; and disseminate those decisions to all concerned agencies and individuals. Generally located at the headquarter level of an organization.

component_details.title: Information Management (IM)
component_details.description: Ability to manage information including requesting, receiving, analyzing and disseminating as per its procedures and partner requirements (IFRC and public authorities in particular). There should be a clear digital/paper trail that documents what, when and how the NS has acted and provides key information for the development of Emergency Plan of Actions. Includes IM between levels, between departments and Situational Reports, mapping, visualisation of data, GO platform (IFRC).

component_details.title: Testing and Learning
component_details.description: Drills and Simulations allow the organization to test, identify and learn from the results of these type of exercises and incorporate learning into future preparedness and response planning.

component_details.title: Activation of regional and international support
component_details.description: Procedures for requesting and accepting regional and international support in operations, including triggering coordination mechanisms for funding, materials and human resources deployments.

component_details.title: CHEMICAL, BIOLOGICAL, RADIOLOGICAL AND NUCLEAR (CBRN) EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS
MANAGEMENT OF DEAD BODIES TO FACILITATE THEIR IDENTIFICATION
NS-specific areas of intervention
component_details.description: Sector-specific or services provided by the NS in case of emergencies, it is in line with the NS mandate and legislation in country. It includes Community Based DP/DRR, Evacuation, Health in Emergencies, Epidemic and Pandemic, First aid, WASH, Food security and Livelihoods, Search and rRescue, Shelter, Management of dead bodies, RFL, Transition to recovery, and CBRN preparedness.

component_details.title: Coordination with local community level responders
component_details.description: Engagement with Community Disaster Response Teams (CDRTs), through training, coordination, and the development of community disaster preparedness and response plans.

component_details.title: Cooperation with private sector
component_details.description: Mechanism that allows cooperation with private sector that often plays a strong role in response, particularly if there is impact on their staff and businesses. There is often a willingness to donate goods and services. Advance agreements help to expedite response actions.

component_details.title: Coordination with External Agencies and NGOs
component_details.description: Mechanism that facilitates coordination and collaboration with Non-Governmental Organization (NGO), both local and international NGOs, civil society organizations (CSOs) and United Nations agencies in country.

component_details.title: Civil Military Relations
component_details.description: Dialogue and interaction with military actors, essential to protect and promote humanitarian principles, avoid competition, minimize inconsistency and, when appropriate, pursue common goals.

component_details.title: Coordination with Movement
component_details.description: Mechanisms that facilitate the coordination with ICRC, IFRC, and PNS in-country.

component_details.title: Coordination with authorities
component_details.description: Mechanism that facilitates coordination and cooperation with local and national authorities. It is connected to the NS auxiliary role for humanitarian assistance.

component_details.title: Staff and volunteer management
component_details.description: Well-functioning staff and volunteer management systems and practices allow for effective recruitment, supervision, support and encouragement of staff and volunteers.

component_details.title: Safety and security management
component_details.description: Addresses policy and procedures to ensure the safety of staff and volunteers. This include awareness, effective recruitment, training and management processes in place to ensure that personnel are capable of undertaking the roles demanded of them (from NS operational, management and leaders) according to the Stay Safe (IFRC) and Safer Access (ICRC). Based on safer access framework, including concepts of access, perception, identification and acceptance, and protection and violence prevention.

component_details.title: Communication in emergencies
component_details.description: Incorporates a system of public messaging to enable the NS to share timely, accurate information before, during, and after a disaster or crisis.

component_details.title: Operations Monitoring, Evaluation, Reporting and Learning
component_details.description: The PMERL is designed to implement a results-based planning, monitoring and evaluation system that provides an evidence base of NS performance, including relevance, efficiency, effectiveness, sustainability and impact. A reliable and trusted organization is accountable, providing transparent and timely information and building systems to strengthen data collection and reporting. It is data-driven, analytical and results-based.

component_details.title: Finance and Admin policy and emergency procedures
component_details.description: Overall budgeting, accounting, treasury, assets, financial reporting and financial services operations. it also includes the efficient delivery , cost effective and timely services to the NS. Pre-approved, auditable, expedited procedures that allow for flexibility during a disaster/crisis. These must meet transparency, oversight and accountability standards. Procedures may include faster approval processes, fewer signatures, different authority levels. The Emergency Procedures are activated for a specific period of time.

component_details.title: Information and Communication Technology (ICT)
component_details.description: Refers to technologies that provide access to information through telecommunications. This includes the Internet, wireless networks, mobile phones, radios and other communication mediums.

component_details.title: Resource Mobilisation
component_details.description: A documented strategy for raising domestic funds from the government, private sector, general public and other in-country actors to support the national society’s response. This would include allocation of responsibilities, practical mechanisms for accepting funds and for being accountable on funds.

component_details.title: DRM Strategy
component_details.description: An outline of the overall goal that the NS seeks to achieve in its disaster and crisis response operations. The goal considers: context analysis, ongoing/regular all-hazards risk assessments: it may define the target proportion of affected population that will be reached, and a definition of the areas/sectors where a NS will usually respond during an emergency.

component_responses.notes: Documents of strategies on DRM exist, however, strategies need to be updated and reviewed. But also not sure whether it has been implemented (staff). The heads of the department need to become familiar and disseminate the documents.

component_details.title: DRM Policy
component_details.description: Reflects the NS mission, RCRC principles and mandate. It acknowledges other relevant NS policies, and aligns with the government policy (where applicable), incorporating the general rules that the NS will obey in order to achieve something (i.e mandate, strategy, etc.)

component_responses.notes: on NS level there are no DRM policies, however, on National level there are existing CDM policy, draft Emergency shelter policy, National Sustainable Development Policy

component_details.title: DRM Laws, Advocacy and Dissemination
component_details.description: Designed to support the NS in improving legal preparedness for disasters and crisis and to promote the use of the IDRL Guidelines in order to reduce human vulnerability.

component_responses.notes: The BRCS has leverage/Entitlements due to working with CDEMA and the government but non-existing document on this. Need to find the actual Act exempting BRCS from taxes during responses.

component_details.title: Resource Mobilisation
component_details.description: A documented strategy for raising domestic funds from the government, private sector, general public and other in-country actors to support the national society’s response. This would include allocation of responsibilities, practical mechanisms for accepting funds and for being accountable on funds.

component_details.title: Staff and volunteer management
component_details.description: Well-functioning staff and volunteer management systems and practices allow for effective recruitment, supervision, support and encouragement of staff and volunteers.

component_details.title: Safety and security management
component_details.description: Addresses policy and procedures to ensure the safety of staff and volunteers. This include awareness, effective recruitment, training and management processes in place to ensure that personnel are capable of undertaking the roles demanded of them (from NS operational, management and leaders) according to the Stay Safe (IFRC) and Safer Access (ICRC). Based on safer access framework, including concepts of access, perception, identification and acceptance, and protection and violence prevention.

component_details.title: Communication in emergencies
component_details.description: Incorporates a system of public messaging to enable the NS to share timely, accurate information before, during, and after a disaster or crisis.

component_details.title: Operations Monitoring, Evaluation, Reporting and Learning
component_details.description: The PMERL is designed to implement a results-based planning, monitoring and evaluation system that provides an evidence base of NS performance, including relevance, efficiency, effectiveness, sustainability and impact. A reliable and trusted organization is accountable, providing transparent and timely information and building systems to strengthen data collection and reporting. It is data-driven, analytical and results-based.

component_details.title: Finance and Admin policy and emergency procedures
component_details.description: Overall budgeting, accounting, treasury, assets, financial reporting and financial services operations. it also includes the efficient delivery , cost effective and timely services to the NS. Pre-approved, auditable, expedited procedures that allow for flexibility during a disaster/crisis. These must meet transparency, oversight and accountability standards. Procedures may include faster approval processes, fewer signatures, different authority levels. The Emergency Procedures are activated for a specific period of time.

component_details.title: Information and Communication Technology (ICT)
component_details.description: Refers to technologies that provide access to information through telecommunications. This includes the Internet, wireless networks, mobile phones, radios and other communication mediums.

component_details.title: Hazard, Context and Risk Analysis, Monitoring and Early Warning
component_details.description: Describes how the NS monitors and maps past, present and potential hazards, disasters and crises (e.g. hazard, vulnerability assessments, gathering information from communities and government authorities) and systematically evaluates the damage that could be caused by a potential disaster/crisis, the frequency, severity of the impact, and the alert the relevant areas to scale the preparedness actions to reduce population vulnerability.

component_responses.notes: ●	NEMA has a daily hazard recording system and share info directly with MRCS branches and at-risk communities.  ●	MRCS branches also directly receive EWs from meteorological organisations.  ●	There is an existing EAP in place for Dzuds. One of the early actions identified includes branches sending SMS alerts to at-risk communities. The EAP includes thresholds for early actions, EW and EAs, ●	MRCS’ SG is a member of the national emergency commission (NEMA) and MRCS branches are also part of the provincial / local emergency commissions (LEMA) who are also capable of disseminating information on potential hazards. ●	MRCS relies on NEMA for information and analysis on political trends and when action should be taken ●	MRCS established CP for pre-election preparedness and response for potential internal disturbance during post-election period in coordination with the ICRC.  ●	EAP has established early actions and thresholds for Dzuds ●	MRCS does not have a consolidated national multi-hazard risk analysis and maps. They do however have existing risk analysis and maps for Dzud, which are captured in the EAP ●	Annually MRCS do receive information from the Disaster Research Institute (part of NEMA) and the Geophysical Disaster Organisation on hazards. ●	Currently, as part of the government mandate provinces, districts and local levels (which includes MRCS branches) need to conduct community level risk assessments.  ●	MRCS is in the process of signing an agreement with the government registration office to have access to disaggregated data on vulnerability and capacity on high-risk communities

component_details.title: Scenario planning
component_details.description: A set of practical operation plans that closely mirror the generic disaster or crisis response plan but are tailored to a specific hazard type (e.g. earthquake, dengue epidemic, floods, cyclone) and a specific scenario (i.e. number of people affected, their locations and other important factors).

component_responses.notes: ●	Please refer to General Considerations section, explaining the usage of MRCS’s All-Hazard Contingency Plan in relation to this component ●	The scenario of an earthquake was updated in 2019 following the nation-wide simulation exercise for an earthquake. The Dzud scenario is captured in detail in the EAP (which includes specific triggers, but not specific geographic areas) ●	Branches have their own separate Disaster Preparedness Plans as contingency plans (which includes preparedness, response) specific to hazards that are relevant to each location ●	LEMA require all local actors to have contingency plans that cover floods, fires, earthquakes, fire, Dzud, strong windstorm and animal and human diseases. MRCS HQ request these contingency plans to be updated every year, but officially is reviewed by LEMA every 2 years.  The contingency plans include a mapping of resources/capacity of mid-level branches, how many volunteers they have and what stock they have pre-positioned ●	As of right now, MRCS does not have a scenario on epidemics, but now starting to look at developing a contingency plan for influenza in coordination with Australian Red Cross ●	It was noted that in general the branch CPs are strong, but the HQ CPs need to be improved because the current CP is mostly general and contains many elements of key DM documents. Also, there have been many changes within the structure of MRCS, so each department needs to review their own specific parts of the CP. It was further noted that the CP also needs to better to define the role of the branches in supporting the HQ in the case of a large-scale disaster. It also needs to include regional considerations in the plan

component_details.title: Risk management
component_details.description: A mapping of the potential risks in every area, along with its related mitigation measures. Including financial, reputational, organizational risks etc.

component_responses.notes: ●	There is no specific focal person or team dedicated to managing overall organisational risk. Instead responsibilities are delegated to specific departments; for example, Admin and finance team manages operational risks, communication manages reputational risk, finance committee is responsible for finance risks and oversees organisational risk ●	In MRCS, reputational risks are seen as the responsibility of each individual staff members and is captured in each staff job description. In addition, Risk management was identified as a weakness in the OCAC assessments (especially risk management of volunteers). In 2019, the latest OCAC review demonstrated that MRCS risk management component improved from B to C criteria ●	MRCS has a Corruption Prevention procedure overseen by the compliance committee. Staff have received training on this. Fraud and corruption training has been translated, but it could not be uploaded on to MRCS web-based training platform due to technical issues  ●	Within MRCS risk management is not done in a preventive way, if there is a particular organisational risk the governing board becomes involved

component_details.title: Preparedness plans and budgets
component_details.description: Plans identifying organisational resources, determining roles and responsibilities, and developing policies, procedures and activities in order to reach a level of preparedness to be able to respond effectively to a disaster or crisis. Budgets ensure that the necessary financial support is secured to allow capacities to be built and readiness maintained.

component_responses.notes: ●	Please refer to General Considerations section, explaining the usage of MRCS’s All-Hazard Contingency Plan in relation to this component ●	The MRCS focal person for preparedness is the DM manager. Since the DRCE in 2016 MRCS has aimed to identify, prioritise and take action for its preparedness gaps through a capacity strengthening plan (RCEP- Response Capacity Enhancement Plan). These efforts continue through the PER process ●	The DRCE process was used to mobilise resources to support the RCEP (e.g. BRC FbA). Going forward the PER process and work-plan can be used as a marketing document to mobilise resources and coordinate support from partners ●	MRCS does not have specific allocation of budget for emergency preparedness however capacity building elements are present within projects and there are also specific community-based programmes

component_details.title: Business continuity
component_details.description: A strategy to counter any potential or anticipated obstacles to effective functioning of the NS, with an eye to ensuring that personnel and assets are protected and able to function in the event of a disaster/crisis.

component_responses.notes: ●	Please refer to General Considerations section, explaining the usage of MRCS’s All-Hazard Contingency Plan in relation to this component ●	MRCS does not have a business continuity plan. However, it is noted in the CP that if there is a major incident the youth camp has been identified as an alternative location/base to HQ ●	MRCS has identified who will be available if a key person is absent so that the function is continued, this have been captured in the MRCS multi-hazard contingency plan ●	There are no set procedures to communicate with donors to repurpose funds for unexpected or emerging needs

component_details.title: Emergency Response Procedures (SOPs)
component_details.description: Written guidelines that describe duties and rights of personnel, command structures, coordination with other organizations, and reporting requirements, etc. Includes detailed organogram, decision-making flow chart, and defined roles and responsibilities.

component_responses.notes: ●	Please refer to General Considerations section, explaining the usage of MRCS’s All-Hazard Contingency Plan in relation to this component. ●	Currently, there is no MRCS HQ level DM SOP that outlines all of the DM procedures in one place. There are dispersed/separated HQ level SOPs that focus on: ●	how to activate emergency response teams (NDRTs and BDRTs),  ●	cash assistance ●	SOPs for early action are captured in the EAP this includes role of MRCS, partners and other relevant stakeholders in the case of dzud ●	NDRT SOPs and MRCS multi-hazard CP defines operational roles and responsibilities. ●	MRCS organogram has HQ roles and responsibilities defined in the multi-hazard contingency plan. ●	MRCS still need to develop SOPs for support services (logistics, finance and admin) ●	MRCS has an emergency committee (SG and DM manager are part of this committee) this is activated at the request of the SG and DM manager, but there are no set triggers or procedures for when this committee is convened. ●	It is general practice for the SG to activate the emergency committee when there is a state of emergency declared, but this is not written down.

component_details.title: Response and recovery planning
component_details.description: A documented set of procedures for the disaster/crisis response and recovery process. Including use of local capacities, transition to recovery, type of activities and serivices provided during response and recovery activities and exit strategies, procedures for DREF & EA, and templates for planning, budgeting and accessing funds.

component_responses.notes: ●	Please refer to General Considerations section, explaining the usage of MRCS’s All-Hazard Contingency Plan in relation to this component ●	There is no specific / separate MRCS multi-sectoral response plans. However, response options are captured in MRCS ‘contingency plan’. The first page of the CP states how the plan is in line with FPs ●	There are national / Gov response plans (Disaster protection plans) and MRCS’ role is defined within these.  ●	MRCS is part of the state services and are called upon by Gov to provide assistance   ●	The government response plans and MRCS CPs do not consider gender, age, disability and diversity complexities and community capacities specifically, but these categories are considered in the targeted populations (see within the MRCS DM Programme Manual for branches p.12-13).  ●	Furthermore, ENA template for 72 hours include the number of persons affected and the question 11 asks “what are appropriate (culture) clothes, duvets for women, men, children, pregnant women, lactating women and elderlies” ●	As part of the Recovery cluster MRCS contribute to the overall recovery plan. MRCS themselves do not do or consider recovery in their emergency plans and recovery planning does not happen unless it is part of a large EA. In some cases MRCS has separate recovery project that address things like LLHs, usually due to donor requirements. ●	MRCS has developed a proforma for IFRC EPoAs, which is currently sitting with IFRC APRO for approval

component_details.title: Pre-disaster meetings and agreements
component_details.description: A commitment to arrange meetings and agreements with Movement stakeholders and external actors to identify, plan for and address gaps for any upcoming disaster season (e.g. monsoon, floods or cyclones, or for any generic disaster/crisis event (e.g Epidemic, pandemic, confilict situations). Pre-disaster agreements should set out each partner's role in the event of a disaster/crisis.

component_responses.notes: ●	There is an existing pre-disaster agreement (MoU) between NEMA and MRCS, who meet annually, as well as when the need arises. ●	MRCS also has existing pre-agreements with MoH, social welfare, NEMA, Trade Dev Bank (TDB), APU (commercial water company), Monas pharmacy, Khan bank, as well as a number of media channels (Mongolian national broadcast and three other channels). ●	Key staff are familiar with all of the agreements and how to operationalise them and depending on the content / nature of an agreement MRCS staff will operationalise the agreements during a response. ●	MRCS coordinate frequently with other stakeholders as part of the HCT (with UNICEF, Save the Children and World Vision) as well as with NEMA and LEMA. They also participate in all of the clusters. There is also a State-Red Cross Cooperation Council headed by the Deputy Prime Minister and members include relevant State Secretaries of the Ministries. This structure is duplicated at local levels and they meet twice a year. ●	In Sep 2018 MRCS held their first pre-disaster meeting. During this meeting they carried out a capacity mapping of Movement partners, which is documented in the meeting minutes. MRCS also holds a “Partnership Meeting” every two year, during which they carry out programme and partnership mapping. However, no pre-disaster agreements or Movement coordination agreement has been signed. ●	Contractors do not sign CoC, but within contracts / agreements there are articles that refer to parts of CoC and FPs.  ●	While there is no specific agreement with public authorities to facilitate expedited import of humanitarian aid and visas for incoming personnel there are 2 x legal acts and specific laws on expedited customs process for the purpose of humanitarian assistance.  ●	MRCS has no formal agreements in place for goods. However, they are currently in discussion with suppliers. They do however have agreements with banks to provide money transfer services.  ●	MRCS has no formal agreement with social protection systems. But they receive this from National Statistics Department (updated every year).

●	MRCS does not have Food Security as a standalone project /programme/objective or priority and therefore does not monitor food security levels in-country ●	However, as part of an MRCS livelihoods assessment, there was an analysis conducted on main food and agricultural markets and based on these findings MRCS was able to do an analysis on food security levels on which they could then plan activities. ●	MRCS is currently a member of the food security cluster (led by World Vision) and coordinate closely with Local Emergency Management Agencies. ●	One of the key activities that MRCS conducts during disasters is food distribution
Not applicable to MRCS.

●	MRCS ensures active participation of communities and reflects the needs and strengths of the local population in the assessment, design, planning of community-based preparedness activities through existing DRR and resilience projects.  ●	MRCS branches conduct regular awareness raising, public education and training on disasters or crises with LEMA. These are reflected in the branch manuals. Part of this awareness raising includes “Be Ready” ●	Community based EWEA is in place. Branches receive information / updates directly from LEMA, NEMA and Met services and then send EW messages to communities who are aware and trained in what early actions they can take.  ●	CDRTs are trained and equipped to handle local responses in partnership with local actors. The Branch disaster protection plan, outlines actions for CDRTs to take ●	Community risk assessments are done in an inclusive gender diverse way. MRCS has even translated EWEA into braille, as well as having people who can do sign language.

component_details.title: Mapping of NS capacities
component_details.description: A list of the NS capacities including HR (staff, response teams and volunteers) and equipment that are available for disaster/crisis response. Teams could include branch and national response teams. This should be defined by technical speciality where relevant.

component_responses.notes: ●	Please refer to General Considerations section, explaining the usage of MRCS’s All-Hazard Contingency Plan in relation to this component. ●	MRCS Human Resource capacities are mapped and focal points, through NDRTs, are identified for specific areas of intervention.  ●	All the NDRT members have profiles which identifies the trainings they taken. ●	PMER team has excel based database which contain HR and equipment resources. For branches, they also record a list of equipment. There is a regional database that is updated by branches. ●	Capacities are not mapped against response levels.  ●	Every year mapping of resources from the resource database is done to identify gaps. Every 2 years branch also do a branch assessment to identify gaps. Annual planning then includes activities to address the gaps identified.

●	In general, HiE is a new area for MRCS and there is only one scenario for influenza, which does not include multi country scenarios. ●	There are currently no procedures for specific HiE, but MRCS is working towards this.   ●	In general MRCS has data collection procedures and feedback mechanisms, but nothing yet specific to health outbreaks - MRCS staff have however participated in a training on how to prevent outbreaks and currently MRCS is implementing a project on TB surveillance ●	There are no existing procedures in place to manage and respond to rumours. There are protocols for staff or volunteers on infection prevention and control within epidemics, but depending on response MRCS distribute necessary protection equipment (e.g.  masks for those who are responding to TB) or hand sanitizers. However, no training has been carried out on use or safe disposal of PPE ●	NS have identified their role within epidemics. These are clearly defined in the statutes of MRCS as well as MoU with MoH. As they work closely with the MoH they know what technical capacity is available and support can be provided ●	MRCS is the member of the Health Cluster; however, cluster is not active ●	MRCS do not do dead body management

component_details.title: Early Action Mechanisms
component_details.description: Designed to translate warnings into anticipatory actions to help reduce the impact of specific disaster or crisis events. They focus on consolidating available forecasting information and putting procedures in place to ensure that a NS can act ahead of any disaster/crisis. Forecast-based financing is included within the scope of this area.

component_responses.notes: ●	MRCS has recently approved Early Action Protocol for dzud hazards. ●	At the national level, the government has initiated the discussion on Early Warning and Early Action strategies and preparedness, with different methods to send out alerts for at-risk people. ●	At the local level, the branches collaborate with the meteorological office and receives monthly, weekly and 3-day information on potential threats; branches produce material on how to prevent and prepare for the main hazards (fires, floods) for communities. ●	Currently MRCS does not have a mass messaging system for sending alerts at a nation level, however MRCS is considered/testing using the TERA system to send messages via SMS. Additionally, branches (with information from the Met Office) send SMS alerts, and Facebook messages to communities. At the provincial level, they can pay around 35CHF telecommunication messages to specific target groups at risk (via SMS by e.g. unitel, mobicom major operators). No agreement with the telecommunication company at the moment ●	The NS uses the national emergency commission as the body to help anticipate and respond. Also noted that there are national regulations for providing early action alerts using television, radios, etc.

component_details.title: Cash Based Intervention (CBI)
component_details.description: An effective and flexible way, including all forms of cash and voucher-based assistance, to support people affected by emergencies, maintaining their dignity and choice, while fostering local economies. Cash should also be mainstreamed into other sectors (including Relief, shelter, livelihoods) and services (Logistics, Finance, etc.)

component_responses.notes: ●	MRCS Cash SOPS/Guidelines developed with guidance from the IFRC Cash Toolkit (containing cash in emergencies principles, plan and specific steps, roles and responsibilities). Cash guidelines/SOPs are at draft version and therefore, not yet finalised nor approved or disseminated to BDRTs and branches yet. ●	MRCS has organogram for cash, how to select beneficiaries (using a matrix), has a commission to select the beneficiaries and how to prioritise, how to validate information, what are the beneficiaries’ documentation to receive cash support. ●	MRCS conducted a cash feasibility study and believes that MRCS cash-based interventions are considerate of cultural differences and social dynamics.  ●	MRCS co-leads the Cash sub-cluster.

component_details.title: Emergency Needs Assessment
component_details.description: Assess the extent and impact of the damage caused by the disaster/crisis and the degree of vulnerability of the affected population. The first step in any emergency response, such an assessment will identify the needs that require external intervention and the gaps to be filled. It is a vital component of the programme-planning process.

component_responses.notes: ●	MRCS differentiated between immediate, rapid, detailed and continual assessments within their NDRT and BDRT SOPs. ●	“DM Program Manual for Branches” contains a standardised template for emergency needs assessment. ●	MRCS believes that ENAs are well done at the branches and BDRTs are well trained on the ENA ●	MRCS is looking to standardise all the templates, which needs to be approved ●	MRCS has also used Magpi for data collection ●	MRCS 24-72h immediate and rapid ENAs are more generic. A second assessment contains more detailed data which captures gender, age, disability and other vulnerabilities of the affected population.

component_details.title: Affected population selection
component_details.description: Identification and selection of target Affected population for interventions, using a pre-defined set of criteria based on need and vulnerability. This includes consideration of specific vulnerabilities such as disability, age and gender.

component_responses.notes: ●	MRCS has agreed selection criteria for different hazards approved at senior management level and reflected in branch manuals and EAP for dzuds ●	The selection criteria is communicated to communities through the primary branches as well as broadcasting messages on local media channels ●	Selection criteria does consider different vulnerabilities and all responders are trained on data collection methods. Standardised templates for beneficiary data collection are also included in the branch manuals ●	Data collected is not shared with third parties unless it is part of a joint assessment or to ensure targeting is not duplicated. However, digital data systems are not protected. This is an area that MRCS feels needs strengthened ●	MRCS has different tools to verify beneficiary data

component_details.title: Emergency Operations Centre (EOC)
component_details.description: A central command and control facility responsible for carrying out disaster/crisis management functions at a strategic level in an emergency situation. The common functions are to collect and analyze data; facilitate decision making that protects life and livelihoods; and disseminate those decisions to all concerned agencies and individuals. Generally located at the headquarter level of an organization.

component_responses.notes: ●	The MRCS DM Programme Manager has formally been appointed as the EOC focal point ●	During the 2016 DRCE the EOC was identified as an important component for MRCS to strengthen. Since then MRCS has appointed an EOC focal person (DM manager) as well as a location / room with equipment at HQ. They also have a back-up EOC location (MRCS Youth Centre) in case the primary location is not accessible ●	MRCS has EOC SOPs which are in the process of being approved by Secretary General ●	The members of the EOC are NDRTs and it is activated by the SG. The trigger for activation of the EOC is the same as the trigger for activating NDRTs ●	Contact details for the EOC are captured in the CP not the EOC SOPs  ●	While the EOC is equipped there is no back-up or emergency infrastructure (i.e. back-up electricity, water), however there are SAT phones ●	As the EOC has not been activated yet there has not been an opportunity to test it

component_details.title: Information Management (IM)
component_details.description: Ability to manage information including requesting, receiving, analyzing and disseminating as per its procedures and partner requirements (IFRC and public authorities in particular). There should be a clear digital/paper trail that documents what, when and how the NS has acted and provides key information for the development of Emergency Plan of Actions. Includes IM between levels, between departments and Situational Reports, mapping, visualisation of data, GO platform (IFRC).

component_responses.notes: ●	At HQ MRCS is aware of the IFRC IM templates. The branches however use simplified templates (developed by MRCS) to then share data with HQ who then populate the IFRC templates. ●	MRCS has a number of SharePoints that can be used to share information, however these are not often utilised. ●	MRCS has the capacity to compile, visualise and share information via emails and paper-based mails with IFRC offices and partners and internally with different branches. ●	High risk areas are updated regularly especially at the branch level, who get the information from National Statistics Department (updated every year). MRCS also has access to demographic, socio-economic data disaggregated by age, gender and disability in high risk areas. ●	Based on OCAC 2016 results, MRCS improved its archiving capacities organised by the National Archiving Office.

component_details.title: Testing and Learning
component_details.description: Drills and Simulations allow the organization to test, identify and learn from the results of these type of exercises and incorporate learning into future preparedness and response planning.

component_responses.notes: ●	MRCS regularly tests response systems through a number of exercises including:  •	Government table-top exercise every 2 years •	Government simulation / field exercises every 4 years  •	Gobi Wolf exercise exchange, organised every year by the US Army/Embassy •	MRCS branch drills and simulations conducted by LEMA ●	Recent experiences, include MRCS organised earthquake simulation 2018 as part of EU funded project ●	The simulations that have been organised and participated by the MRCS include injects that address issues such as security, access, but not perception or acceptance of the NS. ●	MRCS does not conduct cross border simulations. ●	Lessons learned from such simulations and drills are used to revise plans and procedures.

component_details.title: Activation of regional and international support
component_details.description: Procedures for requesting and accepting regional and international support in operations, including triggering coordination mechanisms for funding, materials and human resources deployments.

component_responses.notes: ●	MRCS has an advantage compared to other international organisations in-country of calling for international assistance without national declaration of emergency. ●	MRCS is generally aware of available IFRC / ICRC support and corresponding procedures. They have launched Emergency Appeals (EA) and frequently (at least once a year) requests Disaster Relief Emergency Funds (DREF). Recent EA is from 2016 and 2018 DREF for cold wave, 2019 DREF influenza N1H1 ●	MRCS does not have SOPs on how to activate international assistance, but this information is instead reflected in the multi-hazard Contingency Plan. The decision on whether to request international support is taken by the SG who coordinates/communicates with the CCST. ●	Information, updates and requests are communicated via the GO Platform, two DM staff have GO accounts. ●	MRCS has already developed proforma EPoA (i.e. pre-filled EPoA), which is now with the IFRC for feedback/approval.

component_details.title: CHEMICAL, BIOLOGICAL, RADIOLOGICAL AND NUCLEAR (CBRN) EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS

component_responses.notes: ●	Livelihoods is articulated in MRCS Strategy 2020 as the first strategic objective, to support livelihoods of Mongolians that are vulnerable. Noted there is no DRM Strategy. ●	MRCS has a nationwide livelihood programme ●	There is a nation-wide program called “Livelihoods support programme” which is implemented in most provinces. MRCS is usually part of these programmes. Additionally, there is a “Social Protection Law” with a clause to protect livelihoods and those who are vulnerable. ●	MRCS does not have a focal point for LLH and Food Security

●	Nation-wide, there is an agreement (including with government) that ‘gers’ are the most appropriate shelters.  ●	Currently within MRCS, there are no pre-positioned gers as they are difficult to store due to the materials they are made of, however, in high risk areas ger suppliers have been identified and MRCS is in the process of establishing framework agreements with those suppliers.  ●	MRCS has a standard list of NFI kits to be prepositioned. ●	Shelter cluster lead during non-emergency time with technical support from Global Shelter Cluster

component_details.title: MANAGEMENT OF DEAD BODIES TO FACILITATE THEIR IDENTIFICATION

component_responses.notes: ●	MRCS has a functioning RFL service and RFL FP who has dealt with a number of RFL requests (3 active cases). ●	The RFL FP frequently attends trainings with the ICRC. MRCS also has signed a cooperation agreement with ICRC to provide additional RFL technical support if necessary

●	Only a few staff are familiar with the key recovery principles ●	MRCS’s mandate is to support every phase of the DM cycle. However, it does not explicitly outline their mandate specifically in recovery ●	In practice DREF and EA operations include recovery activities and considerations ●	MRCS does not have enabling systems for the smooth transition from relief to longer-term recovery activities ●	MRCS does joint needs assessments with public authorities ●	MRCS consider how to integrate sector interventions to have the maximum impact on affected communities

component_details.title: NS-specific areas of intervention
component_details.description: Sector-specific or services provided by the NS in case of emergencies, it is in line with the NS mandate and legislation in country. It includes Community Based DP/DRR, Evacuation, Health in Emergencies, Epidemic and Pandemic, First aid, WASH, Food security and Livelihoods, Search and rRescue, Shelter, Management of dead bodies, RFL, Transition to recovery, and CBRN preparedness.

component_responses.notes: ●	While evacuation is not specified in the strategy or CP, the volunteer guidelines mention specific responsibilities for carrying out evacuations. For example; relocation of people to pre-established camps / assembly points and setting up of safe spaces for PSS and first aid.  ●	As part of the local commission MRCS branch staff are involved in overall evacuation process

●	MRCS is very active in First Aid, which is part of their NS's response strategy and different scenarios. FA is also included in the responsibilities of both NDRTs and BDRTs ●	First aid is part of the Be Ready program ●	In addition to trainings, MRCS provides first aid packages to branches ●	MRCS also carries out mass social media campaigns on first aid

●	WASH is included in MRCS all-hazard CP as one of the 4 key priority areas ●	MRCS is part of the WASH cluster, however in practice this cluster is not so active and does not meet frequently ●	Doing sanitation training and refreshers as part of last DREF therefore key staff are familiar at HQ level. But prior to this they had little capacity and they are not clear on what WASH activities in emergencies should look like ●	Some bilateral projects on WASH in certain branches (Netherlands RC and UNICEF) - so some understanding in some branches - finished 3-4 years ago

●	MRCS currently does not have a community health contingency plans, nor concrete systems and procedures on proper reporting of health events from volunteers and branches to the Ministry of Health or relevant health facilities. ●	Previously, the volunteers at the HQ have been trained on the CBHFA through a programme and have been active in several districts of the capital of Ulaanbaatar. Nevertheless, they have not been refreshed on the CBHFA and not actively engaging on the simulation planning, implementing and evaluating at the moment.

component_details.title: Coordination with local community level responders
component_details.description: Engagement with Community Disaster Response Teams (CDRTs), through training, coordination, and the development of community disaster preparedness and response plans.

component_responses.notes: ●	MRCS branches representatives describe that all the response design, implementation and monitoring is considerate of communities’ feedback. Because of good collaboration with local emergency management agencies, MRCS branches have capacities to obtain information from them to make decisions. ●	MRCS branches have close relations with community level responders, regulations are in place on how to establish, structure and train these teams.

component_details.title: Cooperation with private sector
component_details.description: Mechanism that allows cooperation with private sector that often plays a strong role in response, particularly if there is impact on their staff and businesses. There is often a willingness to donate goods and services. Advance agreements help to expedite response actions.

component_responses.notes: ●	MRCS has various partnerships with private sector including companies such as APU, Khan bank, Trade Development Bank, and others. ●	In 2018 MRCS received the IFRC due diligence checklist and documents / agreement templates (including an annex of emblem use). These were all translated into Mongolian and have been used (e.g. to scope a possible partnership with Rio Tinto). ●	MRCS systematically ensures appropriate use of emblem as it is one of the clauses of the agreement that it makes with companies. ●	There has also been some collaboration with private sector in some branches.

component_details.title: Coordination with External Agencies and NGOs
component_details.description: Mechanism that facilitates coordination and collaboration with Non-Governmental Organization (NGO), both local and international NGOs, civil society organizations (CSOs) and United Nations agencies in country.

component_responses.notes: ●	MRCS coordinates and collaborates with other Humanitarian organisations working in Mongolia primarily through monthly HCT meetings: WV Mongolia, UNICEF, Mercy Corps, Save the Children, Caritas etc. MRCS also have agreements with key response organisations.

component_details.title: Civil Military Relations
component_details.description: Dialogue and interaction with military actors, essential to protect and promote humanitarian principles, avoid competition, minimize inconsistency and, when appropriate, pursue common goals.

component_responses.notes: ●	For MRCS, to date, there has not been a need to collaborate with the military as there has not been a large-scale emergency. ●	Currently, MRCS branches work with the military in peacetime mainly on simulations, training and sensitisation (e.g. go to local military schools to talk about what MRCS role and activities), and collaborate on blood donation services ●	MRCS is part of two major simulation exercises which involves internal and foreign military: Khan Quest and Gobi Wolf. ●	For emergency response there is an agreement which is under discussion with the Ministry of Defence ●	Civil Military Relations are not described in the MRCS multi-hazard CP/SOPS however MRCS has appointed a focal point (DM Manager)

component_details.title: Coordination with Movement
component_details.description: Mechanisms that facilitate the coordination with ICRC, IFRC, and PNS in-country.

component_responses.notes: ●	In the Mongolian Disaster Protection Law (amended in 2017), MRCS is a sole humanitarian organisation that can call for international assistance from the Movement in times of disaster and crisis prior the national declaration of emergency. Therefore, MRCS has been able to apply for available Movement assistance. ●	There is IFRC Country Office in Mongolia with 2 staff (Finance and admin, and a driver). MRCS coordinates with CCST for DREF or Emergency Appeals. ●	There are no legal frameworks for receiving assistance for major disasters with the Movement partners, however there is a good environment for collaboration and partnerships in place. In practice in the event of an emergency, there is good coordination. They have however never had to test this for a large-scale emergency.  ●	MRCS believes that there is a lack of reference materials for coordination mechanisms with the Movement

component_details.title: Coordination with authorities
component_details.description: Mechanism that facilitates coordination and cooperation with local and national authorities. It is connected to the NS auxiliary role for humanitarian assistance.

component_responses.notes: ●	MRCS is formally part of the national humanitarian coordination system in-country. It collaborates and coordinates with National Emergency Management Agency and MRCS branches with the Local Emergency Management Agency. ●	MRCS is part of State and Local Emergency Commission ●	As a member of a Humanitarian Country Team, MRCS is part of clusters and sub-clusters, playing leading roles in some of the clusters. ●	Key NS interventions have collaborations with local authorities at National and Local levels. This is formalised through emergency commission, and also at State-Red Cross Cooperation Council.

component_details.title: Staff and volunteer management
component_details.description: Well-functioning staff and volunteer management systems and practices allow for effective recruitment, supervision, support and encouragement of staff and volunteers.

component_responses.notes: ●	Please refer to General Considerations section, explaining the usage of MRCS’s All-Hazard Contingency Plan in relation to this component ●	Responders are deployed and equipped at both HQ and branch level. Branch guidelines and the NDRT ToR refer to required equipment, which is provided by MRCS HQ to branches ●	MRCS has a learning pathway for responders to obtain required qualifications and skills according to competencies and role profiles and BDRTs are able to advance from BDRTs to NDRTs once they have completed the relevant trainings and gained relevant experience ●	Responders are trained in the majority of quality and accountability standards: ○	SPHERE - NDRTs and BDRTs receive training in SPHERE,  ○	CoC - are signed every year by volunteers and staff ○	CHS - translated into Mongolian and is being disseminated   ○	Child protection policy - exists and has been disseminated to branches ○	SGBV - no specific training yet   ○	Fundamental Principles - Volunteers receive annual refreshers, trainings and orientations  ●	MRCS staff have ID and all volunteers receive visibility items that are recognised by authorities ●	In general, responders are not insured. However, during IFRC DREF and EA operations all volunteers are insured through IFRC insurance. MRCS is in discussion with a Mongolian Insurance Company to insure their active volunteers ●	Procedures exist to activate, deploy and manage branch and national response teams ●	MRCS has contact details of all responders and branches maintain HR profiles, which includes list of trainings and certificates for each person. However, this information is not consolidated in a single/accessible database. If needed, HQ would request information from the branch ●	MRCS does not have procedures for deploying spontaneous volunteers. This gap was also identified during DRCE, but MRCS has not yet taken actions ●	MRCS has specific HR procedures to scale-up or down. At national and branch levels, the volunteer policy describes recruitment, retention and recognition ●	There is no regular training on self-care, violence and harassment in the workplace is completed and psychosocial support is not systematically available for staff and volunteers during and after emergencies and crises. However, a stress management training took place for NDRT members previously ●	There is no documentation that formally communicates an expenses policy for responders, but in practice HQ covers volunteer these costs

component_details.title: Safety and security management
component_details.description: Addresses policy and procedures to ensure the safety of staff and volunteers. This include awareness, effective recruitment, training and management processes in place to ensure that personnel are capable of undertaking the roles demanded of them (from NS operational, management and leaders) according to the Stay Safe (IFRC) and Safer Access (ICRC). Based on safer access framework, including concepts of access, perception, identification and acceptance, and protection and violence prevention.

component_responses.notes: ●	Safety and security procedures developed, it is in draft and not approved yet. ●	No clear assigned focal points at HQ however at branches, the branch manager does take safety and security measures by providing equipment and guidance on how to ensure safety. ●	Context and risk analysis info is provided to responders on an ad hoc basis (e.g. through a whatsapp groups); nothing is formalised. ●	Safety and security analysis not happening at HQ level. ●	SAF has been translated and disseminated to branches. Stay Safe has been developed in Mongolian version but has had issues uploading it. ●	No concrete communication mechanism for staff and volunteers to report risks and incidents (although it is noted that the NDRT has function to report incidents).

component_details.title: Communication in emergencies
component_details.description: Incorporates a system of public messaging to enable the NS to share timely, accurate information before, during, and after a disaster or crisis.

component_responses.notes: ●	MRCS has a dedicated communications team at HQ and at the branch level and branch managers will act as the communications focal point. ●	In an emergency the SG is the assigned spokesperson for MRCS (if the SG is not available this responsibility is passed to the DM manager)  ●	MRCS also has informal system, for “humanitarian journalists”, trained journalists from televisions, newspapers, websites on humanitarian issues. ●	MRCS NDRTs attended a simulation exercise on communications in emergencies ●	MRCS has strong capacity and consistently monitor social media, but they do not have a specific social media policy.

component_details.title: Operations Monitoring, Evaluation, Reporting and Learning
component_details.description: The PMERL is designed to implement a results-based planning, monitoring and evaluation system that provides an evidence base of NS performance, including relevance, efficiency, effectiveness, sustainability and impact. A reliable and trusted organization is accountable, providing transparent and timely information and building systems to strengthen data collection and reporting. It is data-driven, analytical and results-based.

component_responses.notes: ●	MRCS has a dedicated PMER function for Operations as part of Disaster Management Programme. Also, there is an organisational PMER department consisting of 2 staff members who are part of NDRT and could also support PMER operations if needed. ●	Due to number of DREF and EA operations MRCS conducts various operational PMER, however, for smaller scale disasters or as a part of organisational culture through concrete PMER framework could be strengthened. ●	In general, MRCS believes that reporting, monitoring and evaluations are done in quality and timely manner according to the agreements with the IFRC, Partners and other relevant donors. Operational learnings are used by the MRCS to plan and update the future/current operations.

component_details.title: Finance and Admin policy and emergency procedures
component_details.description: Overall budgeting, accounting, treasury, assets, financial reporting and financial services operations. it also includes the efficient delivery , cost effective and timely services to the NS. Pre-approved, auditable, expedited procedures that allow for flexibility during a disaster/crisis. These must meet transparency, oversight and accountability standards. Procedures may include faster approval processes, fewer signatures, different authority levels. The Emergency Procedures are activated for a specific period of time.

component_responses.notes: ●	MRCS use Diamond accounting software. ●	They have a finance manual, but this does not include procedures for finance in emergencies. ●	MRCS do not have procedures in place to ensure transparency, but there is a statement in MRCS statute about maintaining transparency. ●	There are no systems and procedures for fraud/corruption prevention during emergency.  ●	Relevant admin finance staff and operation managers are familiar with existing emergency related MoUs and agreements for compliance as part of IFRC DREF/Appeals.

component_details.title: Information and Communication Technology (ICT)
component_details.description: Refers to technologies that provide access to information through telecommunications. This includes the Internet, wireless networks, mobile phones, radios and other communication mediums.

component_responses.notes: ●	All staff are required to have functioning mobile phones, SIM cards spare batteries etc, but these are not provided by the MRCS ●	There is a contact list of all the MRCS key staff and contact details, which has been disseminated to branches and used by the branch staff. ●	During response MRCS prefers using FB group chats for internal communication as it is accessible and frequently used.  ●	Externally, it has access to radio frequency that is opened by the Emergency Commission when disaster strikes. ●	MRCS has low frequency radios and some access to satellite phones both at HQ and branches. ●	MRCS currently does not have an up-to-date, approved Emergency Notification Protocol / SOPs that are followed by all staff and volunteers.

component_details.title: Resource Mobilisation
component_details.description: A documented strategy for raising domestic funds from the government, private sector, general public and other in-country actors to support the national society’s response. This would include allocation of responsibilities, practical mechanisms for accepting funds and for being accountable on funds.

component_responses.notes: ●	The MRCS DM department is familiar with RM options available for humanitarian response and preparedness activities. ●	While MRCS has an overarching RM strategy, they do not have one specific to RM in emergencies ●	NS has agreements and mechanisms for collaboration and fundraising with the private sector ●	MRCS currently do not have a national emergency fund. However noted that some MRCS branches have access local budget to pre-position emergency relief stocks at local level. Currently, key emergency funding is available through the EAP, however this is only in the case of Dzuds. ●	MRCS has a bank account specifically to receive DREF and EA funds, however they do not have one to receive public donations. They are currently working with TDB to be able to receive online donations.  ●	There is no system in place to track donations. When there is a DREF/EA, MRCS would look at the bank statement to see where the money is coming from (and also its expenses). Finance staff have access to the bank statements  ●	There is not a predefined list of in-kind donations. Noted that MRCS branches have a list of what to prepositions

component_details.title: RC auxiliary role, Mandate and Law
component_details.description: A constitutional reference to the role of the NS in responding to disasters and crises, which may be legislated or included/ recognized in the National Response System.

component_responses.notes: ●	MRCS has an established auxiliary role and mandate within Mongolia. These are reflected in the following national laws:  1.	Law on Legal Status of Mongolian Red Cross Society 2.	National Disaster Protection Law  3.	Mongolian Donor Law ●	The Fundamental principles are reflected in the MRCS law and statutes of MRCS ●	Staff and volunteers are made aware of these laws and the FPs through a number of trainings including mandatory orientation trainings and online trainings ●	As part of the IHL core working group, MRCS promote IHL to the public authorities (this was only recently established) It was noted that to get from Good to High performing for this component, MRCS could focus on further establishing IHL to make it more prominent within MRCS. Also, it was noted there is a need to do more dissemination/sensitisation of IHL externally with ministries (particularly due to staff turnover).

component_details.title: DRM Strategy
component_details.description: An outline of the overall goal that the NS seeks to achieve in its disaster and crisis response operations. The goal considers: context analysis, ongoing/regular all-hazards risk assessments: it may define the target proportion of affected population that will be reached, and a definition of the areas/sectors where a NS will usually respond during an emergency.

component_responses.notes: ●	Please refer to General Considerations section, explaining the usage of MRCS’s All-Hazard Contingency Plan in relation to this component ●	MRCS currently does not have a dedicated DRM strategy. However, MRCS defines its general DM objectives (e.g. strengthening MRCS capacity and supporting community-based preparedness) within its organisational Strategy 2020 ●	It is noted that more detailed strategic operational objectives specifically for EQs and floods are defined in the all-hazard CP, to provide services such as first aid, psychosocial support, distribution of aid (CP, p.2). This includes details such as number of targeted beneficiaries (i.e. up to 500 households to be reached within 72 hours). Additionally, in line with the Early Action Protocols, operational objective to dzud was included (to reach up to 1000 households) ●	The CP also defines the sectors that MRCS provides services for. It was noted that the operational strategies/objectives in the CP, are not always reflected in EPoAs as the CPs focus on large scale disasters. The CP is reviewed every 2 years

component_details.title: DRM Policy
component_details.description: Reflects the NS mission, RCRC principles and mandate. It acknowledges other relevant NS policies, and aligns with the government policy (where applicable), incorporating the general rules that the NS will obey in order to achieve something (i.e mandate, strategy, etc.)

component_responses.notes: ●	MRCS currently does not have a DRM Policy

component_details.title: DRM Laws, Advocacy and Dissemination
component_details.description: Designed to support the NS in improving legal preparedness for disasters and crisis and to promote the use of the IDRL Guidelines in order to reduce human vulnerability.

component_responses.notes: ●	MRCS works with the IFRC APRO Disaster Law focal point on IDRL ●	In 2015 MRCS was asked by NEMA to support the revision of the national Disaster protection Law to include elements of IDRL. Then in 2017 MRCS worked with NEMA to develop an amendment that covered the entire DRM cycle, including risk management, recovery, and IDRL  ●	Currently MRCS and NEMA have a joint IDRL plan (which is updated annually). MRCS has also carried out dissemination activities and organised a number of trainings on disaster protection and other relevant laws ●	The Law describes certain legal entitlements to accommodate international assistance into the country. However, there are currently no clear visa timelines for international delegates entering the country  in the event of a large scale emergency and there are limitations of how well these laws are understood, due mainly to the turnover of government staff especially when it comes to sudden-onset disasters ●	There have been few opportunities to test IDRL in practice, but lessons were captured during a 2019 National EQ SimEx

component_details.title: Quality and accountability
component_details.description: Describes the essential elements of principled, accountable, and high-quality humanitarian action. The RCRC Movement provides support to the most vulnerable people in line with the Sphere and CHS standards, Code of Conduct for the RCRC Movement and NGOS in Disaster Relief and the Code for Good Partnership of the RCRC Movement, Gender & Diversity, inclusion and protection, BPI/ Do no harm, context-sensitive analysis, violence prevention, accountability to affected population and disability considerations, Community engagement and accountability (CEA).

component_responses.notes: ●	It was noted that while there are no documented procedures/guidelines or templates  in place on how to incorporate community input, in practice, during an emergency, mechanisms are in place and new ones (TERA) being piloted to ensure that MRCS’ BDRTs consult with affected populations during needs assessments and to clearly communicate selection criteria ●	A number of MRCS HQ staff have received training on CEA, however to date MRCS has not identified a CEA focal point ●	MRCS has a safe and accessible feedback and complaints mechanisms in the form of a hotline, established in 2016. MRCS has access to a two-way SMS communication with almost 600,000 G-mobile subscribers through TERA. TERA is free of charge for both the Red Cross and the G-Mobile subscribers who receive or send messages. It was piloted with communities to verify whether cash, food, warm clothes and fuel (in this order of priority) were the most needed relief items. However, contract that was signed between IFRC and G-Mobile, expired and contract could not be extended due to number of reasons including funding ●	Currently MRCS does not have a violence protection/SGBV policy. However, during the pilot project supported by Australian Red Cross (2018), MRCS established multi-disciplinary working group composed of relevant stakeholders and continued the practice of establishing same WGs through the violence prevention project (since 2019) funded by ICRC. This WG includes police, health, social care and health agencies who established SOPs that all agencies have signed up to ●	MRCS has a dedicated focal person for PGI and is currently reviewing the PGI minimum standards, which need to be verified and approved. MRCS is also working to include PGI in BDRT trainings ●	MRCS adheres to SPHERE standards throughout the organisation. Annual training is provided to BDRTs to SPHERE. Generally, it would appear there is a good understanding of SPHERE ●	MRCS has a ‘Child Protection Policy’ and is part of related protection clusters within the country ●	MRCS does not have plans and procedures to actively minimise potential harmful social, economic and environmental impacts of assistance. In practice, these areas have not been identified during responses. Nevertheless, during response planning certain social elements are considered for instance when distributing NFIs and market analysis is conducted

It acknowledges other relevant NS policies, and aligns with the government policy (where applicable), incorporating the general rules that the NS will obey in order to achieve something (i.e mandate, strategy, etc.)

component_responses.notes: CVM precisa de investir (indicar focal point, política definida, treinamento)  nesta componente para que seja eficaz.
