Community review meetings ensure opinions are shared. Reports contain a part on how community was engaged. A framework for receiving complaints and feedback exists based on the context. Feedback might be collected through volunteers or a hotline however there is a risk the information does not come back to the field due to missing links, or comes late or unclear. NS refers to CHS during reviews/evaluations and other standards during MEAL activities. PGI related elements are guided by a Protection Manager. The response is customised and the ""Do no harm” principle is followed. Data is disaggregated for gender and privacy purposes however it does not capture disabilities. Some underlying conditions are included in the assessment."

component_details.title: Business continuity
component_details.description: A strategy to counter any potential or anticipated obstacles to effective functioning of the NS, with an eye to ensuring that personnel and assets are protected and able to function in the event of a disaster/crisis.

component_responses.notes: Business Continuity (BC) plans are triggered by needs; there is no standing BC plans. NS now has a BC plan for COVID-19 (for all levels) which also covers NS health facilitates/services, and this has been tested. In past one was developed for elections. It has not been developing a BC plan for floods. BC plan is led by HR with technical support from DM; approval is made by Head of HR/DSG. Normally, this is not an elaborated document. NS does not have pre-agreed/approved procedures to communicate with donors; this is done after an EW/ emergency.

component_details.title: Emergency Response Procedures (SOPs)
component_details.description: Written guidelines that describe duties and rights of personnel, command structures, coordination with other organizations, and reporting requirements, etc. Includes detailed organogram, decision-making flow chart, and defined roles and responsibilities.

component_responses.notes: "SOPs exist but not for all areas. SOPs are updated regularly and are well institutionalized. Branches adapt NHQ and MoH SOPs. There are SOPs for RCATS. There is need to update SOPs after COVID-19 response/ experience. SOPs are disseminated through training sessions. At field level, not everyone knows about SOPs; this needs enhancement, especially to new staff and volunteers.   In general, SOPs describe the roles and responsibilities of various responders at different levels however, there are some missing links in some sectors. SOPs include all stages of a response until earl recovery. Standardised templates are included. SOPs do not include procedures to scale alert levels up and down; this is very much guided by managers' decision based on a situation. SOPs are general however. these very well guide the epidemic situations."

component_details.title: Response and recovery planning
component_details.description: A documented set of procedures for the disaster/crisis response and recovery process. Including use of local capacities, transition to recovery, type of activities and serivices provided during response and recovery activities and exit strategies, procedures for DREF & EA, and templates for planning, budgeting and accessing funds.

component_responses.notes: "NS develops multi-hazard and multi-sectoral contingency plan (CP) (more generic/countrywide) through a consultative process in March which is reviewed in September, every year. More detailed and specific (to an imminent risk e.g. floods) CP is developed closer to an emergency. Head of DM approves the plans. NS develops a proper deployment plan. During assessment and planning, groups with special needs are considered and targeted efforts are made. KRCS beneficiary tracker include PGI considerations (pregnancy, age, disability). However, NS faces some challenges in this regard due to turnover of volunteers and a need for capacity building of new volunteers.  Plan is developed by a bottom-up process. Counties provide significant inputs to March planning workshop through consultations with various stakeholders. Sharing with IFRC and other partners happens in case of escalation and in case of a response. NS does not follow any standard check list (or a systematic process) for adherence of CP to Principles and Rules, DRM policy and Fundamental principles; this gets ensured through the trained staff by default. Synergies with plans of other actors mostly takes place when coordination mechanism (led by government) is activities after a disaster.  NS analyses secondary risk (e.g. contamination, interruption of services)  during response and recovery planning during response and early recovery planning however, in many instances, it is unable to move to recovery phase because of lack of resources. NS has SOPs to carry our AAR; it can make this element more effective by enhancing the involvement of partners. NS has SOPs and uses MoH guidelines to manage donation of medical items "

component_details.title: Pre-disaster meetings and agreements
component_details.description: A commitment to arrange meetings and agreements with Movement stakeholders and external actors to identify, plan for and address gaps for any upcoming disaster season (e.g. monsoon, floods or cyclones, or for any generic disaster/crisis event (e.g Epidemic, pandemic, confilict situations). Pre-disaster agreements should set out each partner's role in the event of a disaster/crisis.

component_responses.notes: "KRCS has the operational lead in response nationally and in counties, due to the lack of Government capacity. Meetings are planned before predictive disasters (cyclical, seasonal). The platform ""Kenya Humanitarian Partnership"" brings together humanitarian actors to discuss actions. Meetings happen once a month. If there is an issue, partners will have subsequent meetings to plan for a particular disaster. A partnership coordination forum also happens between Movement partners (PNS – IFRC – ICRC) and UN for sharing. KRCS is the lead for disaster and post-disaster data. Others depend on it. The Mass Casualty Incident Protocol guides mass responses. When needs go beyond the county's capacity, then the national mechanism calls key actors and they come out with a response plan through a committee. Contingency planning is also done jointly at county level and nationally, allocating tasks to all actors for preparedness and response.  Agreements are formalised in the shape of documents standing agreements, plans, protocols or contingency plans developed jointly. They are disseminated and explained internally; some are shared with the IFRC. Agreements for data sharing are signed with ministries on need basis. Regions know the agreements, and dissemination to branches happens in coordination meetings. Branches are part of contingency plans' development, so they cascade information locally. A table mapping strategic areas of support of PNS – ICRC – IFRC and other actors exists with the partnership FP. Mapping of the different capacities during epidemics and pandemics should be done. Framework agreements are in place in order to avoid procurement. NFIs have a mechanism for activation. Most of the suppliers sign the code of conduct. One-time suppliers don't. Epidemic control measures and insurance should be considered for suppliers.  Entrance of emergency teams and materials is made easy through the connections with the Government, without having any official document stating tax exemptions and facilitated procedures. The NS is including this point in the disaster law being developed with the IFRC."

component_details.title: Hazard, Context and Risk Analysis, Monitoring and Early Warning
component_details.description: Describes how the NS monitors and maps past, present and potential hazards, disasters and crises (e.g. hazard, vulnerability assessments, gathering information from communities and government authorities) and systematically evaluates the damage that could be caused by a potential disaster/crisis, the frequency, severity of the impact, and the alert the relevant areas to scale the preparedness actions to reduce population vulnerability.

component_responses.notes: "Different teams work on analysis. The capacity to analyse exists but it needs to be enhanced in countries. 5 people do it at HQ and 24 at counties. Some progress can be made on: Who are the users of this data? Can they take decisions based on this data? Because of the auxiliary role, KRCS needs to see how others' analysis feeds into the RC's work, for them not to be working in silos. The data management team is responsible for the risk assessment and anticipatory actions for recurrent disasters based on past data. They inform the DM team on scenarios. Risk monitoring and preparedness for immediate action is done by the teams on the ground for the different areas. The interagency team KRA (Red Action Team) does the rapid assessment. On the ground, trained volunteers collect data which feeds into the risk monitoring system (ex: for floods). Teams coordinate information. The DM team reviews the contingency plan twice a year; there is a matrix that helps understand risks and vulnerability in relation to the location, the likelihood and resources needed. In counties, risks have been identified. Program frameworks contain a risk analysis. There is a monitoring and early warning system for cyclical and seasonal hazards (floods, fires, droughts, recurrent epidemics and for some counties, armed conflicts). For epidemics, KRCS is working with the Gov on a system that actively does surveillance for epidemics alert. Alert raised are investigated by the Government and KRCS county’s health FP. Data collection was improved by using technology like smart phones and Kobo. No much paperwork. Primary and secondary data is used for anticipation, then triangulation happens. This helps a direct response. Counties with an EOC have better data collection and analysis.  A feasibility study was done in 2018 and this has been informing data preparedness capacities with the objective of being a data driven society but also understanding the hazards, risks and impacts based on historical impacts. Gaps and risk are very context specific. Team works on safe access and security, using technology for getting inaccessible data: GIS, satellite technology, drones. There is no written procedure on how to analyse acceptance and security risks. KRCS is moving from a reactive to an active institution. Early Action protocol including early warning and thresholds is ready for floods. It is linked to the department of meteorology and water resource management authorities. Communication Strategies have been developed for 7 counties out of 47 (river basin). For droughts, it is being developed in contribution with different stakeholders and considers conflicts from migration. Fire sensors were also place in some counties to detecting raise in temperature and inform response teams before the fire starts. In some counties there is a mailing list for early warning, it is also done through radios. Communication strategy was missing however it is getting better now. Risk analysis and mapping are co-developed with branches, relying on volunteers and community leaders. Connectors and dividers are not systematically analysed. Maps are shared with all active branches. Those existing for fundraising purposes are not as aware. VCA is continuously done with communities. VCA informs project design. Once in a while, the NS does a “Mapathon” to allow community to participate in the development of multi-hazard maps.  Data disaggregation and management, especially in epidemics, and cross-boarder coordination can be enhanced and systemized. Recognition and early action for epidemics can be strengthened at volunteer level. Mapping of health facilities and their capacities needs to be updated, and the coordination between the data management and health teams should be enhanced. "

component_details.title: Scenario planning
component_details.description: A set of practical operation plans that closely mirror the generic disaster or crisis response plan but are tailored to a specific hazard type (e.g. earthquake, dengue epidemic, floods, cyclone) and a specific scenario (i.e. number of people affected, their locations and other important factors).

component_responses.notes: "NS develops multi-hazard and multi-sectoral contingency plan (CP) (more generic/countrywide), based on scenarios, through a consultation process in March which is reviewed in September, every year. CP includes preparedness plan as well as response plan and response strategy. Focus of CP is more on emergency relief and underlying risks are considered during planning for long-term recovery. Sometimes, at county level, there is a great plan but activation and resource allocation becomes a problem due to limited resources. Elements like NS acceptance, security and access are considered during CP process but are not captured comprehensively; these are more considered during planning for and in actual response.   Plan is aligned with other agencies' plans through KRCS' participation in multi-agency contingency planning process, and sharing and coordination. Activation of CP is tied with scenarios and escalation of situation. Trigger mechanism is not very structured. Specific framework for coordination with neighbouring NSs does not exit; necessary coordination is done once an emergency has happened.    Epidemics are one of four disasters that are considered in NS CP and related scenarios. "

component_details.title: Risk management
component_details.description: A mapping of the potential risks in every area, along with its related mitigation measures. Including financial, reputational, organizational risks etc.

component_responses.notes: "Currently, Audit Manager is replacing Risk & Compliance Manager on an interim basis; risk function will be separated from Audit department. Audit & Risk Committee is comprised of heads of departments and focus on strategic risks; same structure during operations. However, risk management during emergency operations is more rapid. Team works closely with SG and reports to board on risks management every quarter; this also includes reputational risks. At branches, governance and technical team manage risks, with periodic meetings, risk monitoring and risk matrix. Risk identification is done before engaging in operations and projects. Follow-up is still not fully institutionalised. Whistleblowing hotline and complaints mechanism going straight to SG (but not to an external party). All reports are logged and given to Audit and Risk committee.  Identification and mitigation of risks is part of risk management template. This is happening in an ad hoc way and lessons learnt can be strengthened. Engagement with stakeholders is done and potential risks are identified at the start of operations and programmes, sometimes also linked closely with resource mobilisation e.g. political interference. However, this is not always done in a systematic way. To prevent fraud and corruption, systems, policies and procedures are in place, and are revised and updated regularly. There are limits at branch and regional level to authorise expenditures (especially around procurement and contracting). NS ensures protection of first responders, taking into account the impact of fear, stigma and diseases-specific precautions."

component_details.title: Preparedness plans and budgets
component_details.description: Plans identifying organisational resources, determining roles and responsibilities, and developing policies, procedures and activities in order to reach a level of preparedness to be able to respond effectively to a disaster or crisis. Budgets ensure that the necessary financial support is secured to allow capacities to be built and readiness maintained.

component_responses.notes: NS has a preparedness FP at HQ. There are preparedness and response FPs in every county. These are mostly County Coordinators or RCAT leaders who are trained in preparedness and actual response and recovery and are critical in the development and review of NS multi-hazard CP. Preparedness gaps are discussed during CP process; these are also communicated to respective departments and to other stakeholders. There is a need to systematise identification and prioritization of financial gaps for preparedness and early actions and putting a resource mobilisation strategy is in place.

KRCS has the ability to offer food security assistance through various means and coordination is strong between cash and logistics departments when deciding on the most appropriate modality. KRCS is a trusted partner of WFP for distributing food assistance. National standards are followed when determining levels of assistance. Food security as a technical sector could still be strengthened and is mostly dependent on projects.

Search and rescue is part of the NS' response strategy and is identified in different scenarios. NS has improved its capacity for this service over time however, it lacks specialized equipment and associated training, and adequate PPEs. Epidemic risk and potential absence of S&R personnel is under consideration after COVID-19.

KRCS achieves the participation of the community through establishing, training and equipping, and supporting the Community DRR teams (CMDRR). CMDRR teams are recognised as the first responders. The CMDRR teams are well integrated as part of the local response structures and local authorities. KRCS volunteers are recognised as playing a key role as part of the communities, communicating vulnerabilities, needs, and early warnings to KRCS branches. There is also an effective system of managing rumours in cases of epidemics. Empowering the community to be able to respond by themselves has changed the perception – no longer just “beneficiaries” but have capacity and contribute. However, lack of resources at community-level often hinder the implementation of various plans and measures.

component_details.title: Mapping of NS capacities
component_details.description: A list of the NS capacities including HR (staff, response teams and volunteers) and equipment that are available for disaster/crisis response. Teams could include branch and national response teams. This should be defined by technical speciality where relevant.

component_responses.notes: "NS has focal points for all areas of intervention and services to provide technical guidance and support, and staff and volunteers are trained and kept up to date in line with operational needs. However, high turnover of volunteers and retention of HR and skills is a big challenge. NS has a database to manage record of its staff, volunteers and action/response teams.  Stock is prepositioned in line with annual contingency plan and based on needs but there are always gaps in resources. NS does not have an efficient online system in place to track its stock. At this stage, HQ approval for the disbursement of NFIs (in line with assessment) is helping to ensure accountability and some oversight. Mechanisms are in place to share resources between counties or regions with the approval of HQ. Between sister NS, this has happened through IFRC or a PNS.   NS capacities are not mapped in line with different levels of response or types of epidemics, in a systematic way. "

KRCS Emergency Health is embedded into DM department to ensure multi-sectorality in response. Health data is collected as a standard part of the response. Rumour management is a strong component and addressed through various channels. Procedures for safe and appropriate use and disposal of PPE exist, however processes for Management of the Dead in epidemics not yet fully formalised. Volunteer safety is regarded as paramount. KRCS auxiliary role in epidemics is not always fully clear as NS can end up filling gaps MoH is not able to cover.

component_details.title: Early Action Mechanisms
component_details.description: Designed to translate warnings into anticipatory actions to help reduce the impact of specific disaster or crisis events. They focus on consolidating available forecasting information and putting procedures in place to ensure that a NS can act ahead of any disaster/crisis. Forecast-based financing is included within the scope of this area.

component_responses.notes: "NS early warning early action system includes o Forecast-based Financing and disease surveillance and is an integral part preparedness system. NS conducts mapping of disasters and their trends; this is fed into multi-hazard contingency planning. Contingency plan details all actions needed to be done. Constant surveillance through EOC helps in this regard. NS uses available information, and activate early action base on contingency planning. NS tests and makes use of new technologies appropriate for the context and audiences for sending alert messages related to early action (e.g. radio for CBS, mailing list, WhatsApp groups). NS has procedures and personnel available to communicate alerts and initiate early action at all levels of the NS.  Trained and equipped CBDRTs continuously monitor hazards. It is their responsibility to warn community and provide them to right information. There is a unit with CBDRTs that was established in every community. They are the ones providing information to communities about relevant hazards including epidemics. CBDRTs are supported by frontline staff (through e.g. Red spots, WhatsApp groups, SMS, Facebook). Sometimes competition between KRCS and authorities and lack of clarity on mandate. Early Action mechanism in case of epidemics (e.g. cholera) is often quite clear but is not always formalized with MoH."

component_details.title: Cash Based Intervention (CBI)
component_details.description: An effective and flexible way, including all forms of cash and voucher-based assistance, to support people affected by emergencies, maintaining their dignity and choice, while fostering local economies. Cash should also be mainstreamed into other sectors (including Relief, shelter, livelihoods) and services (Logistics, Finance, etc.)

component_responses.notes: "KRCS is an active member (co-chair) of cash working group and influence government for use of cash. NS prioritises the use of cash in early action and in early response. Cash and Voucher Assistance (CVA) is incorporated in the national plan. There is an agreement with a service provider (Safari Com) who has authorised KRCS manage the payment platform; this makes transfers efficient. NS is looking for innovative approaches to improve cash programming like DIGITS Digital identities and Community Inclusion Currencies (CIC) digital currencies that circulate within a community. There is an internal cash working group for CVA that is working on strengthening the system e.g. exploring cash vendors beyond Safari Com for direct cash, updating database and trying to decentralise capacities.   Staff from various departments and volunteers (including action teams) were trained in various counties. They are added in the database exists.  NS has a plan to do a session targeting governance and Senior Management Team (SMT) and Regional Managers for strategic positioning and scaling up the use of cash in the institution. Market analysis and integration are areas that need strengthening.   NS has been able to readily tailor cash programming in response to epidemics. During COVID-19 and Ebola, cash has been the most preferred modality.  "

component_details.title: Emergency Needs Assessment
component_details.description: Assess the extent and impact of the damage caused by the disaster/crisis and the degree of vulnerability of the affected population. The first step in any emergency response, such an assessment will identify the needs that require external intervention and the gaps to be filled. It is a vital component of the programme-planning process.

component_responses.notes: "NS uses standardised templates and procedures for needs assessment and reporting. This information includes essential PGI elements, is backed-up by secondary data and guides the development of emergency plan. NS engaged multi-sectoral emergency assessment team (RCATs) in a timely manner. Trained personnel from other agencies are also part of network/ system to collect data in a holistic way, in a multi-agency approach.  NS analyses accessibility, availability, quality and use of goods and services during needs assessment. Demonstration to beneficiaries on how to use relief items is also considered. Some of the secondary effects and local coping mechanisms are taken into account during assessments but there is no formal system to process/document that.   Standardised tools and procedures are used to cover epidemics or their likeliness. There is potential to further improve these tools (e.g. information about people living with chronic illnesses, systematisation to institutionalise data collection methods). "

component_details.title: Affected population selection
component_details.description: Identification and selection of target Affected population for interventions, using a pre-defined set of criteria based on need and vulnerability. This includes consideration of specific vulnerabilities such as disability, age and gender.

component_responses.notes: "NS uses community interest/entry strategies, engages community gatekeepers and base affected population selection on a clear criteria. For a distribution, selection criteria is shared and agreed with communities and justified. For this purpose, community committees are organised and consulted to build acceptance and gain support during distribution. NS also explains limitations in resources. Selection criteria includes essential PGI elements.   NS uses consent forms during data collections, clearly explains the purpose and protects data. Action/response teams are trained in data collection, using standard templates. Verification of potential beneficiaries is done through coordination mechanism to avoid double-targeting, without compromising data protection. Data for epidemics is collected by using MoH tools and kept under their strict data protection practices."

component_details.title: Emergency Operations Centre (EOC)
component_details.description: A central command and control facility responsible for carrying out disaster/crisis management functions at a strategic level in an emergency situation. The common functions are to collect and analyze data; facilitate decision making that protects life and livelihoods; and disseminate those decisions to all concerned agencies and individuals. Generally located at the headquarter level of an organization.

component_responses.notes: "The national EOC is active 24/7 with a formal FP, defined shifts, the capacity to function without stopping regular activities, SoPs that include technical sectors and clear levels of authorities, a back-up location and mechanism in case the main facilities cannot be accessed, the equipment needed and a regular display of information. There is a need for more people at HQ and for systems usage to be revised regularly as the digital world changes fast. Strategic decisions are based on the situational analysis. The national EOC is in direct contact with Government’s and counties’ EOCs for coordination. Military and police are contacted through mobile phones. The radio system is not used by KRCS in emergency response. Phone numbers of staff are saved in the system since on-boarding as briefings and SMS alerts are regularly sent to staff. Sometimes, local EOCs are set up in response areas. Those might lack of essential needs in remote areas (connection, water, sleeping space, etc…) Some key staff know their role (mainly for recurrent disasters), other don’t. As for epidemics, the role of health staff is only defined in times of epidemics and upon need. The “Mass Casualty Incident Protocol” describes the neutral protocol and defines technical lead based on the type of hazard. Specific roles for epidemics are defined when response in time of epidemics occurs. The protocol does not detail pre-analysed plans, special considerations and the connection with the Ministry of Environment during epidemics. "

component_details.title: Information Management (IM)
component_details.description: Ability to manage information including requesting, receiving, analyzing and disseminating as per its procedures and partner requirements (IFRC and public authorities in particular). There should be a clear digital/paper trail that documents what, when and how the NS has acted and provides key information for the development of Emergency Plan of Actions. Includes IM between levels, between departments and Situational Reports, mapping, visualisation of data, GO platform (IFRC).

component_responses.notes: "There are hard and soft copy templates of which people are aware. Equipment to view and share data exists at the national EOC, some is ready for deployment in large scale response and most branches have the needed equipment. Response data is shared on a cloud system. The “Community risk analysis dashboard” provides non-disaggregated data. This dashboard is not disseminated yet. Some secondary data is taken from the Government, DHIS and secondary sources. This info is aggregated by age and gender however not disability. Data is available over time. Decisions are documented however are not archived be readily available upon need. There is a tendency to rebuild.  Sitrep template exists, it is used and informs response. It includes guidelines on every section for people to know what should be captured. It even covers the action plan and lessons learned however summary is not extracted in an automated system. It is saved within a department and no archiving happens; thus database might be lost.  Guidelines on information sharing and authorisation exist however they are not as effective as they should be. Data is kept in silos within departments. There is no central place to access or request documents. In large scale emergencies with a task force in place, sharing of data happens. But outside the taskforce, the information is not captured well. There are no special data sharing guidelines for epidemics. During COVID, the NS was forced to think of the way they should work and discuss, and of their approval processes while not in the office. "

component_details.title: Testing and Learning
component_details.description: Drills and Simulations allow the organization to test, identify and learn from the results of these type of exercises and incorporate learning into future preparedness and response planning.

component_responses.notes: "Early action protocols are in process of development. Simulations are conducted time to time especially during training; regular simulations do not happen. Lessons learned are part and parcel of adjustment and planning of future response. Aspects like access, acceptance and security are covered during SAF related simulations. For regular simulations, main focus is a particular technical/thematic area. Branches test their response system where feasible and RCAT leaders are involved in planning and implementation of drills.  Simulations and drills are conducted with national authorities and communities. These exercises do not happen with neighbouring NS; only coordination takes place when an emergency has hit. IPC for staff and volunteers is included in simulations."

component_details.title: Activation of regional and international support
component_details.description: Procedures for requesting and accepting regional and international support in operations, including triggering coordination mechanisms for funding, materials and human resources deployments.

component_responses.notes: "Almost half of NS key staff are familiar with technical, financial, material and HR support available from Movement partners, with designated counterparts. Staff know available resources (and tools/templates) but not fully familiar with deployment and activation of them. Frequent update of tools/templates sometimes is a challenge for NS to be on top of. SOPs include procedures to request and incorporate regional and global support into their response system, and focus mainly coordination within NS. NS informs IFRC within 24 hours for which assistance may be required.  For bilateral assistance requests, NS uses PNS guidelines; there is no coordination framework in place. For medical supplies and personnel, NS uses MoH and IFRC technical guidelines."

component_details.title: CHEMICAL, BIOLOGICAL, RADIOLOGICAL AND NUCLEAR (CBRN) EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS

component_responses.notes: "The NS’s mandate in CBRN events is to provide first aid and evacuation. The response role and some guidance on safety and risks exist. There is no official focal point nationally and capacity at HQ and branches is very limited. In the past years' hazard mapping, the NS has identified the need for CBRN preparedness to be strengthened. There is a need to strengthen and equip responders at various levels of the mandated response. Very minimal protection equipment exist, there are no public messages that are ready to disseminate and there is no coordination with neighboring NSs on cross-border response, however the NS is part of the national network for technical support.  The needs for international support in responding to CBRN is not shared with Movement partners."

KRCS positions itself as part of both the response and long-term coordination mechanisms on livelihoods. A lot of sensitisation work has been done in urban and rural markets during COVID. Livelihoods are included in KRCS and county-level contingency plans, however they are not always realised due to lack of resources (including some in the floods operation). Capacity could be strengthened at branch level.

"Fixed emergency shelter kits that follow IFRC standards are used by the NS. Nevertheless, in rural areas, the design is adapted to preference and existence of material. The assessment aims to understand the best shelter's structure based on the composition and ethnic group of the household. Reconstruction has a different procedure since assessment stage.  The NS is expected to respond to 150000 people before seeking support from other agencies. This represents 30000 household approximately for which the NS tries to pre-position items in the 8 regional warehouses based on projected needs. Real requirements are higher every year and replenishment is not being easily done by partners, therefore, these figures cannot be reached sometime.  Agreements with providers mention standards and prices however they do not guarantee the availability of material at any given time.  Shelter champions exist in branches for operational advise. In times of epidemics, health colleagues guide teams on the replacement and destruction of contaminated items. There are no existing SoPs that inform this mechanism."

component_details.title: MANAGEMENT OF DEAD BODIES TO FACILITATE THEIR IDENTIFICATION

component_responses.notes: Management of dead bodies is part of KRCS auxiliary role and it is carried out in coordination with authorities who are responsible for identification. Sometimes KRCS is the sole provided of this service. Safe and Dignified Burials not needed in KRCS operations thus far. DBM services activated during floods operation.

RFL offered as a key service in areas of high displacement as well as in refugee camps but not in all areas of Kenya. Implementation of RFL supported by ICRC. Epidemic constraints taken into account with service. RFL not required in floods operation.

NS has adapted IFRC's Community Resilience for their recovery design. Recovery is assessed through individual sectors’ assessment which might need to look at a systemized way to integrate sectors for a more impactful recovery planning. The NS’s role in recovery is not formalised with authorities however the coordination with ministries and other actors exists.The community is fully engaged for recovery, and stigma is reduced by making sure the real information is reaching communities. Staff and volunteers in branches understand the recovery strategy and response SoPs cover the transition to recovery phase however there is no general guidance on transition to recovery explaining actions in chronological order and mapping link-ups to be done.When the NS faces needs that are not strategic, they mobilise resources and needed skills to be able to respond.

component_details.title: NS-specific areas of intervention
component_details.description: Sector-specific or services provided by the NS in case of emergencies, it is in line with the NS mandate and legislation in country. It includes Community Based DP/DRR, Evacuation, Health in Emergencies, Epidemic and Pandemic, First aid, WASH, Food security and Livelihoods, Search and rRescue, Shelter, Management of dead bodies, RFL, Transition to recovery, and CBRN preparedness.

component_responses.notes: Evacuation is part of all KRCS response plans and takes place as per humanitarian needs. Emphasis is on pre-emptive evacuation. KRCS auxiliary role is clear in epidemics. In the floods operation, KRCS assumed the lead for evacuations due to lack of resources and capacities of authorities.
First Aid is a strong part of KRCS services. No epidemic policy/guidelines in existence.

WASH is a strong part of KRCS response including epidemics (especially cholera) though there is a shortage of volunteers trained for WASH in epidemics. RCATs have been trained and support from professional volunteers (e.g. engineers) and authorities is also available. KRCS is also part of the national WASH coordination mechanisms.

"Target communities especially in fragile counties have contingency plans which are led by communities and linked to multiple actors. NS identifies and trains local volunteers in CBHFA. They collect data which helps to determine disease trends, and support identification of priorities.   Considering limited available resources, selected volunteers from high-risk communities or nearby areas are trained in CBHFA. There is a mechanism to train newly inducted volunteers or refresh trained ones, and trainings are mostly tied with projects. NS follows IFRC standard training curriculum. This includes necessary skills for reporting of suspect events to MoH, and simulations; separate simulation exercises are not conduced. CBHFA volunteers are trained in community engagement and making referrals. NS is implementing selected components of ICCM. Capacity in communicable diseases/epidemic control exist in some counties.  Only selected volunteers including RCATs are trained in basic FA because of limited resources; this situation also affects refresher plans. Annual training needs are determined based on available resources."

component_details.title: Coordination with local community level responders
component_details.description: Engagement with Community Disaster Response Teams (CDRTs), through training, coordination, and the development of community disaster preparedness and response plans.

component_responses.notes: Community engagement is practised through KRCS volunteers and branches and supported by RCATs during response, strongly underpinned by the CEA framework. All stages of the disaster cycle are covered through engagement with communities. A clear mechanism is in place for communication between different parts of the organisation. Community engagement may be restricted through lack of resources at branch level.

component_details.title: Cooperation with private sector
component_details.description: Mechanism that allows cooperation with private sector that often plays a strong role in response, particularly if there is impact on their staff and businesses. There is often a willingness to donate goods and services. Advance agreements help to expedite response actions.

component_responses.notes: KRCS Partnership Policy guides engagement with private sector including appropriate use of emblem. KRCS benefits from several professional vokunteers though there isn't a separate mechanism/strategy in place to support this.

component_details.title: Coordination with External Agencies and NGOs
component_details.description: Mechanism that facilitates coordination and collaboration with Non-Governmental Organization (NGO), both local and international NGOs, civil society organizations (CSOs) and United Nations agencies in country.

component_responses.notes: KRCS is a well-established organisation within the Kenyan humanitarian network and partners with UN and other agencies based on strategic interest and alignment and reach. KRCS is able to establish bilateral partnerships and coordination between the different organisations happens at all levels through the NS.

component_details.title: Civil Military Relations
component_details.description: Dialogue and interaction with military actors, essential to protect and promote humanitarian principles, avoid competition, minimize inconsistency and, when appropriate, pursue common goals.

component_responses.notes: KRCS has strong practices around coordinating with the military and police and use military logistical capacity when needed as a last resort as guided and approved by leadership and senior management. Dissemination also happens through trainings. KRCS role has been recognised in many restrictive situations (e.g. during COVID-19 curfews) with access and movement granted to KRCS. Coordination mechanisms and not formalised through a policy/guidelines and the capacity is not fully institutionalised.

component_details.title: Coordination with Movement
component_details.description: Mechanisms that facilitate the coordination with ICRC, IFRC, and PNS in-country.

component_responses.notes: Movement coordination in-country takes place with IFRC, ICRC and PNSs through regular meetings and exchanges between counterparts. Partnership meetings to share operational updates recently established. For international assistance and coordination with neighbouring NSs, reliance on IFRC coordination and processes.

component_details.title: Coordination with authorities
component_details.description: Mechanism that facilitates coordination and cooperation with local and national authorities. It is connected to the NS auxiliary role for humanitarian assistance.

component_responses.notes: KRCS has strong coordination mechanisms with national and local authorities and is integrated into the national response mechanisms through the National Disaster Operations Centre (NDOC). Engagement with authorities is continuous and not limited to disasters or emergencies; contingency planning process plays an important part in this. Sometimes authorities rely on KRCS to take the lead due to their own limited resources (human and financial). While there is a high level of emblem awareness, there are no specific guidelines for this.

component_details.title: Staff and volunteer management
component_details.description: Well-functioning staff and volunteer management systems and practices allow for effective recruitment, supervision, support and encouragement of staff and volunteers.

component_responses.notes: "KRCS has a large web of volunteers made of 200,000 people with a very regular rotation, making it impossible to manage all volunteers in the same way. Therefore, systems related to database, training, equipping, ensuring visibility and formalising are more focused on the RC Action Teams (RCAT), who have formal guidelines containing everything from responsibilities to deployment procedures. Deployment happens based on the skills needed in particular areas. Database exists at counties and HQ, but updates depend on counties. When there is a need for more help or specialised skills during large responses, counties set desks to accept spontaneous volunteers and those with the needed professional skills. A person usually handles dissemination to those volunteers. To improve practice, the NS can have a checklist to incorporate spontaneous volunteers, meeting the minimum screening procedures. RCAT have visibility vests and a RC IDs. In case there is a need for more active volunteers, then IDs are prepared at HQ and delivered to branches. When deployed, RCAT receive a briefing session including equipment providing, explanation of the situation, insurance and safe access. They are divided in shifts. These teams have a specific training but no visible training path or choice of the areas they would like to master. Remaining volunteers receive the dissemination session but do not have a training path.  The code of conduct is explained and signed during the induction session, but other policies are not known. Only RCAT members might be aware of more policies due to practice. There should be an ongoing system that ensures policies are known and put into practice. Volunteers’ expenses are covered and when insurance does not cover an incident, KRCS tries to cover it from its budget. This procedure takes time but it works in some cases. In serious conditions, the NS cannot help. It should look at other resources to repurpose funds. When response needs are intensified, more volunteers are added to the response. Volunteer recognition is done at county level during the National volunteer award. A specific award is given for exceptional work. Written procedures are not grouped under one policy. Some are some in the HR policy, others in volunteers policy, volunteer management guidelines, youth policies, Incident Command Protocol and the security policy. Some of the mechanisms and processes are also not formalised (scaling up and down, rotation and retention strategy, …). There is a PSS team that supports staff and volunteers during and after a response. The team also offers support in peace time. Regular training on epidemic prevention and control are not systemised however it happened regularly for COVID. It might be helpful to have this point as part of the training and refresher mechanism."

component_details.title: Safety and security management
component_details.description: Addresses policy and procedures to ensure the safety of staff and volunteers. This include awareness, effective recruitment, training and management processes in place to ensure that personnel are capable of undertaking the roles demanded of them (from NS operational, management and leaders) according to the Stay Safe (IFRC) and Safer Access (ICRC). Based on safer access framework, including concepts of access, perception, identification and acceptance, and protection and violence prevention.

component_responses.notes: KRCS has security focal points at HQ level and a security handbook. Stay Safe is compulsory for responders and Safer Access is being implemented in certain areas. Some RCATs have also received Safer Access training. Security processes are mostly known and applied by staff and volunteers though impacted by turnover. KRCS is responsible for security arrangements for its own staff and volunteers but also a number of partner staff in country. SOPs are currently being developed but there is no overall Security Policy.

component_details.title: Communication in emergencies
component_details.description: Incorporates a system of public messaging to enable the NS to share timely, accurate information before, during, and after a disaster or crisis.

component_responses.notes: "Focal points for comms and official spokespersons are identified. The protocol is well understood. Trainings on the guidelines and policy are done at on-boarding of staff and volunteers, and refreshers are regularly done at HQ however not often at county level.  KRCS uses social media, press statements, press tours and radio programs to inform the public on needed actions, raise awareness on the needs of the affected population or even to respond to rumors.  Templates exist for key messages related to usual disasters or diseases, press releases and some reports along with ready forms for photos consent and beneficiary data management. There is no general plan for comms in emergencies nor written guidelines to provide information to the public within 24 hours of the disaster, however KRCS is able to update their communities as soon as information is available, thanks to its branches and web of volunteers. A full time social media officer exists for tracking, monitoring, and directing negative messages to the related department. A regular coordination with IFRC and ICRC exists.   For institutionalisation of those practices, the team is advised to develop a strategy and an emergency plan for the communication that should happen within few hours of a disaster."

component_details.title: Operations Monitoring, Evaluation, Reporting and Learning
component_details.description: The PMERL is designed to implement a results-based planning, monitoring and evaluation system that provides an evidence base of NS performance, including relevance, efficiency, effectiveness, sustainability and impact. A reliable and trusted organization is accountable, providing transparent and timely information and building systems to strengthen data collection and reporting. It is data-driven, analytical and results-based.

component_responses.notes: "There is a MEAL department at HQ with a head of department and 4 MEAL Officers in the regions (for 8 regions). A MEAL manual also exists. The NS collects Lessons Learned to feed into future operations. There is an indicator tracking table which is linked to response activities.  7% of the budget is dedicated to MEAL activities. This does not include salary of MEAL staff and fees related to evaluations. Compilation and sharing with the Movement is currently happening. It was absent before. There are no specific guidelines for MEAL in epidemics with an analysis of the capacity to monitor and report with a limited number of people. This was managed during COVID-19 through a Business Continuity plan and based on MoH guidelines. An accountability framework is in place. KRCS needs to update its strategy/framework in line with IFRC CEA Strategy which was revised last year."

component_details.title: Finance and Admin policy and emergency procedures
component_details.description: Overall budgeting, accounting, treasury, assets, financial reporting and financial services operations. it also includes the efficient delivery , cost effective and timely services to the NS. Pre-approved, auditable, expedited procedures that allow for flexibility during a disaster/crisis. These must meet transparency, oversight and accountability standards. Procedures may include faster approval processes, fewer signatures, different authority levels. The Emergency Procedures are activated for a specific period of time.

component_responses.notes: "The NS uses professional systems to manage and keep track of financial and in-kind donations. Some personnel at HQ and counties is trained to use the systems and to deal with finance emergency procedures. The emergency period is officially defined for procedures to be followed. Transparency is maximized through the automated systems, internal and external audits, voluntary on-spot audits, public M&E, reporting and a hotline for feedback.  The NS is auxiliary to county and national authorities. It has a number of MoUs with authorities, stakeholders and suppliers. Finance and Admin emergency procedures consider measures that ensure essential functions are covered with minimum presence, automated online approval where possible, virtual meetings, cloud sharing of documents, etc."

component_details.title: Information and Communication Technology (ICT)
component_details.description: Refers to technologies that provide access to information through telecommunications. This includes the Internet, wireless networks, mobile phones, radios and other communication mediums.

component_responses.notes: KRCS has HF and VHF radios available in most vehicles and in key locations. The NS also has satellite communications capacity for emergencies. Communication is often done through WhatsApp groups; some dedicated WhatsApp groups exist now for specific responses though practice is not formalised. WhatsApp and social media are used to communicate response updates. Some of the equipment is not usable due to lack of maintenance. Communications branches do not have much ITC capacity or are dependent on projects.

component_details.title: Resource Mobilisation
component_details.description: A documented strategy for raising domestic funds from the government, private sector, general public and other in-country actors to support the national society’s response. This would include allocation of responsibilities, practical mechanisms for accepting funds and for being accountable on funds.

component_responses.notes: "The RM system is partially working well and can still be strengthened based on the strong infrastructure in KRCS. International RM options are well known, donors and partners are managed at each level from HQ to regions and branches, however there is not RM strategy or plan that institutionalises procedures, nor RM pre-disaster agreements signed. NS has developed Early Action Protocols for floods (and soon other disasters) and have integrated funds-repurposing section to be able to respond in cases of crisis or disasters. Repurposing funds is communicated between DM, PRD and PMER however there is no written mechanism for that. Contact with donors is done case by base, and for more general collaboration, the NS has an agreement with Kenya's Private Sector Alliance to strengthen DRM in the country. The NS’s RM role is made official under article 4 and 59 of the constitution which tackles investments in the objectives of financing RC work however, the NS is short on funds for early action. Emergency fund management guidelines also states diversification of fundraising streams however this did not happen allover the territory yet. There is no remote or digital donation platform. The NS is developing a digital fundraising platform and looking into possibilities to accept donations through MPESA and PayPal. KRCS’s constitution refuses donations stemming from revenues which activities are contrary to the RCRC’s Fundamental Principles. As for in-kind donations, a list of acceptable items and criteria are shared with main donors and private companies willing to donate. Practically, individual in-kind donations are accepted on a desk which keeps track.  KRCS has an RM table, tracks funds and IKDs, is able to capture donor funds/IKDs. The NS also has a proposal tracker. Tools are only for internal use so far."

KRCS has a dedicated Logistics function with items strategically prepositioned based on hazard mapping and contingency plans. At branch level, technical capacity for logistics is often not present. (4)//KRCS coordinate their stock and equipment with other actors in country and follows Movement standards for stock. Stock is released to operations based on assessment needs and SitReps and through Requisitions. Procedures are in place to accept or reject IKDs and for import. KRCS pays no duty or VAT. (5)//Procurement activities are guided by the Procurement manual, which also includes emergency procurement provisions. Pre-qualified suppliers (done every two years) exist at all levels; additional procurement support for branches is available through Regions and HQ. Currently there are no Framework Agreements in place because of COVID but they are standard practice. It is possible to blacklist suppliers. All suppliers have signed a Supplier Code of Conduct. (5)//KRCS has a comprehensive Fleet manual, disseminated to staff. Vehicles have the necessary equipment and documentation, including logbooks. Vehicles are comprehensively insured and regularly maintained and only driven by authorised drivers. New drivers are vetted and tested and regular drivers tested and re-trained regularly (including First Aid and SAF). Driver hours are guided by the manual but there are no specific provisions for emergencies. Vehicles suppliers are mapped but mostly exist in Nairobi. At branch level, there is a lack of vehicles. There is no written policy on weapons in vehicles. (3)//KRCS has a Warehouse manual and standardised templates for receipt, storage and dispatch of items. Warehousing capacity is sufficient and spread throughout the country though not all branches have dedicated storage space. Epidemic considerations taken into practice during COVID but not yet documented. (4)

component_details.title: DRM Strategy
component_details.description: An outline of the overall goal that the NS seeks to achieve in its disaster and crisis response operations. The goal considers: context analysis, ongoing/regular all-hazards risk assessments: it may define the target proportion of affected population that will be reached, and a definition of the areas/sectors where a NS will usually respond during an emergency.

component_details.title: DRM Policy
component_details.description: Reflects the NS mission, RCRC principles and mandate. It acknowledges other relevant NS policies, and aligns with the government policy (where applicable), incorporating the general rules that the NS will obey in order to achieve something (i.e mandate, strategy, etc.)

component_details.title: DRM Laws, Advocacy and Dissemination
component_details.description: Designed to support the NS in improving legal preparedness for disasters and crisis and to promote the use of the IDRL Guidelines in order to reduce human vulnerability.

component_details.title: Quality and accountability
component_details.description: Describes the essential elements of principled, accountable, and high-quality humanitarian action. The RCRC Movement provides support to the most vulnerable people in line with the Sphere and CHS standards, Code of Conduct for the RCRC Movement and NGOS in Disaster Relief and the Code for Good Partnership of the RCRC Movement, Gender & Diversity, inclusion and protection, BPI/ Do no harm, context-sensitive analysis, violence prevention, accountability to affected population and disability considerations, Community engagement and accountability (CEA).

component_details.title: RC auxiliary role, Mandate and Law
component_details.description: A constitutional reference to the role of the NS in responding to disasters and crises, which may be legislated or included/ recognized in the National Response System.

component_details.title: Hazard, Context and Risk Analysis, Monitoring and Early Warning
component_details.description: Describes how the NS monitors and maps past, present and potential hazards, disasters and crises (e.g. hazard, vulnerability assessments, gathering information from communities and government authorities) and systematically evaluates the damage that could be caused by a potential disaster/crisis, the frequency, severity of the impact, and the alert the relevant areas to scale the preparedness actions to reduce population vulnerability.

component_details.title: Scenario planning
component_details.description: A set of practical operation plans that closely mirror the generic disaster or crisis response plan but are tailored to a specific hazard type (e.g. earthquake, dengue epidemic, floods, cyclone) and a specific scenario (i.e. number of people affected, their locations and other important factors).

component_details.title: Risk management
component_details.description: A mapping of the potential risks in every area, along with its related mitigation measures. Including financial, reputational, organizational risks etc.

component_details.title: Preparedness plans and budgets
component_details.description: Plans identifying organisational resources, determining roles and responsibilities, and developing policies, procedures and activities in order to reach a level of preparedness to be able to respond effectively to a disaster or crisis. Budgets ensure that the necessary financial support is secured to allow capacities to be built and readiness maintained.

component_details.title: Business continuity
component_details.description: A strategy to counter any potential or anticipated obstacles to effective functioning of the NS, with an eye to ensuring that personnel and assets are protected and able to function in the event of a disaster/crisis.

component_details.title: Emergency Response Procedures (SOPs)
component_details.description: Written guidelines that describe duties and rights of personnel, command structures, coordination with other organizations, and reporting requirements, etc. Includes detailed organogram, decision-making flow chart, and defined roles and responsibilities.

component_details.title: Response and recovery planning
component_details.description: A documented set of procedures for the disaster/crisis response and recovery process. Including use of local capacities, transition to recovery, type of activities and serivices provided during response and recovery activities and exit strategies, procedures for DREF & EA, and templates for planning, budgeting and accessing funds.

component_details.title: Pre-disaster meetings and agreements
component_details.description: A commitment to arrange meetings and agreements with Movement stakeholders and external actors to identify, plan for and address gaps for any upcoming disaster season (e.g. monsoon, floods or cyclones, or for any generic disaster/crisis event (e.g Epidemic, pandemic, confilict situations). Pre-disaster agreements should set out each partner's role in the event of a disaster/crisis.

component_details.title: Mapping of NS capacities
component_details.description: A list of the NS capacities including HR (staff, response teams and volunteers) and equipment that are available for disaster/crisis response. Teams could include branch and national response teams. This should be defined by technical speciality where relevant.

component_details.title: Early Action Mechanisms
component_details.description: Designed to translate warnings into anticipatory actions to help reduce the impact of specific disaster or crisis events. They focus on consolidating available forecasting information and putting procedures in place to ensure that a NS can act ahead of any disaster/crisis. Forecast-based financing is included within the scope of this area.

component_details.title: Cash Based Intervention (CBI)
component_details.description: An effective and flexible way, including all forms of cash and voucher-based assistance, to support people affected by emergencies, maintaining their dignity and choice, while fostering local economies. Cash should also be mainstreamed into other sectors (including Relief, shelter, livelihoods) and services (Logistics, Finance, etc.)

component_details.title: Emergency Needs Assessment
component_details.description: Assess the extent and impact of the damage caused by the disaster/crisis and the degree of vulnerability of the affected population. The first step in any emergency response, such an assessment will identify the needs that require external intervention and the gaps to be filled. It is a vital component of the programme-planning process.

component_details.title: Affected population selection
component_details.description: Identification and selection of target Affected population for interventions, using a pre-defined set of criteria based on need and vulnerability. This includes consideration of specific vulnerabilities such as disability, age and gender.

component_details.title: Emergency Operations Centre (EOC)
component_details.description: A central command and control facility responsible for carrying out disaster/crisis management functions at a strategic level in an emergency situation. The common functions are to collect and analyze data; facilitate decision making that protects life and livelihoods; and disseminate those decisions to all concerned agencies and individuals. Generally located at the headquarter level of an organization.

component_details.title: Information Management (IM)
component_details.description: Ability to manage information including requesting, receiving, analyzing and disseminating as per its procedures and partner requirements (IFRC and public authorities in particular). There should be a clear digital/paper trail that documents what, when and how the NS has acted and provides key information for the development of Emergency Plan of Actions. Includes IM between levels, between departments and Situational Reports, mapping, visualisation of data, GO platform (IFRC).

component_details.title: Testing and Learning
component_details.description: Drills and Simulations allow the organization to test, identify and learn from the results of these type of exercises and incorporate learning into future preparedness and response planning.

component_details.title: Activation of regional and international support
component_details.description: Procedures for requesting and accepting regional and international support in operations, including triggering coordination mechanisms for funding, materials and human resources deployments.

component_details.title: CHEMICAL, BIOLOGICAL, RADIOLOGICAL AND NUCLEAR (CBRN) EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS
MANAGEMENT OF DEAD BODIES TO FACILITATE THEIR IDENTIFICATION
NS-specific areas of intervention
component_details.description: Sector-specific or services provided by the NS in case of emergencies, it is in line with the NS mandate and legislation in country. It includes Community Based DP/DRR, Evacuation, Health in Emergencies, Epidemic and Pandemic, First aid, WASH, Food security and Livelihoods, Search and rRescue, Shelter, Management of dead bodies, RFL, Transition to recovery, and CBRN preparedness.

component_details.title: Coordination with External Agencies and NGOs
component_details.description: Mechanism that facilitates coordination and collaboration with Non-Governmental Organization (NGO), both local and international NGOs, civil society organizations (CSOs) and United Nations agencies in country.

component_details.title: Civil Military Relations
component_details.description: Dialogue and interaction with military actors, essential to protect and promote humanitarian principles, avoid competition, minimize inconsistency and, when appropriate, pursue common goals.

component_details.title: Coordination with Movement
component_details.description: Mechanisms that facilitate the coordination with ICRC, IFRC, and PNS in-country.

component_details.title: Coordination with authorities
component_details.description: Mechanism that facilitates coordination and cooperation with local and national authorities. It is connected to the NS auxiliary role for humanitarian assistance.

component_details.title: Coordination with local community level responders
component_details.description: Engagement with Community Disaster Response Teams (CDRTs), through training, coordination, and the development of community disaster preparedness and response plans.

component_details.title: Cooperation with private sector
component_details.description: Mechanism that allows cooperation with private sector that often plays a strong role in response, particularly if there is impact on their staff and businesses. There is often a willingness to donate goods and services. Advance agreements help to expedite response actions.

component_details.title: Staff and volunteer management
component_details.description: Well-functioning staff and volunteer management systems and practices allow for effective recruitment, supervision, support and encouragement of staff and volunteers.

component_details.title: Safety and security management
component_details.description: Addresses policy and procedures to ensure the safety of staff and volunteers. This include awareness, effective recruitment, training and management processes in place to ensure that personnel are capable of undertaking the roles demanded of them (from NS operational, management and leaders) according to the Stay Safe (IFRC) and Safer Access (ICRC). Based on safer access framework, including concepts of access, perception, identification and acceptance, and protection and violence prevention.

component_details.title: Communication in emergencies
component_details.description: Incorporates a system of public messaging to enable the NS to share timely, accurate information before, during, and after a disaster or crisis.

component_details.title: Operations Monitoring, Evaluation, Reporting and Learning
component_details.description: The PMERL is designed to implement a results-based planning, monitoring and evaluation system that provides an evidence base of NS performance, including relevance, efficiency, effectiveness, sustainability and impact. A reliable and trusted organization is accountable, providing transparent and timely information and building systems to strengthen data collection and reporting. It is data-driven, analytical and results-based.

component_details.title: Finance and Admin policy and emergency procedures
component_details.description: Overall budgeting, accounting, treasury, assets, financial reporting and financial services operations. it also includes the efficient delivery , cost effective and timely services to the NS. Pre-approved, auditable, expedited procedures that allow for flexibility during a disaster/crisis. These must meet transparency, oversight and accountability standards. Procedures may include faster approval processes, fewer signatures, different authority levels. The Emergency Procedures are activated for a specific period of time.

component_details.title: Information and Communication Technology (ICT)
component_details.description: Refers to technologies that provide access to information through telecommunications. This includes the Internet, wireless networks, mobile phones, radios and other communication mediums.

component_details.title: Resource Mobilisation
component_details.description: A documented strategy for raising domestic funds from the government, private sector, general public and other in-country actors to support the national society’s response. This would include allocation of responsibilities, practical mechanisms for accepting funds and for being accountable on funds.

component_details.description: Dialogue and interaction with military actors, essential to protect and promote humanitarian principles, avoid competition, minimize inconsistency and, when appropriate, pursue common goals.

component_details.title: Coordination with Movement
component_details.description: Mechanisms that facilitate the coordination with ICRC, IFRC, and PNS in-country.

component_details.title: Coordination with authorities
component_details.description: Mechanism that facilitates coordination and cooperation with local and national authorities. It is connected to the NS auxiliary role for humanitarian assistance.

component_details.title: Coordination with local community level responders
component_details.description: Engagement with Community Disaster Response Teams (CDRTs), through training, coordination, and the development of community disaster preparedness and response plans.

component_details.title: Cooperation with private sector
component_details.description: Mechanism that allows cooperation with private sector that often plays a strong role in response, particularly if there is impact on their staff and businesses. There is often a willingness to donate goods and services. Advance agreements help to expedite response actions.

component_details.title: Staff and volunteer management
component_details.description: Well-functioning staff and volunteer management systems and practices allow for effective recruitment, supervision, support and encouragement of staff and volunteers.

component_details.title: Safety and security management
component_details.description: Addresses policy and procedures to ensure the safety of staff and volunteers. This include awareness, effective recruitment, training and management processes in place to ensure that personnel are capable of undertaking the roles demanded of them (from NS operational, management and leaders) according to the Stay Safe (IFRC) and Safer Access (ICRC). Based on safer access framework, including concepts of access, perception, identification and acceptance, and protection and violence prevention.

component_details.title: Communication in emergencies
component_details.description: Incorporates a system of public messaging to enable the NS to share timely, accurate information before, during, and after a disaster or crisis.

component_details.title: Operations Monitoring, Evaluation, Reporting and Learning
component_details.description: The PMERL is designed to implement a results-based planning, monitoring and evaluation system that provides an evidence base of NS performance, including relevance, efficiency, effectiveness, sustainability and impact. A reliable and trusted organization is accountable, providing transparent and timely information and building systems to strengthen data collection and reporting. It is data-driven, analytical and results-based.

component_details.title: Finance and Admin policy and emergency procedures
component_details.description: Overall budgeting, accounting, treasury, assets, financial reporting and financial services operations. it also includes the efficient delivery , cost effective and timely services to the NS. Pre-approved, auditable, expedited procedures that allow for flexibility during a disaster/crisis. These must meet transparency, oversight and accountability standards. Procedures may include faster approval processes, fewer signatures, different authority levels. The Emergency Procedures are activated for a specific period of time.

component_details.title: Information and Communication Technology (ICT)
component_details.description: Refers to technologies that provide access to information through telecommunications. This includes the Internet, wireless networks, mobile phones, radios and other communication mediums.

component_details.title: Resource Mobilisation
component_details.description: A documented strategy for raising domestic funds from the government, private sector, general public and other in-country actors to support the national society’s response. This would include allocation of responsibilities, practical mechanisms for accepting funds and for being accountable on funds.

component_details.title: RC auxiliary role, Mandate and Law
component_details.description: A constitutional reference to the role of the NS in responding to disasters and crises, which may be legislated or included/ recognized in the National Response System.

component_details.title: DRM Strategy
component_details.description: An outline of the overall goal that the NS seeks to achieve in its disaster and crisis response operations. The goal considers: context analysis, ongoing/regular all-hazards risk assessments: it may define the target proportion of affected population that will be reached, and a definition of the areas/sectors where a NS will usually respond during an emergency.

component_responses.notes: strategy is there, but dissemination is an issue (EZEN)

component_details.title: DRM Policy
component_details.description: Reflects the NS mission, RCRC principles and mandate. It acknowledges other relevant NS policies, and aligns with the government policy (where applicable), incorporating the general rules that the NS will obey in order to achieve something (i.e mandate, strategy, etc.)

component_details.title: DRM Laws, Advocacy and Dissemination
component_details.description: Designed to support the NS in improving legal preparedness for disasters and crisis and to promote the use of the IDRL Guidelines in order to reduce human vulnerability.

component_details.title: Quality and accountability
component_details.description: Describes the essential elements of principled, accountable, and high-quality humanitarian action. The RCRC Movement provides support to the most vulnerable people in line with the Sphere and CHS standards, Code of Conduct for the RCRC Movement and NGOS in Disaster Relief and the Code for Good Partnership of the RCRC Movement, Gender & Diversity, inclusion and protection, BPI/ Do no harm, context-sensitive analysis, violence prevention, accountability to affected population and disability considerations, Community engagement and accountability (CEA).

component_details.title: Business continuity
component_details.description: A strategy to counter any potential or anticipated obstacles to effective functioning of the NS, with an eye to ensuring that personnel and assets are protected and able to function in the event of a disaster/crisis.

component_responses.notes: need to operationalize the emergency fund

component_details.title: Emergency Response Procedures (SOPs)
component_details.description: Written guidelines that describe duties and rights of personnel, command structures, coordination with other organizations, and reporting requirements, etc. Includes detailed organogram, decision-making flow chart, and defined roles and responsibilities.

component_responses.notes: emergency response protocol exists (2012) but it needs to be disseminated.

component_details.title: Response and recovery planning
component_details.description: A documented set of procedures for the disaster/crisis response and recovery process. Including use of local capacities, transition to recovery, type of activities and serivices provided during response and recovery activities and exit strategies, procedures for DREF & EA, and templates for planning, budgeting and accessing funds.

component_details.title: Pre-disaster meetings and agreements
component_details.description: A commitment to arrange meetings and agreements with Movement stakeholders and external actors to identify, plan for and address gaps for any upcoming disaster season (e.g. monsoon, floods or cyclones, or for any generic disaster/crisis event (e.g Epidemic, pandemic, confilict situations). Pre-disaster agreements should set out each partner's role in the event of a disaster/crisis.

component_details.title: Hazard, Context and Risk Analysis, Monitoring and Early Warning
component_details.description: Describes how the NS monitors and maps past, present and potential hazards, disasters and crises (e.g. hazard, vulnerability assessments, gathering information from communities and government authorities) and systematically evaluates the damage that could be caused by a potential disaster/crisis, the frequency, severity of the impact, and the alert the relevant areas to scale the preparedness actions to reduce population vulnerability.

component_details.title: Scenario planning

component_details.title: Preparedness plans and budgets
component_details.description: Plans identifying organisational resources, determining roles and responsibilities, and developing policies, procedures and activities in order to reach a level of preparedness to be able to respond effectively to a disaster or crisis. Budgets ensure that the necessary financial support is secured to allow capacities to be built and readiness maintained.
