component_details.title: Early Action Mechanisms
component_details.description: Designed to translate warnings into anticipatory actions to help reduce the impact of specific disaster or crisis events. They focus on consolidating available forecasting information and putting procedures in place to ensure that a NS can act ahead of any disaster/crisis. Forecast-based financing is included within the scope of this area.

component_responses.notes: La SN actualmente no tiene procedimientos de alerta temprana, sin embargo se realizan tarea puntuales y existe interés en trabajar la línea

component_details.title: Cash Based Intervention (CBI)
component_details.description: An effective and flexible way, including all forms of cash and voucher-based assistance, to support people affected by emergencies, maintaining their dignity and choice, while fostering local economies. Cash should also be mainstreamed into other sectors (including Relief, shelter, livelihoods) and services (Logistics, Finance, etc.)

component_responses.climate_environmental_considerations: No
component_responses.notes: La SN trabaja en CBI en respuesta de emergencia con fondos internacionales, se cuenta con kits generados en la SN y actualizados con las lecciones aprendidas.

component_details.title: Emergency Needs Assessment
component_details.description: Assess the extent and impact of the damage caused by the disaster/crisis and the degree of vulnerability of the affected population. The first step in any emergency response, such an assessment will identify the needs that require external intervention and the gaps to be filled. It is a vital component of the programme-planning process.

component_responses.climate_environmental_considerations: No
component_responses.notes: Existen plantillas y falta formación para equipos de evaluación

component_details.title: Coordination with External Agencies and NGOs
component_details.description: Mechanism that facilitates coordination and collaboration with Non-Governmental Organization (NGO), both local and international NGOs, civil society organizations (CSOs) and United Nations agencies in country.

component_responses.climate_environmental_considerations: Necesita mejorar. Se comenzó ha identificado socios estratégicos mediante el proyecto Irish Aid. Participación en reunión de difusión de evaluación nacional del riesgo climático, elabordo en cooperación con el centro del clima
component_responses.notes: El SINAE está trabajando para conformar una instancia de comunidad humanitaria en el país, por el momento no existe. Existen acuerdos de colaboración, como el del Movimiento Scout del Uruguay.

component_details.title: Civil Military Relations
component_details.description: Dialogue and interaction with military actors, essential to protect and promote humanitarian principles, avoid competition, minimize inconsistency and, when appropriate, pursue common goals.

component_responses.notes: El contacto con el ejército es mediante el SINAE, CDE Y CECOED

component_details.title: Coordination with local community level responders
component_details.description: Engagement with Community Disaster Response Teams (CDRTs), through training, coordination, and the development of community disaster preparedness and response plans.

component_responses.climate_environmental_considerations: Se comenzó realizando experiencias pilotos, como en Soriano, San José, Paysandú. (Proyectos comenzados)
component_responses.notes: No se cuenta con equipos comunitarios de respuesta (CDRT) identificados, no existen procedimientos para la gestión de procedimientos formales entre la filial y la comunidad.

component_details.title: Cooperation with private sector
component_details.description: Mechanism that allows cooperation with private sector that often plays a strong role in response, particularly if there is impact on their staff and businesses. There is often a willingness to donate goods and services. Advance agreements help to expedite response actions.

component_responses.notes: Los socios firman documentos para asegurar la transparencia de los activos y hacer un buen uso del emblema.

component_details.title: Coordination with Movement
component_details.description: Mechanisms that facilitate the coordination with ICRC, IFRC, and PNS in-country.

component_responses.climate_environmental_considerations: Se tiene conocimiento de la existencia y se ha contactado con el Centro Climático pero actualmente no existen proyectos conjuntos (Comunicaciones formales, Dref Sequías)
component_responses.notes: Se dan todos estos pasos, está muy mecanizado, pero faltaría documentar los procesos

component_details.title: Coordination with authorities
component_details.description: Mechanism that facilitates coordination and cooperation with local and national authorities. It is connected to the NS auxiliary role for humanitarian assistance.

component_responses.climate_environmental_considerations: Existe parcialmente. Cuando se coordina con el Sinae, ellos están involucrados, sin embargo, no existen acuerdos o reuniones directamente con los entes
component_responses.notes: Existen procedimientos no formalizados, sin embargo se detecta la necesidad de firma de acuerdos de entendimientos y cooperación de trabajos

▫ A clear logistics function exists within PRC, managing procurement, warehousing, transportation and fleet. However, it is noted that many of the PRC service departments (e.g. DMS, Health, WASH) have their own parallel logistic functions. ▫ Procurement lacks uniformity in the procedural management, each department appears to have its own way of doing procurement. E.g. WASH unit has a focal person for all WASH related procurement and logistics, who centralizes and processes documents to ensure coherence with the organization’s procedural uniformity. ▫ Procurement team suggested regular orientation/training of new staff on procedures and timelines as well as the broad logistics functions at the chapter level. ▫ As per the desk review, there seem to be clear SOPs and procedures in place, with specific reporting lines and action point e.g. PRC‐PROC 03‐02 Procurement of Goods and Services Procedure which includes a flow for emergency procurement need. However, most procedures reviewed refer to "normal times/business as usual situation”. ▫ Logistics manual developed and well circulated NS wide. However, needs improvement in warehouse management, fleet maintenance and suppliers’ identification with established agreements for bulk purchase during disasters. There are no contracts/framework agreements in place for frequent or cyclic procurement. Survey results indicate there are still some gapsto be addressed in terms of long lead time and centralized and heavy approval processes. ▫ Logistics capacity varies from chapter to chapter. ▫ It was noted that delivery of supplies from NHQ to Chapters has been timely during the past disasters. However, electronics (laptop/projector) essential in reporting and dissemination purposes could take 2‐3 months to be delivered. Survey responses also indicated facing some supply chain difficulties due to geographical landscape.

component_details.title: Staff and volunteer management
component_details.description: Well-functioning staff and volunteer management systems and practices allow for effective recruitment, supervision, support and encouragement of staff and volunteers.

component_responses.notes: ▫ PRC has developed Volunteer Services manual (still in draft form but on its final printing stage for circulation nationwide. Soft copies will be uploaded in PMER dashboard regarding Knowledge Management Module. It is undergoing copyright registration.). ▫ Draft Volunteer Services manual stipulates that a database of skilled/specialized volunteers will be maintained and updated regularly. It outlines proceduresfor mobilization and retention of volunteers as well as the Code of Conduct to be signed by all NS volunteers. ▫ PRC takes measures to protect staff and volunteers during epidemics by limiting their risk of exposure. ▫ NS has expedited procedures to incorporate spontaneous volunteers during emergencies which meet minimum screening procedures and comply with its volunteer in emergency policy. ▫ Survey findings indicate that no consolidated and accessible database exists showing HR/VR information, trainings, capacities, etc. Databases exist in many different locations among different departments. NHQ confirms that the OVD exists and is available under the PMER dashboard. ▫ Some chapters have their own system in which every response unit can recruit, train and manage its own volunteers independent of other units. ▫ HR has a roster of all staff, containing general information (contact details, name, gender, religion) but this database is incomplete, and only updated on an ad hoc basis upon request of management. ▫ The importance to revaluate recruitment and retention strategies due to high turnover of staff and volunteers was highlighted in multiple survey responses. ▫ Volunteers need to pay their own insurance which may discourage volunteer engagement

component_details.title: Safety and security management
component_details.description: Addresses policy and procedures to ensure the safety of staff and volunteers. This include awareness, effective recruitment, training and management processes in place to ensure that personnel are capable of undertaking the roles demanded of them (from NS operational, management and leaders) according to the Stay Safe (IFRC) and Safer Access (ICRC). Based on safer access framework, including concepts of access, perception, identification and acceptance, and protection and violence prevention.

component_responses.notes: ▫ PRC NHQ has an internal Safety Security TWG and a focal point (FP) for Safety and Security matters. Chapters do not have dedicated staff to oversee this however, the responsibility is with the Chapter Administrators. ▫ PRC implements Safer Access and has appropriate security systems in place to protect staff and volunteers. Safer Access and security protocols are integrated in volunteers’ trainings. ▫ PRC managers completed Security management training. ▫ At chapter level, PRC is actively disseminating Safer Access among its responders and reminds them of Code of Conduct during deployments. ▫ Volunteer services manual contains a section mentioning Safer Access: 6.4.5 Volunteers shall observe the policies and guideline concerning “Safer Access” particularly in areas affected by armed conflict. Refer to ICRC Safer Access Manual  ‐ this indicates that there is a Safer Access policy in place. ▫ Safety and Security FP keeps tracks of security issues in the field. However, there are still gaps in regular reporting of security concerns as these are only submitted on as‐needed basis. In addition, there is no clear collection of data related to safety and security incidents

component_details.title: Communication in emergencies
component_details.description: Incorporates a system of public messaging to enable the NS to share timely, accurate information before, during, and after a disaster or crisis.

component_responses.notes: ▫ PRC's Chairman and Secretary General are the official designated spokespersons in an emergency – based on desk review. ▫ Survey findings indicate that external communication is strong. In times of emergencies,social media is used widely and efficiently to disseminate information to public. In addition, high quality press releases are issued. ▫ Communications department has good relationships with media contacts to correct misinformation when it occurs. ▫ Public awareness messages are also shared with staff during emergencies. ▫ Reliance on technology can be a barrier, especially if there is internet/phone disruption during an emergency. ▫ PRC has a limited number of VSATs available to install during disasters to restore communication links in the most damaged areas. ▫ PRC has in‐house Tower Public Announcement System which is not implemented due to limited funds.

component_details.title: Operations Monitoring, Evaluation, Reporting and Learning
component_details.description: The PMERL is designed to implement a results-based planning, monitoring and evaluation system that provides an evidence base of NS performance, including relevance, efficiency, effectiveness, sustainability and impact. A reliable and trusted organization is accountable, providing transparent and timely information and building systems to strengthen data collection and reporting. It is data-driven, analytical and results-based.

component_responses.notes: ▫ PRC has designated MEAL staff at NHQ and reporting focal persons are deployed in field during operations, as needed.  Some templates, forms, and guidelines are in place. ▫ NS operates an M&E system at the field level to collect, manage and report on data to branches, NHQ and IFRC against the set objectives of the operation. ▫ Operation Sheet is used to monitor all response actions and includes damage and needs, 3W, deployments, situational updates, and other operational data. The data is contained in a single source (i.e. excel) and accessible on Google Drive by all NHQ DMS Staff. ▫ Operational plans are updated with more accurate figures from the damage and needs assessments. ▫ The Learning component seems to be missing i.e. learnings from the past operations are not widely shared or incorporated in applicable policies and/or plans. ▫ Reporting flow during a disaster response can be unclear at times with staff reporting the need to respect lines of management and chain of command ▫ Data collection seemsto remain an issue. Lack of a specific template leads to duplication of data and burdensome reporting on the same topic.

component_details.title: Finance and Admin policy and emergency procedures
component_details.description: Overall budgeting, accounting, treasury, assets, financial reporting and financial services operations. it also includes the efficient delivery , cost effective and timely services to the NS. Pre-approved, auditable, expedited procedures that allow for flexibility during a disaster/crisis. These must meet transparency, oversight and accountability standards. Procedures may include faster approval processes, fewer signatures, different authority levels. The Emergency Procedures are activated for a specific period of time.

component_responses.notes: ▫ There is an identified need to improve Finance in Emergencies procedures i.e., a ‘fast‐lane’ to expedite procedures during emergencies. ▫ The desk review identified only one SOP related to finances and logistics (not specifically related to emergencies). Existing procedures and SOPs for "normal" situations are the same as for emergency, leading to delays during an emergency. ▫ NS has trained personnel in Finance and Admin emergency support procedures. Deployment of finance people should be contained at some degree since most chapters are trained on finance procedures. The finance team is continuously conducting finance technical training to services and chapters to strengthen their capacity during operations in terms of the organization’s accounting and finance procedures. ▫ The survey clearly indicates that delays are always prevalent, even in emergencies, due to the very burdensome and centralized procedures. Approvals are required at a very high level ‐ up to Chairman office ‐ which slows down the process. ▫ The WASH Unit has a sector focusing on WASH‐related emergency operations, in order to monitor and expedite the procedure to respond effectively in the affected area. Parallel to other offices or services which have a team focusing on emergencies, establishment of a WASH response team who will prioritize the response will contribute to effective operations.

component_details.title: Information and Communication Technology (ICT)
component_details.description: Refers to technologies that provide access to information through telecommunications. This includes the Internet, wireless networks, mobile phones, radios and other communication mediums.

component_responses.notes: ▫ NS has trained IT support focal points able to support with technical issues and equipment (e.g. computers, software, phones, cameras, GPS) and provide maintenance. ▫ Volunteers should be properly equipped (with mobile phone or walkie talkie) according to the draft Volunteer Services manual. ▫ The survey results indicate that all staff and volunteers are not equally equipped, and that stock is limited. For example, radios are only with DMS. Note that the issuance of assets is based on the functions of the services. Since PRC only have limited stocks and items, and equipment is allocated to services who usually use them. ▫ Not all chapters have stable Internet connection and appropriate equipment (e.g. satellite phone, radio) functioning or belonging. Satellite phones are particularly needed in times of emergencies when all services are disrupted. ▫ Some challenges were noted with approving phone bills during times of emergencies. The approval of the excess phone bill needs to be done by ASG and SG. ▫ IT needs improvement in digital back up of the accounting system. ▫ Availability of knowledge, training and capacity differs from one chapter to another.

component_details.title: Resource Mobilisation
component_details.description: A documented strategy for raising domestic funds from the government, private sector, general public and other in-country actors to support the national society’s response. This would include allocation of responsibilities, practical mechanisms for accepting funds and for being accountable on funds.

component_responses.notes: ▫ PRC fund generation webpage Ways to donate is launched and provides easy access to donate funds through several means. For example, online (PayPal, Lazada, Shopee), Mobile Wallet (Gcash, Paymaya JUSTPAY.TO and Grabrewards) and through the listed banks. ▫ PRC has Fund Generation Policy which defines its roles and responsibilities (including for chapters), guiding principles, and procedures. ▫ PRC relevant staff is aware of general practices for accepting in‐kind goods and this is documented in the Fund Generation Policy. ▫ Although document strategy and new fundraising channels (for example GCash) exist, several findings mention a need for improvements and greater accountability of funds received by donors: private or governmental. ▫ Survey results indicate a strong mobilization of donors in times of major calamities as opposed to other type of emergencies i.e. pandemic. ▫ Some indication that chapters seem to be in favour of having access to fundslocally, by having the ability to fundraise and collectsupport locally.

component_details.title: DRM Laws, Advocacy and Dissemination
component_details.description: Designed to support the NS in improving legal preparedness for disasters and crisis and to promote the use of the IDRL Guidelines in order to reduce human vulnerability.

component_responses.notes:
▫ PRC provided technical support to the executive review of national Philippine 2016 DRM Law and in the legal drafting of the National DRRMC executive review in 2016. As member of DRRMC, PRC and IFRC provided input on Philippines International Humanitarian Assistance (PIHA) Guidelines.  
▫ Pursuant to Republic Act 10121 the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Plan (NDRRMP) 2020‐2030 was established with the support of PRC ‐ therefore indicating an ongoing dedicated support from PRC to the drafting of national DRM law.  
▫ PRC is a member of National DRRMC, and Local DRRMCs (Province, Municipal and City). PRC is a part of any ongoing reviews of DRRM policy at National level.

component_details.title: Quality and accountability
component_details.description: Describes the essential elements of principled, accountable, and high-quality humanitarian action. The RCRC Movement provides support to the most vulnerable people in line with the Sphere and CHS standards, Code of Conduct for the RCRC Movement and NGOS in Disaster Relief and the Code for Good Partnership of the RCRC Movement, Gender & Diversity, inclusion and protection, BPI/ Do no harm, context-sensitive analysis, violence prevention, accountability to affected population and disability considerations, Community engagement and accountability (CEA).

component_responses.notes:
▫ PRC has mechanisms in place to ensure the affected populations are involved in all stages of the response (including decision‐making) to ensure assistance is appropriate and meets their needs and priorities. Various groups e.g. RC 143, RCAT, BARCOM, etc. are established as frontline responders to ensure engagement of affected population.  
▫ PRC also has a telephony project, the Operations Centre, Beneficiary satisfaction survey, the hotline, etc. That are platformsto scale up quality and accountability.  
▫ PRC is currently working on other elements that would improve its response to the most vulnerable including the approval of PSEA and PGI policy. PSEA is included as part of the Performance, Quality and Accountability (PQA) assessment tool for chapters.
▫ In addition, it is noted in the introduction of Contingency Planning Guidelines: "always remembers the Quality and Accountability principles and practices of the Philippine Red Cross."
▫ PRC developed CEA Guidelines. NHQ level training was conducted. The PER Survey findings (collected in January 2022) indicate that there may have been a lack of dissemination and/or training of these guidelines at some levelsin the chapters. However, it was confirmed that copies of CEA Guidelines were fully disseminated and received by all chapters in February 2022 (CEA Post Activity Training Report).
▫ PRC adheres to Sphere Standards to meet the quality of humanitarian needs of the most vulnerable population during emergency.

component_details.title: RC auxiliary role, Mandate and Law
component_details.description: A constitutional reference to the role of the NS in responding to disasters and crises, which may be legislated or included/ recognized in the National Response System.

component_responses.notes:
▫ PRC operates within a strong legal base.
▫ Mandate and role of the NS are clearly articulated in the Republic Act (RA) 10072.
▫ PRC is a recognized partner of the government being the only permanent humanitarian and non‐governmental member of the Disaster Risk Reduction Management Councils (DRRMCs) at the national, regional, provincial, city, municipality, and barangay levels (RA 10121).  
▫ NS mandate is aligned with RCRC Fundamental Principles and reflected in various NS documents (Emergency and Disaster Response Policy (EDR) & SOP Manual).
▫ PRC has a clear role as auxiliary to the government, however, needs to create a stronger advocacy strategy to be better understood by the public on its mandate. The public often perceives PRC as a government agency

component_details.title: DRM Strategy
component_details.description: An outline of the overall goal that the NS seeks to achieve in its disaster and crisis response operations. The goal considers: context analysis, ongoing/regular all-hazards risk assessments: it may define the target proportion of affected population that will be reached, and a definition of the areas/sectors where a NS will usually respond during an emergency.

component_responses.notes:
▫ PRC 2021‐2025 Strategic Plan is the organization‐wide tool having integrated approach with clear and ambitious objectives. The document clearly articulates the goals, strategic objectives, performance indicators with a risk analysis, Disaster Management Strategy (with KPIs) and all relevant services.
▫ The Strategic Plan is disseminated and understood. Further guidance to chapters to contextualize, operatize and report on the Plan with necessary capacities will help its effective implementation – acknowledging there are varying capacities/means of various chapters.
Yearly, operational plan and priority programs are disseminated to all chapters.
▫ 2020 Operational plan and expected deliverables outlines core programs, objectives and outcomes(with KPIs), programs and projects, capacity and previous years deliverables and accomplishments.
▫ Strategic Plan should be aligned with the government strategy/plans especially for the capacity building such as training programs.
▫ Clarity on focal point for climate change would help the implementation of relevant elements of the Plan.

component_details.title: DRM Policy
component_details.description: Reflects the NS mission, RCRC principles and mandate. It acknowledges other relevant NS policies, and aligns with the government policy (where applicable), incorporating the general rules that the NS will obey in order to achieve something (i.e mandate, strategy, etc.)

component_responses.notes:
▫ The 2020 Emergency Disaster Response Policy and SOP Manual broadly defines guiding principles behind overall assistance and activities under emergency response. It outlines legal framework, relationship with movement partners, international agencies and government/military, and it sets general guiding principles for emergency response at various levels ‐ tools and systems.
▫ PER Survey findings indicate a lack of clarity around what the DRM Policy is – as much as there is a lack of understanding of what document exactly stands as the DRM Policy.
▫ Survey findings further points out that an existing Disaster Management Services (DMS) Manual of Operations is outdated with certain provisions during operations missing (for example, augmentation, provision of relief). Manual is currently under review to address new challenges to date based on lessons learned most recently i.e., weather conditions, needed equipment, operations and communications, radio deployment, etc.

component_details.title: Scenario planning
component_details.description: A set of practical operation plans that closely mirror the generic disaster or crisis response plan but are tailored to a specific hazard type (e.g. earthquake, dengue epidemic, floods, cyclone) and a specific scenario (i.e. number of people affected, their locations and other important factors).

component_responses.notes:
▫ The Survey findings show that some mechanisms exist as well as contingency planning for specific hazards such as typhoons.
▫ Contingency Plans (CPs) exist at chapter levels based on their respective specific situation and the desk review confirms the existence of guidelines to develop a CP (2019).  
▫ A Disaster Preparedness Response Technical Working Group (DPR TWG) was in place until end of 2021 to develop CPs.  
▫ Survey finding suggests that practical operational plans are not in place at different levels especially at some chapters.
▫ The survey indicates the existence of a mechanism at NHQ level supporting branches to develop scenario planning, but it is not widely known/used.

component_details.title: Risk management
component_details.description: A mapping of the potential risks in every area, along with its related mitigation measures. Including financial, reputational, organizational risks etc.

component_responses.notes:
▫ There is reference to establishing PRC Risk assessment team in the context of COVID‐19. It is a group of 5 people ensuring that screening for test related to COVID is evaluated and endorsed, discuss testing guidelines, quarantine and protocols related to COVID 19.
▫ Risks are recognized and risk mapping is documented in the Strategic Plan, but there is no specific mechanism in place to address them. Survey finding indicates that there is no regular and systematic mapping of financial, reputational and organizational risks yet in place. The survey results further indicate that there may be a reputational risk linked to the
fact that the PRC is working with the government and at times might be perceived being directly associated with it.  
▫ Tight financial controls (e.g., signing authorities) and layers of administrative processes acts to reduce financial risks are in place however, this increases operational risks (e.g., delays).

component_details.title: Preparedness plans and budgets
component_details.description: Plans identifying organisational resources, determining roles and responsibilities, and developing policies, procedures and activities in order to reach a level of preparedness to be able to respond effectively to a disaster or crisis. Budgets ensure that the necessary financial support is secured to allow capacities to be built and readiness maintained.

component_responses.notes:
▫ PRC has a trained focal point for disaster preparedness.
▫ PRC has many institutional preparedness and response capacity projects (in DMS) but also within other departments.
▫ Preparedness actions are updated every second year as stipulated under EDR Policy and SOP Manual – as such, it should be planned in 2022 accordingly.
▫ PRC has initial planned budget set for disaster preparedness and emergency, however, there appears to be difficulty in accessing and releasing the funds (long processes leading to delays). There is currently ongoing review of Internal communications and coordination system
within PRC to address this.
▫ NHQ prepositions support to chapters before a disaster strikes through regular inventory of resources and capacities of chapters. However, the survey findings indicate a gap in preparedness between NHQ and the chapters  ‐  especially when it comes to budget. Plans are reportedly mainly made at NHQ levels which may create a gap with regard to the
actual needs of a specific chapter for preparedness.

component_details.title: Business continuity
component_details.description: A strategy to counter any potential or anticipated obstacles to effective functioning of the NS, with an eye to ensuring that personnel and assets are protected and able to function in the event of a disaster/crisis.

component_responses.notes:
▫ Survey findings display thatsome chapters have business continuity plans for some specific hazards/risks which are not updated, while others do not.  
▫ Business Continuity Plan for COVID‐19 exists and is valid nation‐wide.
▫ During 2022 Assessment findings validation session, participants highlighted the need to have comprehensive Business Continuity Plan in place (covering multiple hazards/risks).

component_details.title: Emergency Response Procedures (SOPs)
component_details.description: Written guidelines that describe duties and rights of personnel, command structures, coordination with other organizations, and reporting requirements, etc. Includes detailed organogram, decision-making flow chart, and defined roles and responsibilities.

component_responses.notes:
▫ The EDR Policy and SOP Manual in many ways implies the existence of ER procedures and showcase a structure in place. It includes decision making flowchart which assigns decision making responsibility accordingly at each level. Selected SOPs are available, for example epidemic response, emergency assessment and response planning.
▫ 2020 EDR Policy and SOP manual contains an organigram outlining role and responsibilities, however, contact details are missing.  
▫ Communication and information requests from NHQ to chapters is duplicated at times, with different NHQ departments contacting chapters requesting similar information.
▫ Survey findings indicate the lack of clarity when it comes to this component. Some seem to know about the existence of procedures, but they are out‐dated or not approved/not well disseminated.  
▫ Chapter Administrators (CA) are knowledgeable of their roles and responsibilities during a response however, it is not documented but based more on experience and trainings. The risk is that a Chapter may become less functional during a response if the CA is unavailable.
▫ Decision‐making authority and budget approvals often significantly affects the quality and timeliness of service delivery.

component_details.title: Response and recovery planning
component_details.description: A documented set of procedures for the disaster/crisis response and recovery process. Including use of local capacities, transition to recovery, type of activities and serivices provided during response and recovery activities and exit strategies, procedures for DREF & EA, and templates for planning, budgeting and accessing funds.

component_responses.notes:
▫ CEA guidelines highlight that communities to be involved in the disaster response planning.
▫ The DMS manual's SOPs are the reference for the response planning.
▫ The general trends in relation to the consultation method as outlined in the 2018 assessment have remained the same i.e. less consultations happen during response, while longer‐term recovery involves greater consultation.  
▫ PER Survey findings point out that the Barangay Recovery Committees (BaReCom) mentioned in the 2018 assessment do not exist. However, PRC HQ confirmed that it does exist. This needs to be clarified internally to ensure common knowledge.  
▫ Survey findings indicates a gap between NHQ and chapters/volunteers' knowledge of the existence ofsuch planning procedures which points out that while documents exist, they are not known by all or disseminated optimally.  
▫ We could not find any evidence about this component in the desk review.

component_details.title: Pre-disaster meetings and agreements
component_details.description: A commitment to arrange meetings and agreements with Movement stakeholders and external actors to identify, plan for and address gaps for any upcoming disaster season (e.g. monsoon, floods or cyclones, or for any generic disaster/crisis event (e.g Epidemic, pandemic, confilict situations). Pre-disaster agreements should set out each partner's role in the event of a disaster/crisis.

component_responses.notes:
▫ Annual pre‐disaster meetings occur among departments and with RCM partners.
▫ Coordination and agreements exist between PRC, Movement partners and external stakeholders setting out each other's roles and responsibilities (NGOs, INGOs, UN agencies, public authorities etc.).
▫ Before an onset of a disaster meetings are conducted among agencies, discussing strengths and support that can be extended to communities that will be affected.
▫ PIHA guidelines exist at the national level.
▫ Regular pre‐disaster meetings and advisories are done only before a disaster. Regular meetings have been conducted with partners during COVID‐19, improved partners’ 
 communication; this has also been demonstrated during Typhoon Odette.
▫ Survey findings reflect that there is a need to update some of the agreements, as well as some new agreements need to be developed at NHQ and across the chapters.
▫ Survey findings indicate that meetings and agreements exist  ‐ however there still seem to be no framework agreement with suppliers. The validation session expressed that some draft agreements are underway but nothing final.

component_details.title: Hazard, Context and Risk Analysis, Monitoring and Early Warning
component_details.description: Describes how the NS monitors and maps past, present and potential hazards, disasters and crises (e.g. hazard, vulnerability assessments, gathering information from communities and government authorities) and systematically evaluates the damage that could be caused by a potential disaster/crisis, the frequency, severity of the impact, and the alert the relevant areas to scale the preparedness actions to reduce population vulnerability.

component_responses.notes:
▫ PRC has various effective toolsin place and several documentsin the desk review indicate that monitoring and Early Warning is strong for PRC as related to hydrometeorological emergencies (e.g., typhoons, flooding).
▫ PRC monitors disasters and crisesthrough the Operations Centre (OpCen) that provides round the clock monitoring and dissemination of warnings through various channels.
▫ Early warning messaging is distributed through the Hazard App and through other means (WhatsApp, Viber, Phone).
▫ DMS tools such   as   Rapid   Damage   and   Needs   Assessment (RDANA), VCA, and Emergency Needs assessment (ENA – in draft) are available (as referenced in the CEA Guidelines). However, overall, there is a gap between what is existing and what is implemented in the chapters – either a lack of means to implement or training or both. Some chapters do not have the financial means as required.  
▫ PRC does not appear to have a centralized and accessible database/mapping of previous disasters or have completed analysis of trends.
▫ Hazard data is not made widely accessible and shared with chapters and/or other departments.
▫ Risk analysis as part of an emergency assessment is included in the draft 2021 ENA SOPs and Guidelines.

component_details.title: Cash Based Intervention (CBI)
component_details.description: An effective and flexible way, including all forms of cash and voucher-based assistance, to support people affected by emergencies, maintaining their dignity and choice, while fostering local economies. Cash should also be mainstreamed into other sectors (including Relief, shelter, livelihoods) and services (Logistics, Finance, etc.)

component_responses.notes: ▫ Cash transfer program is part of PRC’s services under Disaster Management Services. ▫ PRC has agreements with financial service providers; LBC can cater 200 beneficiaries per day while Globe and PhilPost can cater 3,000 beneficiaries in 3 hours. PRC has had agreements since 2012, which have been renewed until today. ▫ PRC has an up‐to‐date database of CBI trained and experienced staff and volunteers at headquarter and branch levels across sectors and support services to implement CBI within the response cycle. ▫ 2020 EDR Policy & SOP Manual mentions cash resources for operations and cash transfer programming flow (annex 4.5)  ‐  and Finance and RedRose (RR). However, a need to simplify and develop user‐friendly procedures was identified in the survey results. ▫ Survey results noted that availability of funds can be challenging, and chapters might have to pay from their own funds or may have to wait a considerable amount of time before funds become available. ▫ Survey results noted the absence of protocol in terms of Cash and Vouchers Assistance (CVA). ▫ SOP and Guidelines for Cash Transfer Program are in working draft. Voucher system is still not yet being utilized. PRC needs to create centralized team to handle VCA. ▫ Needs to strengthen implementation of VCA in other sectors, such as WASH. ▫ PRC has been implementing cash assistance during response and recovery phases, though it still relies on hard cash that needs to be withdrawn from banks, and raises security concerns (temporary safekeeping, transport). ▫ The findings further indicate that this may be different from one chapter to the next, as there is, at the chapter level, a Disaster Response Fund (DRF), established through local memo, is advanced to CSR‐DMS and can be used anytime subject to replenishment once depleted or threshold is met. ▫ There are concerns that scaling‐up CTP for large emergencies would be challenging due to financial, administrative, logistics and IT bottlenecks, as well as not having procedures to mitigate security risk. ▫ Guidelines for Cash in Envelopes exist (memo 2020‐03‐56) outlining the steps, responsible persons and special considerations and control procedures.

component_details.title: Emergency Needs Assessment
component_details.description: Assess the extent and impact of the damage caused by the disaster/crisis and the degree of vulnerability of the affected population. The first step in any emergency response, such an assessment will identify the needs that require external intervention and the gaps to be filled. It is a vital component of the programme-planning process.

component_responses.notes: ▫ PRC has a trained multi‐sectorial emergency assessment team available to deploy in a timely manner. ▫ The Rapid Damage Needs Assessment form is used at primary stages of the assessment which is then reported to NHQ through DMS and OpCen. ▫ PRC guidelines for emergency needs assessment on its final draft for approval. Tools such as the PRC SOP and Guidelines for Disaster Needs Assessment exist. ▫ 2020 EDR SOP contains templates collecting several types of data related to an emergency needs assessment, as well as the elements related to rapid deployment of teams on the ground. So does the Contingency Planning guidebook. These manuals contain information related to emergencies and needs assessments in various forms (templates or flow chart for communication lines). ▫ However, the survey findings reveal that this component still needs improvement in numerous ways. For example, the slow submission of reports from affected areas and need for faster RDNA was flagged.

component_details.title: Affected population selection
component_details.description: Identification and selection of target Affected population for interventions, using a pre-defined set of criteria based on need and vulnerability. This includes consideration of specific vulnerabilities such as disability, age and gender.

component_responses.notes: ▫ NS communicates selection criteria to the affected population using preferred communication channels and involves community leaders/representatives. ▫ PRC uses Barangay Recovery Committees (BaReCom) to aid in the identification of those affected. Results are presented back to communities at assemblies. ▫ Data collection templates exist in CEA guidelines and EDR Policy. ▫ The draft Volunteers services manual implies that appropriate training is delivered to allow volunteers to fill these templates properly. ▫ Survey resultsindicate thatselection of beneficiariesis done according to criteria however, findings also indicate that it is varying between chapters,some doing this efficiently in coordination with local authorities to avoid duplication, others mention lack of consistency

component_details.title: Emergency Operations Centre (EOC)
component_details.description: A central command and control facility responsible for carrying out disaster/crisis management functions at a strategic level in an emergency situation. The common functions are to collect and analyze data; facilitate decision making that protects life and livelihoods; and disseminate those decisions to all concerned agencies and individuals. Generally located at the headquarter level of an organization.

component_responses.notes: ▫ PRC’s EOC, once activated, is strong RCM example of a cross‐ departmental central command and control facility responsible for carrying out disaster/crisis management functions. The EOC is in part related to the physical space, but its strength reflects the team coordination and collaboration. ▫ There is dedicated space for operational management to convene. ▫ There are assigned staff for ensuring EOC functionality on a 24/7 basis. ▫ The Emergency Dispatch standards guidelines is a strong document used as standard procedures for the EOC ‐ called PRC OpCen. ▫ The guidelines also indicate strong organization and “state‐of‐the‐art” facilities to handle emergencies. Job descriptions, operating procedures and link to national legislation are also part of the guidelines, further indicating the strength of this part. ▫ The survey results indicate that this component is strong however, it is to be noted that communication lines between the chapters and NHQ could be enhanced. ▫ Data management is reported to be needing some improvement.

component_details.title: Information Management (IM)
component_details.description: Ability to manage information including requesting, receiving, analyzing and disseminating as per its procedures and partner requirements (IFRC and public authorities in particular). There should be a clear digital/paper trail that documents what, when and how the NS has acted and provides key information for the development of Emergency Plan of Actions. Includes IM between levels, between departments and Situational Reports, mapping, visualisation of data, GO platform (IFRC).

component_responses.notes: ▫ The desk review did not reveal any evidence for this component ▫ There are some examples of good practices of IM within PRC (e.g. DMS) but in general IM needs to be further developed. ▫ Departments have their own individual databases of information (e.g. volunteer, staff, trainings, deployments) which collect information in different manners, some incomplete other updated without predictable frequency. PRC mentioned examples such as OVD (One volunteer database), PMER Dashboard, and knowledge management dashboard. ▫ Survey findings also indicate some information sharing challenges across the organization between NHQ and chapters including repeated information/ data requests coming from different departments. It was also noted that different services and chapters sometimes restrict access to their data. ▫ No IM guidelines could be found either, indicating a gap in the mechanisms to share information.

component_details.title: Testing and Learning
component_details.description: Drills and Simulations allow the organization to test, identify and learn from the results of these type of exercises and incorporate learning into future preparedness and response planning.

component_responses.notes: ▫ The Survey results indicate that PRC regularly tests its early action and response mechanism through simulations and tabletop exercises. However, there appears to be no formal testing schedule. ▫ PRC is involved in national‐level drill exercises with public authorities. At chapters levels, the drills are usually conducted in coordination with respective LGU's. However, it is not common across all the chapters. ▫ Some of the examples of the exercises mentioned are Earthquake drill that was organized in the past (highlighted in the desk review), tabletop exercise to test CP for typhoon (mentioned in the survey). ▫ Lessons learned after a drill or simulation are mostly not shared, indicating either that such documentation is not done (unlikely) or not disseminated (indicating a gap in terms of IM).

component_details.title: Activation of regional and international support
component_details.description: Procedures for requesting and accepting regional and international support in operations, including triggering coordination mechanisms for funding, materials and human resources deployments.

component_responses.notes: ▫ PRC is well seasoned when it comes to using international coordination and funding mechanisms. International Relations with Strategic Partnership Office (IRSPO) oversees the Activation of Regional and International support. ▫ PRC NHQ coordinates activation of regional and internationalsupport. NS has a significant experience of available IFRC/ICRC supports from past emergencies. ▫ Following Haiyan Response, government formed Philippines International Humanitarian Assistance Cluster (PIHAC) as a "one‐stop shop/welcome centre" to facilitate international assistance. PRC has a role in PIHAC. ▫ Survey results noted that PRC SOPs include procedures to request and incorporate regional and globalsupport. Desk review did not find SOPs or guidelines to further validate this finding.

component_details.title: CHEMICAL, BIOLOGICAL, RADIOLOGICAL AND NUCLEAR (CBRN) EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS

component_responses.notes:
▫ Survey findings demonstrate the absence of guidelines, training and equipment to deal with CBRN hazards.   
▫ Ambulance services as a mean of evacuation of the wounded is available but can only be effective if provided with appropriate PPEs which are not readily available.
▫ Small elements of CBRN protocol are mentioned (e.g. necessity to have PPE and trained personnel to respond in biological hazard) but no plan to address is indicated.
▫ There is no indication that a plan has been developed in coordination with authorities or other stakeholders.

▫ PRC DMS has experience in handling livelihood projects as part of recovery and rehabilitation programs.
▫ No documents described livelihood security and safety nets as one of the available services.
▫ Livelihood planning is present but later in the recovery phase ‐ up to 3‐4 months after a disaster. Assessments are likely to be thorough and supporting local communities in their recovery from a disaster situation.
▫ There may be a gap in the provision of SOPs and guidelines as indicated by survey results

▫ Desk review indicates that NFI kits are available as standard relief items
however, there is no SOP for chapters on how to obtain them specifically.  
▫ Survey results highlight that this service is available more specifically in early recovery and recovery. This is often in partnership with PNS and other partners.
▫ There is a need to strengthen the awareness around available training  
▫ DMS guidelines are reported to be in place forthe supply of Shelteritems.

component_details.title: MANAGEMENT OF DEAD BODIES TO FACILITATE THEIR IDENTIFICATION

component_responses.notes:
▫ PRC is a member of the leading agencies in charge of this service as pe the National Disaster Response Plan within the NDRRMC.
▫ PRC relies on government programs and LGUs guidance. Distribution of cadaver bags is done by some chapters.  
▫ Memo 2020‐04‐36 outlines specifications on PRC Cadaver bags in line with Department of Health and Management of the dead and missing cluster.
▫ Department of Interior and Local Government (DILG) Memo 2016‐139 (Oct 2016) is a policy content and guidelines stipulating that the DILG is the lead agency for the management of the dead and missing persons cluster.  
▫ PRC refers to the Sept 2020 WHO Interim guidance for the infection prevention and control for the safe management of a dead body in the context of COVID‐19
▫ Some staff and volunteers of PRC were trained on Management of the Dead Bodies (MDB) and are considered responders by the LDRRMC.
However, very few people were trained, the rollout of the technical skills is quite slow due to the dependency on Department of the Interior and Local Government. There is an identified lack of training and supplies to perform this task optimally.
▫ Othersurvey responses mentioned that NS can assist in the MDB through preserving the dignity of the deceased by enveloping the body in the body bag and in extreme cases can be refrigerated and referred to LGU/DILG for proper identification.  
▫ Guidelines and equipment (PPEs, relevantsuppliessuch as bags, tags) are needed to perform this activity properly.
▫ There is need to strengthen the awareness around PRC’s role versus national authorities’ mandate as PRC solely is an implementation partner.

▫ PRC is engaged in RFL services at national and chapters’ levels.
▫ RFL is supported by the ICRC due to its presence in the country.  
▫ RFL is one of the activities of Welfare services.  
▫ Focal points are well identified.
▫ Some forms and templates are available in the EDR Policy and SOP manual but without guidelines on how to use and fill them.

▫ The survey highlightsthat PRC is a strong emergency responder however, recovery and rehabilitation programs are not as common unless these are funded by PNS, component partners, or other capable donors.
Findings confirm that due to budgetary constraints, recovery is often a component performed with the support of external stakeholders.
▫ The time between response to recovery is 4‐5 months and is often implemented with support from PNS, in coordination with other sector stakeholders.  
▫ Recovery assessments are known by key staff and happens through thorough assessments and community engagement.
▫ Further training and guidelines may be required here, as indicated by some responses in the surveys.

component_details.title: NS-specific areas of intervention
component_details.description: Sector-specific or services provided by the NS in case of emergencies, it is in line with the NS mandate and legislation in country. It includes Community Based DP/DRR, Evacuation, Health in Emergencies, Epidemic and Pandemic, First aid, WASH, Food security and Livelihoods, Search and rRescue, Shelter, Management of dead bodies, RFL, Transition to recovery, and CBRN preparedness.

component_responses.notes:
▫ Evacuation is part of the PRC response strategy and is present in the different scenarios. Evacuation areas are briefly mentioned in the Contingency Planning Guidebook (but not for epidemic situations). 
▫ Mapping/identification of evacuation areas is done in coordination with LGUs. Due to overpopulation, it’s not always easy to identify the evacuation sites (especially in urban areas). 
▫ Although, select communities have been trained earlier by DMS on evacuation protocols, NS Evacuation services could use more visibility and awareness raising for public knowledge on role of PRC in those services. 
▫ Despite some PRC staff and volunteers being trained to provide evacuation services, more training and awareness is required. 
▫ PRC Evacuation capacity varies across the chapters. 
▫ The Government and LGUs are responsible forthis activity by law and PRC is solely an implementation partner. With this perspective in mind, the assessment highlights the need to strengthen the awareness around this component and PRC’s role versus the national authorities’ role in the implementation of evacuations.

▫ First Aid management is well implemented across the board and is one of the key components of NS emergency response.  
▫ PRC staff and volunteers are receiving an appropriate training, as indicated by the draft Volunteer services manual. Some responders are trained through RCAT and RC143.
▫ PRC has a fleet of 175 ambulances. It has sets of guidelines and laws supporting it, and First Aid is part of the deliverables of all chapters nationwide. Some chapters have trained personnel to be mobilized to the First aid station or be a part of the ambulance crew.
▫ An emergency First Aid lecture is also conducted to increase the knowledge of the individuals in the affected community
▫ Safety protocolsin place forstaff and volunteersfor infection, prevention & control.
▫ Finally, the desk review indicatesthat First Aid is a core component of the NS even if specified in broad terms in the documentation at hand.

▫ WASH is included as one of the key components in emergency responses at national and chapters’ level. PRC has a WASH Unit as a stand‐alone office at the NHQ overseeing the activities implemented under its programs.
▫ During disaster response, PRC initially deploys WASH equipment (water tankers, bladders, etc.) and well‐trained RCAT WASH team ensuring that WASH activities are delivered to the affected areas.
▫ Trained personnel (RCAT WASH) assess the area and reports to the NHQ using the standard assessment tool with their recommendation; this includes assessing possible concerns that may arise such as water‐borne contamination in the drinking supply, availability/placements of makeshift latrines within the communities etc.
▫ Regional WASH hubs are identified and strategically prepositioned. Fleet of WASH equipment and supplies (essential items) is a large part of the response.
▫ Toolkits, WASH assets and equipment are deployed in each major disaster. Those WASH toolkits are pre‐positioned for relief aid but not for long‐term situations.
▫ WASH is part of the EDR policy and SOP manual and coordination with other departments during an emergency is outlined. WASH services have protocols in place. The draft ENA includes WASH in its assessment tool.  
▫ The WASH Unit seems to be responsive and well‐equipped with well‐trained teams deployed during emergencies
▫ Need for more WASH hardware and software was indicated in some survey responses. These needs are based on the assessment of the affected communities.

▫ This component is mainstreamed as the foundation for training Community Health Volunteers and community health implementation in the communities.  
▫ The survey findings indicate a need to improve the component and make it a part of or better than the Barangay Health Workers program of the government to ensure consistency when engaged in DoH‐initiated activities such as vaccination campaigns, health promotions, etc.
▫ PRC volunteers are trained and engaged in various activities related to CBHFA, implementing the programs appropriately with communities.
▫ The CEA guidelines also discusses the capacity to respond to the identified needs related to CBHFA.
▫ Although this seems to be a strong activity, with increased engagement from volunteers as well as more volunteers joining the ranks, results of the survey indicate a gap in respective chapters' capacities. Not all chapters are equally equipped to perform this activity optimally.

▫ Food distributions are one of the PRC services during emergency response, in which it coordinates and engages closely with other organisations active in food distribution. PRC coordinates with Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) for serving needs.
▫ Emergency response food aid is with DMS department.  
▫ Some chapters are engaged in food distribution activities. Some of them have agreements with suppliers to ensure that food items can readily be procured during disasters. Also, food items are received from benevolent parties during a donation drive.
▫ Immediate mobilization of available food trucks to provide hot meals to the affected population in every disaster was also mentioned as a strength in the Survey.

▫ Survey results highlight that this activity seems to have strong anchor across the chapters ‐ even if the capacity varies from one chapter to the next.  
▫ Identified chapters are trained and capacitated when it comes to search and rescue.  
▫ Those chapters that have less capacity may have trained teams deployed from NHQ as a support mechanism.  
▫ This activity is led by the Government; PRC is only an implementation partner by law. The assessment indicates a need to strengthen the awareness around PRC’s role versus the national authorities’ role.

▫ NS CEA guidelines are available. PRC ensures participation of  communities in the assessment, project planning and design, and decision‐making concerning activities as well as opportunities to lead or support the implementation of community‐based DP and DRR activities.  
▫ CEA guidelines highlight some procedures for monitoring and design and planning phases, which could be interpreted as early warning systems through data collection systems. However, the guidelines do not discuss training, CP capacity nor resource management. They do not address epidemic response either.
▫ The Vulnerability Capacity Assessment (VCA) is one of the examples of PRC assessment approaches used by staff in the field.
▫ PRC uses various common channels for sharing information with communities (media, pamphlets, face to face), conduct awareness sessions, etc.  
▫ The survey findings indicate that communities are involved in assessments, design, and implementation of activities, but answers are not the same at all levels which could mean that it is not disseminated /orimplemented at the chapterlevel with the same level of effectiveness.
Lack of training is a concern that is repeated (likely coming from the chapters).

component_details.title: Mapping of NS capacities
component_details.description: A list of the NS capacities including HR (staff, response teams and volunteers) and equipment that are available for disaster/crisis response. Teams could include branch and national response teams. This should be defined by technical speciality where relevant.

component_responses.notes:
▫ Survey findings indicate that databases are available at department levels, and OpCen does have an up‐to‐date mapping of the response assets (HR and materials). The One Volunteer Database (OVD) is also available at NHQ level. The desk review further confirms this element i.e. OpCen is equipped as indicated in the Dispatch Standard procedures and
the Volunteers Services Manual indicates that volunteers can be mobilized when Emergencies occurs.   
▫ CP Guidelines and EDR Policy & SOP manual map the levels of responses, but the survey indicates that this lacks dissemination amongst relevant staff/volunteers.  
▫ The survey further indicates the presence of focal points for this component with technical support and equipment available.
▫ Among chapters, HR resources are often shared but there are seemingly no formal mechanisms in place to organize the sharing of resources across chapters. Lack of available qualified HR across some chapters has been mentioned as a challenge.   
▫ PRC uses Chapter Classification based on income generation (e.g. A‐E) and does not necessarily capture response capacity. Often a chapter with a low classification may have very capable responders, and vice‐versa. The chapter classification provides the number of assets, number of people trained, and identify the number of families it is expected to provide support.

▫ NS has a strong relationship with Government in terms of health emergencies response. PRC is well identified in the “Bayanihan to heal as One Act” (RA 11469) specifying its role in COVID‐19. 
▫ PRC has been responding to various Health Emergencies (e.g. avian flu, COVID‐19, diarrhoea outbreaks).
▫ PRC is engaged in COVID‐19 vaccination, emergency field hospital, outbreak response, deployment of medical tentsto support hospitals and health care facilities. 
▫ PRC has high level of awareness and visibility and engagement of staff and volunteers (especially during pandemic).
▫ PRC works with community volunteers/medical corps, in agreement with different medical related fields. 
▫ Multi‐sectoral response needs are identified for different epidemic scenarios including multi‐country outbreak. 
▫ PRC is building community capacity through Primary Health Care program and Health in Disaster and Emergency (HiDE) program. 
▫ Lack of documented or weak procedures and protocols is a gap. Findings suggest that procedures and protocols exist yet need strengthening and training needs to be enhanced especially at chapter levels.

component_details.title: Early Action Mechanisms
component_details.description: Designed to translate warnings into anticipatory actions to help reduce the impact of specific disaster or crisis events. They focus on consolidating available forecasting information and putting procedures in place to ensure that a NS can act ahead of any disaster/crisis. Forecast-based financing is included within the scope of this area.

component_responses.notes: ▫ Mechanisms are in place to anticipate and respond to major hazards in coordination with the nationalsystem. The coordination with the existing governmental mechanisms of early warning is strong – thanks to the existing strong relationship and legal base. ▫ PRC has the Hazard App which is used to send alerts and early warning messages to users. ▫ Mechanisms are in place at chapter level to warn communities and enable local actions through RC 143 community volunteer network, CHVs, BARCOM, etc. ▫ Strong OpCen capacity and support mechanisms in place. ▫ There are ongoing Forecast‐based Financing (FbF) projects aiming to operationalize anticipatory actions by the end of 2022. ▫ Early action is well‐prepared for when it comes to well‐known hazards (such as typhoons), but not for other types of disasters. OpCen is currently in training with the 510 team to facilitate technology transfer for the trigger models for typhoons. There is a need to extend this initiative beyond the pilot 22 provinces and for other hazards such as droughts. Flood trigger model also needs to be improved. Strong partnership with PNS is reported for this mechanism. ▫ NHQ issues alerts and warnings to chapters based on government information. However, apart from the general expectation to prepare for, there are no specific directives as to pre‐emptive actions such as identification of backup resources, deployment timetables, etc. FbF is an approach that is not yet widely disseminated and implemented. ▫ A need to improve other kinds of channels for communicating with chapters (other than telephone/cell phone) was also flagged in survey results

component_details.title: Civil Military Relations
component_details.description: Dialogue and interaction with military actors, essential to protect and promote humanitarian principles, avoid competition, minimize inconsistency and, when appropriate, pursue common goals.

component_responses.notes: ▫ Although PRC has developed relationships with the military, engaging through meetings and military exercises, it is acknowledged that the Civil Military relations function still needs to be formally established within PRC. ▫ IHL department coordinates with military and has been promoting the role of PRC to military personnel. ▫ Fundamental principles and IHL are reported to be disseminated. ▫ There is an identified need to increase PRC awareness of its role and engagement with the military internally. NS should clarify which department and position is in‐charge of this component. ▫ Not all in the chapters conduct dissemination activities to military units. Communication islimited, though coordination during response activities is usually present

component_details.title: Coordination with Movement
component_details.description: Mechanisms that facilitate the coordination with ICRC, IFRC, and PNS in-country.

component_responses.notes: ▫ PRC has International Relations and Strategic Partnership Office at NHQ responsible for international coordination with movement partners. ▫ The survey results confirm the coordination with Movement is well established and usually managed at the NHQ level. Partners mentioned are specifically IFRC and ICRC. Strong relationship with ICRC at chapter level is reported as well. ▫ PRC has regular meetings with IFRC to discuss issues related to response and rehabilitation activities. IFRC country representatives are also present in OpCen for emergency response when protocols are activated. ▫ Some elements of relationship and coordination mechanisms are briefly mentioned in the PRC 2020 EDR Policy and SOP manual without clear procedures. PIHAC coordination is also briefly discussed in the same document. ▫ An older MoU with Finish RC and American RC presented in desk review showcase coordination, roles and responsibilities, and scope of action indicate that coordination is managed professionally asfar as agreements are concerned. ▫ Survey findings acknowledge that there is a need for a 4W (who, what, where, when) for coordination of preparedness actions, and more structured/regular partner meetings.

component_details.title: Coordination with authorities
component_details.description: Mechanism that facilitates coordination and cooperation with local and national authorities. It is connected to the NS auxiliary role for humanitarian assistance.

component_responses.notes: ▫ PRC role is well articulated in the Republic Act 10072 (i.e., Red Cross Law) as well as the Republic Act 10121 (Philippines DRRM Act of 2010). ▫ PRC is a member of NDRRMC and LDRRMCs and regularly attends meetings at national and local level to coordinate humanitarian response actions. ▫ PRC is part of the PIHAC (2020 EDR Policy). ▫ Strong coordination system with authorities is also outlined in 2020 EDR Policy and SOP Manual. ▫ Coordination with authorities at local level appears to be strong too: chapters regularly cooperate with LGUs. ▫ There is a need to improve the guidelines and protocol for coordination and cooperation with local authorities, as identified in the survey.

component_details.title: Coordination with local community level responders
component_details.description: Engagement with Community Disaster Response Teams (CDRTs), through training, coordination, and the development of community disaster preparedness and response plans.

component_responses.notes: PRC has established effective communication lines with local responders. Generally speaking, information sharing from communities to chapters is effective in practice. ▫ Information is collected from communities to support decision‐making at chapter and NHQ levels, regarding response actions. ▫ PRC chapters are involved in CDTRs training through the RC143 program. ▫ In addition, responsibilities at NHQ and chapters are outlined in EDR Policy/SOP Manual. The CEA guidelines outline how information and collaboration with the community is handled. ▫ PRC has good connections with Barangay Recovery Committees and other local response groups. ▫ RC143 volunteer responders are active members of the community. They often participate in other capacity building activities offered by PRC, such as VCA, DR planning, First aid. ▫ There exist similar volunteers’ functions across different services which may lead to roles’ overlapping. ▫ Coordination could be strengthened through more training ‐ funding was mentioned as a reason for lack of training in certain areas.

component_details.title: Cooperation with private sector
component_details.description: Mechanism that allows cooperation with private sector that often plays a strong role in response, particularly if there is impact on their staff and businesses. There is often a willingness to donate goods and services. Advance agreements help to expedite response actions.

component_responses.notes: PRC’s Fund Generation Policy identifies the profile and characteristics of desirable partnerships when it comes to cooperation with the private sector. General practice is that PRC does not partner with anyone whose core business is deleterious to Health. ▫ There are some examples of cooperation with private sector found as a part of desk review (contracts with NOKIA and PMFTC Inc. – this does not seem to be related to emergencies). ▫ PRC ensures appropriate use of emblem and protects the organization's visual identity. ▫ PRC Davao City mapped the potential partners to identify the type and kind support they could provide should the need arise. ▫ Most ofsurvey responses are linked to funding in general, not specifically to cooperation in terms of emergency response. Some cooperation appears to exist at chapter level, but again, related to funding opportunities.

component_details.title: Coordination with External Agencies and NGOs
component_details.description: Mechanism that facilitates coordination and collaboration with Non-Governmental Organization (NGO), both local and international NGOs, civil society organizations (CSOs) and United Nations agencies in country.

component_responses.notes: ▫ PRC is part of the humanitarian community as per 2020 EDR Policy. ▫ PRC regularly joins UNOCHA meetings, and partners with other NGOs and organizations in various activities such as Forecast‐based Financing initiatives. ▫ At chapter level, PRC also actively coordinates with external agencies, for example it is an active member in Calamian Resiliency Network for coordination and efficiency of multi‐sectoral program and project implementation. ▫ The survey results indicate a good presence of PRC at external meetings, coordination being in place despite the competitive nature of it at times. The coordination with external agencies seems to be happening mostly at local level where chapters have regular meetings and coordination with other NGOs and Local Government Units. The situation tends to differ from one chapter to another. ▫ Findings identify a need for greater information sharing among PRC departments on engagement with external agencies.

component_details.title: RC auxiliary role, Mandate and Law
component_details.description: A constitutional reference to the role of the NS in responding to disasters and crises, which may be legislated or included/ recognized in the National Response System.

component_responses.notes:
Mandat définit dans un statut et adopté par décret. Le nouveau statut doit être transmis au ministère de l’intérieur. 
Le rôle d’auxiliaire de l’état du CRM était relativement connu par les anciennes générations (sécheresse 1970) dans les structures étatiques au niveau central et régional. A présent, les nouvelles générations connaissent moins.
En pratique, les comités sont demandés parfois à faire des choses qui ne relèvent pas du Mandat du CRM ni des principes fondamentaux du Mouvement. 
Le rôle du CRM n’est pas compris par tous les volontaires, qui pour beaucoup, ne sont pas impliqués activement ou ne sentent pas d’appartenance.
La promotion du DIH n’est pas régulière. Se fait dans le cadre des évènements. 

Implications: il n’y a pas de coordination claire et systématique entre comités et autorités locales. Les preneurs de décision à chaque niveau ne comprennent pas le rôle complémentaire du CRM. Les comités sont parfois empêchés de travailler, ou demandés à faire des choses qui ne s’alignent pas aux principes du Mvt et donc mettent à risque la réputation de la SN et les volontaires.

component_details.title: DRM Strategy
component_details.description: An outline of the overall goal that the NS seeks to achieve in its disaster and crisis response operations. The goal considers: context analysis, ongoing/regular all-hazards risk assessments: it may define the target proportion of affected population that will be reached, and a definition of the areas/sectors where a NS will usually respond during an emergency.

component_responses.notes:
Le CRM n’a pas une stratégie de GRC mais le plan stratégique tente de couvrir la partie préparation et réponse. 
Les plans stratégiques ne comprennent cependant pas les indicateurs précis qui peut guider les actions de la SN (et le support des partenaires) en réponse.
La présence d’une stratégie marquerait l’engagement clair des secteurs et services techniques. Elle serait la ligne directrice de tous les plans d’intervention (national – local).
vent guider les actions pratiques de la SN (et du support des partenaires).

Implications: le fait que les objectifs opérationnels n’existent pas et ne couvrent pas la proportion de la population à secourir, la SN ne peut pas avoir de plan de réponse clair ni un plan de préparation qui couvrirait le pré-positionnement ou autres activités, ni même bénéficier d’une action précoce.

component_details.title: DRM Policy
component_details.description: Reflects the NS mission, RCRC principles and mandate. It acknowledges other relevant NS policies, and aligns with the government policy (where applicable), incorporating the general rules that the NS will obey in order to achieve something (i.e mandate, strategy, etc.)

component_responses.notes:
La SN n’a pas de politique de GRC. Elle pourrait utiliser le format créé dernièrement par la FICR, ou adopter le politique de GRC de la FICR.
Bien qu’il n’existe pas de politique GRC, la collaboration entre les départements GRC et santé/wash se fait au niveau central.
Les branches ne sont pas au courant des politiques principales à suivre pour la prise de décision.
Une politique adaptée serait une ligne directrice des plans de réponse.

Implications: le manque de politique pourrait résulter en une incohérence dans les différentes activités du CRM. Une politique adoptée et bien reconnue sert de guider la prise de décision quelque soit le niveau, sans perdre le temps à attendre des consignes centralisées.

component_details.title: DRM Laws, Advocacy and Dissemination
component_details.description: Designed to support the NS in improving legal preparedness for disasters and crisis and to promote the use of the IDRL Guidelines in order to reduce human vulnerability.

component_responses.notes:
La SN ne fait pas un travail particulièrement axé sur le DIH et le IDRL.
En terme de facilitation de l’entrée des secours dans le pays, lorsqu’ils sont au nom du CRM, ils sont exonérés des taxes de la douane mais pas des autres impôts (TVA et une autre taxe), ce qui pose problème à quelques partenaires.
Il serait bénéfique de recevoir la liste de vérification de la FICR et de choisir les points importants à prioriser pour le contexte, en ayant comme objectif de faciliter les opérations.
Une fois le travail sur le DIH et le IDRL enclenché, la SN gagnerait à avoir un point focal par comité pour guider les actions et identifier les besoins. 

Implications: le manque de travail sur le DIH ne met pas la SN dans une position forte de plaidoyer, au cas où un incident survient au cours d’une réponse.

component_details.title: Quality and accountability
component_details.description: Describes the essential elements of principled, accountable, and high-quality humanitarian action. The RCRC Movement provides support to the most vulnerable people in line with the Sphere and CHS standards, Code of Conduct for the RCRC Movement and NGOS in Disaster Relief and the Code for Good Partnership of the RCRC Movement, Gender & Diversity, inclusion and protection, BPI/ Do no harm, context-sensitive analysis, violence prevention, accountability to affected population and disability considerations, Community engagement and accountability (CEA).

component_responses.notes:
La population affectée n’est pas impliquée dans toutes les étapes de l'intervention. Une enquête détaillée pourrait avoir lieu après avoir reçu les listes des autorités, pour une idée plus détaillée sur les besoins. 
Des volontaires sont formés sur l’Engagement Communautaire et la Redevabilité (CEA )mais les comités n'en sont pas au courant. Ils ne gardent pas de record des formations et des formés (le siège non plus).
Pas de mécanisme sûrs pour les réclamations (quelques projets le font), mais ceci n’en réduit pas le besoin: des réclamations se font à présent chez le Hakem ou aux volontaires du CRM, sans pour autant avoir un cadre où l’information est enregistrée et bien gérée (explications, action, etc.).
Une formation sur la protection, le genre et l’inclusion a été faite (2021 sans résultats, et 2023) mais pas de politique adoptée. 
Les branches ne sont pas au courant de normes spécifiques que la SN suit, ni ne prêtent une attention spéciale aux violences liées au genre et aux besoins des personnes handicapées. 
Il n’existe pas une analyse qui assure le « Do no harm » à travers les plans et procédures.
Les bénéficiaires sont choisis par les autorités. Mais à travers les programmes, la SN priorise l’inclusion.

Implications: l’aide risque de ne pas répondre aux besoins, ce qui pourrait pousser les personnes à vendre les aides; des personnes pourraient trouver le choix des bénéficiaires injuste (résidents/migrants); les possibles comportements non-acceptables des volontaires pourraient ne pas être détectés.
