component_details.title: Communication in emergencies
component_details.description: Incorporates a system of public messaging to enable the NS to share timely, accurate information before, during, and after a disaster or crisis.

component_details.title: Operations Monitoring, Evaluation, Reporting and Learning
component_details.description: The PMERL is designed to implement a results-based planning, monitoring and evaluation system that provides an evidence base of NS performance, including relevance, efficiency, effectiveness, sustainability and impact. A reliable and trusted organization is accountable, providing transparent and timely information and building systems to strengthen data collection and reporting. It is data-driven, analytical and results-based.

component_details.title: Finance and Admin policy and emergency procedures
component_details.description: Overall budgeting, accounting, treasury, assets, financial reporting and financial services operations. it also includes the efficient delivery , cost effective and timely services to the NS. Pre-approved, auditable, expedited procedures that allow for flexibility during a disaster/crisis. These must meet transparency, oversight and accountability standards. Procedures may include faster approval processes, fewer signatures, different authority levels. The Emergency Procedures are activated for a specific period of time.

component_details.title: Information and Communication Technology (ICT)
component_details.description: Refers to technologies that provide access to information through telecommunications. This includes the Internet, wireless networks, mobile phones, radios and other communication mediums.

component_details.title: RC auxiliary role, Mandate and Law
component_details.description: A constitutional reference to the role of the NS in responding to disasters and crises, which may be legislated or included/ recognized in the National Response System.

component_responses.epi_considerations:
MRCS has a role in epidemic preparedness and response (focused mainly on risk communication) on both national and regional levels and plays active role in coordination with the authorities. For example, MRCS has been working with the public authorities during  COVID-19 response supporting risk communication, IEC materials distribution, sanitizers installation in public transport.
The role of NS in public health is reflected in NS strategies and plans.
component_responses.notes:
• MRCS’s auxiliary role is established by law: 
1992 – MRCS was recognized by Presidential Decree as an autonomous public organization that carries out its activity based on the Fundamental Principles of the International Movement of Red Cross and Red Crescent
1999 – Law on protection of the Red Cross emblem
2001- Law on the Red Cross Society of Moldova
• MRCS’s mandate is aligned with the RCRC Fundamental Principles, and all activities are carried out with respect to them.
• NS mandate is reflected in policies and is generally known by staff and volunteers; however, this could be reinforced via the additional initial and ongoing trainings for all staff and volunteers.
• Promotion of IHL is 4th Strategic objective of MRCS mentioned in the Strategic Development Plan (2022 – 2026). It was recognized that more trainings are required internally to fulfil.
• NS has a role in epidemic preparedness and response (focused mainly on risk communication) on both national and regional levels and plays active role in coordination with the authorities. 
•	Even though overall, role of MRCS is quite clear, it could be further strengthened and disseminated internally and externally.
•The RC auxiliary role is clear and understood at the high government level, but there are some challenges with acceptance and understanding at the lower government departments. Additional challenge is represented by the staff turnover at the government (need to explain what RC does) constantly.

component_details.title: DRM Strategy
component_details.description: An outline of the overall goal that the NS seeks to achieve in its disaster and crisis response operations. The goal considers: context analysis, ongoing/regular all-hazards risk assessments: it may define the target proportion of affected population that will be reached, and a definition of the areas/sectors where a NS will usually respond during an emergency.

component_responses.epi_considerations: MRCS Strategic Development Plan 2022-2026 identifies some health risks and related strategic goals for development of NS interventions.
component_responses.notes:
• NS doesn’t have DRM Strategy.
• MRCS Strategic Development Plan 2022-2026 and National Disaster Preparedness and Intervention Plan 2017 contain elements of the DRM Strategy, such as analysis of country contexts, strategic objectives for the DM. It’s noted that documents are missing some points, e.g., success indicators or unpacking of all NS activities across DRM Continuum.
• NS documents consider different specific areas of intervention, such as DM, Health, IHL, Psychological support, RFL as well as cross-cutting themes, however, the information needs to updated according to new context, current services offered and put into DRM Strategy format identifying objectives and success indicators.

component_details.title: DRM Policy
component_details.description: Reflects the NS mission, RCRC principles and mandate. It acknowledges other relevant NS policies, and aligns with the government policy (where applicable), incorporating the general rules that the NS will obey in order to achieve something (i.e mandate, strategy, etc.)

component_responses.epi_considerations: No
component_responses.notes:
• MRCS doesn’t have DRM Policy; however, it uses IFRC DM Policy Framework from 2010.
• IFRC DM Policy Framework sets out guiding principles and values that guide decision-making on the response approach and actions, however, there is an updated version available and could be considered by MRCS.
• Specific MRCS overarching Policy priorities identifying for how NS shall conduct all its disaster risk management operations and programs, as well as linkages with various Movement and government frameworks still need to be outlined.

component_details.title: DRM Laws, Advocacy and Dissemination
component_details.description: Designed to support the NS in improving legal preparedness for disasters and crisis and to promote the use of the IDRL Guidelines in order to reduce human vulnerability.

component_responses.epi_considerations: No. NS management understands classification of public health risks and emergencies and  complies with policies regarding epidemics.
component_responses.notes:
• No specific IDRL plans in place or documents signed.
• MRCS has just hired IHL coordinator with the support of ICRC. MRCS includes IHL in its public communication in coordination with the ICRC.
• NS selected branches organize various information dissemination sessions (including on IHL) in schools, colleges etc.
• The government of Moldova supports MRCS with paying annual statutory contribution to IFRC. In addition, humanitarian goods imported to the country are exempt from the tax when government announces State of Emergency.

component_details.title: Quality and accountability
component_details.description: Describes the essential elements of principled, accountable, and high-quality humanitarian action. The RCRC Movement provides support to the most vulnerable people in line with the Sphere and CHS standards, Code of Conduct for the RCRC Movement and NGOS in Disaster Relief and the Code for Good Partnership of the RCRC Movement, Gender & Diversity, inclusion and protection, BPI/ Do no harm, context-sensitive analysis, violence prevention, accountability to affected population and disability considerations, Community engagement and accountability (CEA).

component_responses.epi_considerations: Yes. During COVID-19 MRCS worked with partners to develop health promotion messages and deliver them to the public. The booklets were developed in collaboration with UNICEF, WHO, MoH standards were followed.
component_responses.notes:
• NS has limited mechanisms in place to ensure the affected populations are involved in all stages of the response, however, it’s not systematic or planned through relevant procedures.
• NS doesn’t have trained CEA focal points at branches and HQ. CEA Plan is also not developed. 
• Elements of the feedback collection exist (QR codes on vouchers, volunteers communicating with beneficiaries and passing information), however mechanism could be improved especially in the areas of and analyzing the received information and conducting follow-ups.
• NS is not fully familiar with Sphere and the Core Humanitarian Standards, might need more sensitization.
• MRCS doesn’t have PSEA Policy, but has Code of Conduct and is part of some thematic UNHCR led technical working groups (e.g., Refugee Protection Sector Working Group).
• NS has had experience in providing some protection services, e.g., PSS, RFL and coordinating projects on violence prevention. However, it was noted that currently the capacity is at the development stage.
• MRCS makes sure to support the most vulnerable beneficiaries, however more awareness on Minimum Standards for Protection, Gender and Inclusion in Emergencies might be required.

component_details.title: Business continuity
component_details.description: A strategy to counter any potential or anticipated obstacles to effective functioning of the NS, with an eye to ensuring that personnel and assets are protected and able to function in the event of a disaster/crisis.

component_responses.epi_considerations: Not applicable
component_responses.notes:
• NS does not have an up-to-date, approved business continuity plan for major emergency/crisis situation that would affect its ability to operate.
• MRCS had experience requesting the donor during COVID-19 due to the changing needs identified."

component_details.title: Emergency Response Procedures (SOPs)
component_details.description: Written guidelines that describe duties and rights of personnel, command structures, coordination with other organizations, and reporting requirements, etc. Includes detailed organogram, decision-making flow chart, and defined roles and responsibilities.

component_responses.epi_considerations: No
component_responses.notes:
• MRCS doesn’t have up-to-date, approved SOPs for all specific areas of intervention and support services to respond to disasters and crises.
• Nevertheless, NS has some elements in the SOPs for specific intervention areas, describing roles and responsibilities outlined in the National Disaster Preparedness and Intervention plan (2017) that could be elaborated.

component_details.title: Response and recovery planning
component_details.description: A documented set of procedures for the disaster/crisis response and recovery process. Including use of local capacities, transition to recovery, type of activities and serivices provided during response and recovery activities and exit strategies, procedures for DREF & EA, and templates for planning, budgeting and accessing funds.

component_responses.epi_considerations: No
component_responses.notes:
• NS does not have a pre-disaster plan for potential hazards. NS normally develops its own response plan in collaboration with Movement partners when a disaster or emergency has happened.
• The National Disaster Preparedness and Intervention Plan 2017 has elements of multi-sectoral response plan and includes some procedures for the disaster/crisis response and recovery process. However, needs to be further unpacked.
• The plan is not updated with lessons learned from real time and simulated exercises.

component_details.title: Pre-disaster meetings and agreements
component_details.description: A commitment to arrange meetings and agreements with Movement stakeholders and external actors to identify, plan for and address gaps for any upcoming disaster season (e.g. monsoon, floods or cyclones, or for any generic disaster/crisis event (e.g Epidemic, pandemic, confilict situations). Pre-disaster agreements should set out each partner's role in the event of a disaster/crisis.

component_responses.epi_considerations:
• NS is in the process of signing general MOU with Ministry of Health. More dissemination of the information regarding the role of NS might be required across all ministries. 
• When NS conducts community education sessions on health and epidemics, health officials are always involved in either materials preparation or co-leading (e.g. during COVID-19).
component_responses.notes:
• MRCS participates in coordination meetings with authorities on local and National level. When disaster happens, Crisis Commission is assembled under the lead of General Inspectorate for Emergency Situations (IGSU)  and MRCS is part of it.
• The Collaboration Agreement between the MRCS and IGSU establishes a clear understanding of the NS's responsibilities and authorities and reinforces data exchange and accessing pre-existing databases of vulnerable populations.
• Agreement with MoH is about to be signed.
• It was noted that more agreements might be needed with selected ministries, as well as local NGOs.
• In the current operation some contractors were required to sign IFRC Code of Conduct (e.g., real estate agency). However, not done systematically.
• There are no agreements with key suppliers of goods with an agreed mechanism for activation.
• When government declares the Status of Emergency, humanitarian goods could be imported using expedited procedures, however, no pre-disaster agreement exists between MRCS and specific authorities to ensure the support for expedited import of aid and cases for incoming personnel.

component_details.title: Hazard, Context and Risk Analysis, Monitoring and Early Warning
component_details.description: Describes how the NS monitors and maps past, present and potential hazards, disasters and crises (e.g. hazard, vulnerability assessments, gathering information from communities and government authorities) and systematically evaluates the damage that could be caused by a potential disaster/crisis, the frequency, severity of the impact, and the alert the relevant areas to scale the preparedness actions to reduce population vulnerability.

component_responses.epi_considerations:
No. Some volunteers are trained on the signs of most common epidemics and support information dissemination in the communities. 

NS does not conduct CBS, responsibility of MoH.
component_responses.notes:
• NS has some elements of risk monitoring on national and regional levels. For example, through  information exchange with authorities and monitoring of the secondary data available online.
• It appears there is no risk monitoring focal point in NS nor a formally established risk monitoring system formally established and linked to preparedness and early action.
• MRCS gets secondary data provided by local authorities at the branch level, however, NS is not engaged in primary data collection. Communities and local volunteers don’t contribute to the regular update of the multi-hazard risk mapping and Vulnerability and capacity assessments (VCA).
• Government has Early Warning system is established and activated through radio/telecom messages for early action system. MRCS gets informed and follows government protocols.

component_details.title: Scenario planning
component_details.description: A set of practical operation plans that closely mirror the generic disaster or crisis response plan but are tailored to a specific hazard type (e.g. earthquake, dengue epidemic, floods, cyclone) and a specific scenario (i.e. number of people affected, their locations and other important factors).

component_responses.epi_considerations: No
component_responses.notes:
• NS has a globally clear picture of the hazards in the Country.  In close cooperation with the local authorities, the NS prepares for emergencies. 
• MRCS has gained recent experience for developing scenarios with Movement partners (for example, Movement contingency plan 2023), however, it's not done regularly for all hazards or all high-risk regions.
• Emergency response is managed according to the needs, where the local authorities conduct the assessment and launch a request to the NS on a case-by-case basis.
• Volunteers are trained to support activities with the lead of branch director.  This can be reinforced through the specific strategic response plan for each scenario.

component_details.title: Risk management
component_details.description: A mapping of the potential risks in every area, along with its related mitigation measures. Including financial, reputational, organizational risks etc.

component_responses.epi_considerations: Yes. MRCS uses trusted sources of information to provide data for population (for e.g. MoH).
component_responses.notes:
• NS does not conduct risk management holistically across technical sectors and does not identify or operationalize mitigation measures (including in cases of reputational risks). However, some finance procedures and internal control mechanisms are in place for financial risks. 
• Risk management responsibility has not been assigned to a trained and dedicated staff member. However, critical incidents would be managed by President. 
• MRCS has systems and procedures in place to prevent fraud and corruption.
• Risks are included in the discussions of NS Governing Board meetings.

component_details.title: Preparedness plans and budgets
component_details.description: Plans identifying organisational resources, determining roles and responsibilities, and developing policies, procedures and activities in order to reach a level of preparedness to be able to respond effectively to a disaster or crisis. Budgets ensure that the necessary financial support is secured to allow capacities to be built and readiness maintained.

component_responses.notes:
• Head of DM department is the focal point for disaster preparedness.
• Preparedness gaps and areas for improvement are identified in some NS documents (e.g. MRCS Strategic Development Plan 2022-2026, Ukraine and impacted countries crisis Movement Response Plan and Contingency Plan, OCAC assessment 2022).
• Participation of MRCS in 2022 OCAC, as well as current 2023 PER self-assessment process validates the commitment of MRCS towards preparedness elements.

component_responses.epi_considerations: MRCS has been active in leading hygiene promotion sessions in schools (selected locations), as well as providing other health promotion and risk communication messaging in collaboration with relevant partners and authorities.
component_responses.notes:
• MRCS doesn’t usually conduct the assessments. The needs of the population are assessed by authorities and shared with MRCS. 
• MRCS branch volunteers conduct regular awareness-raising and public education on disasters and crises in their regions. To create a standardized message to be shared with the community.
• There are no established Community Disaster Response Teams  (CDRTs), however, partnership between local authorities and some active branches (led by Branch Directors and volunteers) exists.

component_responses.epi_considerations:
Yes. 
• NS staff and volunteers were trained on the usage of PPEs during COVID-19.
• For now NS is just engaged in public health provision, not specific health care services. However, National Disaster Preparedness and Intervention Plan 2017 section 7.5 mentions First aid provision, as well as Blood donor recruitment as one of the MRCS's functions in Emergency medicine.
• NS conducts  training of volunteers engaged in health/ vaccination promotion sessions on communicable diseases and epidemics.
• NS is in a process of signing MOU with MoH. During COVID-19 MRCS has been attending Crisis Commission meetings to coordinate support with other stakeholders.
component_responses.notes:
• NS Health Coordinator is under recruitment. 
• Personal Protection Equipment is provided to staff and volunteers, mainly during the highest pics of the pandemic
• NS Strategic Development Plan 3rd Strategic Objective is focused on Improving Population Health including health promotion, pre-medical FA, voluntary blood donations promotion. In addition, NS has been exposed a little to PSS services (organizing kids’ room during refugees arrival, conducting various activities in the Ukrainian refugees centers)
• Currently, MRCS response in health is mostly limited to awareness raising. During COVID-19 NS was engaged in sanitizers’ installation in public transport, as well as Information Education Communication (IEC) materials development in collaboration with MoH and UNICEF.

• First Aid is mentioned in NS National Disaster Preparedness and Intervention Plan 2017 as part of NS's response activities, as well as included in the MRCS Development Strategic Plan as one areas of future areas of focus. Specific role of MRCS in FA needs to be further clarified. 
• Some staff and volunteers are trained in pre-medical first aid (FA), however, not officially certified to provide the service during response. Refresher trainings might also be needed. 
• First Aid is considered part of the activities mainly from an educational perspective.  NS offers demo sessions to public, for e.g., schools, universities, kindergartens etc. and has a plan to train one certified FA instructor at HQ.
• The resources and equipment for FA training are limited, which makes it challenging to have a broader capacity to offer the first aid trainings or first aid pre-medical services to the community.

• WASH is considered part of NS response activities and mentioned in key MRCS documents.  However, NS engagement in WASH is mostly related to hygiene promotion and relief activities: distribution of hygiene kits, water filters and water bottles. 
• Some MRCS volunteers have been trained to deliver hygiene promotion sessions in schools and other public establishments.
• NS Head of DM has an understanding on how to obtain hygiene kits and water filters in-country or via IFRC, no SOPs. 
• Doesn’t regularly coordinate with other organizations and networks active in WASH in the country, however, in the Movement CP for Ukraine and impacted countries crisis UNHCR and IFRC are mentioned as partner agencies in WASH.
• Disparity of water conditions in different regions of Moldova were noted during validation workshop, as well as potential need to expend/ enhance NS services in this area.

component_responses.epi_considerations: No
component_responses.notes:
• MRCS doesn't have a technical staff for food assistance, however, Head of DM together with partners does the analysis on the best modality of support (parcels distribution vs voucher support).
• NS doesn’t monitor, analyze and documents food security levels in the country, food-security status of the population/most vulnerable, Argo-meteorological data, supplies and demand in main food and agricultural markets, food reserves. This information could be accessible through authorities. 
• NS is not very engaged with other organizations and networks (clusters) active in food aid distribution (e.g. WFP), but for current Ukraine and impacted countries crisis MRCS participates in UNHCR led meetings.
• NS uses the standard food parcel content for distribution suggested by IFRC, however, was able to make the small adjustments once feedback was received by volunteers and passed to HQ.

• Experience in CVA (i.e. vouchers distribution). However, livelihood activities haven’t been implemented or developed by MRCS. 
• From MRCS Strategic Development Plan 2022-2026: Preparing people in high-risk areas to respond and cope effectively with emergencies and their consequences and to mitigate the impact of disasters on people, the environment, livelihoods and material assets

• MRCS Shelter sector response has been focused on distribution of HH items, NS is not engaged in conducting needs assessment and relies on information received from authorities.
• With support of partners NS has recently received tents that could be used as distribution/ information sites, as well as some generators, high range lamps, furniture and First Aid kits. MRCS has plan to pre-position the items near pre-border areas with Ukraine and other high-risk locations.
• NS doesn’t have identified suppliers of shelter items and NFIs with pre-disaster and framework agreements in place.
• NS is not engaged on standard emergency and temporary shelter designs (probably not applicable to context).
• MRCS doesn’t have dedicated shelter trained staff. NS volunteers are not trained in the use of the prepositioned shelter materials to construct basic shelters (e.g., shelter kit training).

component_details.title: MANAGEMENT OF DEAD BODIES TO FACILITATE THEIR IDENTIFICATION

component_responses.notes:
• This sector of response if under development.
• NS and ICRC have an operating agreement for Protection Family Links program (PFL) to support Ukrainian refugees. The ICRC is responsible for the program.
• Per the agreement, the MRCS volunteers will be paired with the Protection team during monthly field trips and conduct needs assessments using pre-prepared forms and questionnaires. 
• MRCS would be expected to be able to refer beneficiaries to ICRC for PFL/RFL if required.

component_responses.epi_considerations: Not applicable in context so far.
component_responses.notes:
• Elements on transition to recovery to the MRCS Strategic Development Plan 2022-2026, e.g., Red Cross recovery assistance aims to prevent further damage and loss, restore basic services, provide psychological support, restore livelihoods and strengthen food security.  Rehabilitation is carried out in such a way as to reduce vulnerability to future disasters.  
• During current response (Ukraine and impacted countries crisis) MRCS has been engaged in informal PSS support.
• There is some understanding with key staff of key recovery principles, such as detailed assessment, community participation, consideration of cross-cutting issues and strengthening resilience through the response, however, could be strengthened. Additional training might be required.

component_details.title: CHEMICAL, BIOLOGICAL, RADIOLOGICAL AND NUCLEAR (CBRN) EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS
Mapping of NS capacities
component_details.description: A list of the NS capacities including HR (staff, response teams and volunteers) and equipment that are available for disaster/crisis response. Teams could include branch and national response teams. This should be defined by technical speciality where relevant.

component_responses.epi_considerations: No
component_responses.notes:
• Focal points are available for some specific areas of intervention (e.g., CVA together with FA, IHL, DM), however, all personnel play multiple roles. All Branch Directors are volunteers.
• Trainings for staff and volunteers are provided (mostly linked with specific projects), but not regular or consistently. It seems that no regular refresher trainings are provided.
• Response materials and equipment database exists and is managed by stock keeper. Not clear whether gaps are noted and addressed. 
• HR and equipment resources are not sufficient to cover initial response.
• Resources are stored at the Chisinau and could be delivered to the regions (small distances).
• MRCS often attends trainings organized by Romanian RC, however, no other resources have been shared with sister NSs so far.

component_details.title: Early Action Mechanisms
component_details.description: Designed to translate warnings into anticipatory actions to help reduce the impact of specific disaster or crisis events. They focus on consolidating available forecasting information and putting procedures in place to ensure that a NS can act ahead of any disaster/crisis. Forecast-based financing is included within the scope of this area.

component_details.title: Cash Based Intervention (CBI)
component_details.description: An effective and flexible way, including all forms of cash and voucher-based assistance, to support people affected by emergencies, maintaining their dignity and choice, while fostering local economies. Cash should also be mainstreamed into other sectors (including Relief, shelter, livelihoods) and services (Logistics, Finance, etc.)

component_responses.epi_considerations: Only what is related to COVID measures.
component_responses.notes:
• MRCS has an agreement with partners (Swiss RC) to support CVA activities.  As part of the preparedness, the NS conducts market analysis to identify potential CVA interventions.
• Training on CVA has been provided to managers and volunteers involved in this program.  The list of participants of the two branches is available.
• NS is working on a voucher modality, and there are agreements with suppliers where beneficiaries can redeem them (only for the period of specific project).  When there is a need, the authorities provide a list of beneficiaries, and they have one month to pick up the goods at the suppliers' premises.  
• MRCS does not currently do cash deliveries.

component_details.title: Emergency Needs Assessment
component_details.description: Assess the extent and impact of the damage caused by the disaster/crisis and the degree of vulnerability of the affected population. The first step in any emergency response, such an assessment will identify the needs that require external intervention and the gaps to be filled. It is a vital component of the programme-planning process.

component_responses.notes:
• No specific Assessment Team in place. One of the clauses in the Collaboration agreement with authorities states that NS makes available its staff, for the joint activity in the commission for the evaluation of the damages following the exceptional situation, in case of necessity.
• Although MRCS doesn’t have standardized templates used for primary and secondary data collection, NS volunteers were gathering/ verifying some information about affected population needs at the refugee centers.
• Some limited trainings for primary data collection were conducted in selected branches (e.g. Kobo), however, not confirmed whether this capacity still available. It was noted that MRCS volunteers were engaged in needs assessment process with ICRC in Transnistria region.

component_details.title: Affected population selection
component_details.description: Identification and selection of target Affected population for interventions, using a pre-defined set of criteria based on need and vulnerability. This includes consideration of specific vulnerabilities such as disability, age and gender.

component_responses.epi_considerations: MRCS's Collaboration agreement with authorities includes a clause on sharing and exchanging information. In addition, NS follows data protection law of country.
component_responses.notes:
• Local authorities are the only ones authorized to collect ID and address information from the population.
• The authorities make the selection of beneficiaries.  Then they consult with the respective branches about their availability to support the communities in need.  When the capacity of the NS is known, the authorities provide a list of beneficiaries for the respective interventions.
• NS identifies criteria based on existing vulnerability and taking into consideration gender, diversity, age and disabilities when requesting the beneficiary list from government (e.g. people with 1st group of disability)
• Before distributing humanitarian aid to beneficiaries, MRCS volunteers call people on the provided list to verify whether they indeed met criteria and if aid is still required (e.g. when distributing aid to the host families).

component_details.title: Emergency Operations Centre (EOC)
component_details.description: A central command and control facility responsible for carrying out disaster/crisis management functions at a strategic level in an emergency situation. The common functions are to collect and analyze data; facilitate decision making that protects life and livelihoods; and disseminate those decisions to all concerned agencies and individuals. Generally located at the headquarter level of an organization.

component_details.title: Information Management (IM)
component_details.description: Ability to manage information including requesting, receiving, analyzing and disseminating as per its procedures and partner requirements (IFRC and public authorities in particular). There should be a clear digital/paper trail that documents what, when and how the NS has acted and provides key information for the development of Emergency Plan of Actions. Includes IM between levels, between departments and Situational Reports, mapping, visualisation of data, GO platform (IFRC).

component_responses.epi_considerations: Data protection laws of the country are observed.
component_responses.notes:
• NS HQ has access to equipment to compile, visualize and share information, however, the equipment other than laptops is not available across all branches.
• NS has a system to store and share files (archive at the HQ), however, no digitalized IM system is used. 
• Secondary data (e.g. from local authorities) is the main source of information regarding hazards and high-risk areas. Some limited trainings for primary data collection were conducted in selected branches (e.g. Kobo), however for now primary data is not collected or analyzed.
• NS  doesn’t have a standardized Situation Report format that includes information on situation, NS response, other actors' response, challenges, achievements and gaps.

component_details.title: Testing and Learning
component_details.description: Drills and Simulations allow the organization to test, identify and learn from the results of these type of exercises and incorporate learning into future preparedness and response planning.

component_responses.epi_considerations: No
component_responses.notes:
• NS doesn’t regularly test its internal response system through simulation and drills.
• However, MRCS participates in various simulations and drills organized by local authorities and General Inspectorate for Emergency Situations (IGSU). 
• Lessons drawn from drills, simulations and responses doesn’t inform revisions in the NS emergency procedures.

component_details.title: Activation of regional and international support
component_details.description: Procedures for requesting and accepting regional and international support in operations, including triggering coordination mechanisms for funding, materials and human resources deployments.

component_responses.epi_considerations: No. MRCS follows MoH regulations and laws. Donations come through MoH.
component_responses.notes:
• NS key staff are familiar with IFRC support available (have been working on procurement, logistics, DREF requests in multiple responses). 
• MRCS has good coordination with the IFRC Cluster and Movement partners.
• MRCS is familiar and have been using DREF and Emergency Appeals funding mechanisms.
• MRCS Head of DM works as a focal point to act as counterpart to regional/international responders.

component_details.title: Cooperation with private sector
component_details.description: Mechanism that allows cooperation with private sector that often plays a strong role in response, particularly if there is impact on their staff and businesses. There is often a willingness to donate goods and services. Advance agreements help to expedite response actions.

component_responses.epi_considerations: No
component_responses.notes:
• NS always ensures due diligence in terms of accepting funds, items, goods. Before acceptance, background checks are done, research on website, offices, locations etc.  However, no checklist in place to list the items accepted by NS.
• NS ensures appropriate use of emblem , however, there have been some cases of the emblem misuse by some agencies. Once misuse is noted, it's being communicated to the companies by MRCS.

component_details.title: Coordination with Movement
component_details.description: Mechanisms that facilitate the coordination with ICRC, IFRC, and PNS in-country.

component_responses.notes:
• Strengthening movement coordination and cooperation principles (SMCC) are observed by NS. The work of movement partners is aligned and coordinated.
• Movement coordination meetings are happening once every few months, mechanism to share information is established through some specialized technical working groups, e.g., CVA, Contingency plan working group.
• MRCS exchanges information with neighboring NSs (e.g., Romanian RC), during current Operation MRCS regularly communicates with other affected countries to discuss response activities and updates. 
• It was noted that regular volunteer exchanges with other NSs could have been useful.

component_details.title: Coordination with authorities
component_details.description: Mechanism that facilitates coordination and cooperation with local and national authorities. It is connected to the NS auxiliary role for humanitarian assistance.

component_responses.epi_considerations: Yes. First 2 epi benchmarks yes, 3rd NA
component_responses.notes:
• MRCS features in the national humanitarian coordination systems and partners with Inspectorate for Emergency Situations (IGSU), MoH, The Ministry of Labor and Social Protection and various Primarias (City Halls) across country. They work hand in hand on activities within the country and are provided with info of RCRC capacities during emergencies. 
• NS is mentioned in the National State Disaster Management Plan.  In addition, there is an Agreement between Civil Protection and Exceptional Situations Service.
• There is Law regarding the use and protection of the Red Cross emblem (Nr.673-XIV). This act has helped the NS gain control on the use of the emblem. The Military and Ambulance have also access to the use of the emblem. The NS also have control over assets, resources and can use such according to NS plans and agreements.
• Engagement with authorities at national and local level could be strengthened for a better positioning of the NS on regional and national levels (e.g. NS is not always invited to important coordination meetings).

component_details.title: Coordination with External Agencies and NGOs

component_details.title: Safety and security management
component_details.description: Addresses policy and procedures to ensure the safety of staff and volunteers. This include awareness, effective recruitment, training and management processes in place to ensure that personnel are capable of undertaking the roles demanded of them (from NS operational, management and leaders) according to the Stay Safe (IFRC) and Safer Access (ICRC). Based on safer access framework, including concepts of access, perception, identification and acceptance, and protection and violence prevention.

component_responses.notes:
• MRCS follows Working place safety policy  (mandated by State Law). All employers must follow and provide Safety policy to employees, it includes clauses on the behavior at the office, evacuation procedures and critical numbers to call in case of emergency.
• NS staff or volunteers didn’t receive security training.
• Currently the ICRC is in the process of supporting MRCS with the Safer Access Framework in selected high-risk locations (for e.g. Transnistria region).
• NS has some informal communication mechanisms available for staff and volunteers to report safety and security risks and incidents and to share to share security information, however, the quality of feedback system for the staff and volunteers could be increased. 
• Safety and security management will be strengthened if a policy, a compliance system, and regular training are developed. The systematic analysis will improve safety and security of staff and volunteers.

component_details.title: Operations Monitoring, Evaluation, Reporting and Learning
component_details.description: The PMERL is designed to implement a results-based planning, monitoring and evaluation system that provides an evidence base of NS performance, including relevance, efficiency, effectiveness, sustainability and impact. A reliable and trusted organization is accountable, providing transparent and timely information and building systems to strengthen data collection and reporting. It is data-driven, analytical and results-based.

component_responses.epi_considerations: No
component_responses.notes:
• NS doesn’t have a dedicated PMER staff, currently IHL Coordinator plays PMER focal point role with support of Head of DM. In addition, staff in charge of the different projects are responsible to report their activities. 
• MRCS does timely reporting on the templates agreed to with partners. 
• MRCS refers to and uses lessons from previous operations in response planning, but does not systematically conduct evaluations or record the recommendations. 
• Some elements of monitoring community feedback exists but needs strengthening. 
• MRCS collects some data and does regular reporting, however, needs to explore more on the ways to measure the impact of the operations.

component_details.title: Finance and Admin policy and emergency procedures
component_details.description: Overall budgeting, accounting, treasury, assets, financial reporting and financial services operations. it also includes the efficient delivery , cost effective and timely services to the NS. Pre-approved, auditable, expedited procedures that allow for flexibility during a disaster/crisis. These must meet transparency, oversight and accountability standards. Procedures may include faster approval processes, fewer signatures, different authority levels. The Emergency Procedures are activated for a specific period of time.

component_responses.epi_considerations:
MRCS is able to maintain finance and admin related procedures during epidemic. 
NS has experience with providing voucher assistance, but no expertise in mobile money.
component_responses.notes:
• MRCS has an automated accounting and financial system (1C). National Society has only one legal entity, all the accounting is performed at the central level. 
• NS has peacetime financial procedures, which they have used during response. Do not have dedicated emergency financial procedures. 
• NS follows its Finance manual (2010), as well as IFRC Procurement procedures.
• NS has mechanisms to prevent fraud and corruption.
• NS assesses alternative payment possibilities (e.g. voucher distribution) but not mobile money.

component_details.title: Information and Communication Technology (ICT)
component_details.description: Refers to technologies that provide access to information through telecommunications. This includes the Internet, wireless networks, mobile phones, radios and other communication mediums.

component_responses.epi_considerations: No. During COVID-19 staff were asked to use their own equipment.
component_responses.notes:
• MRCS recently purchased phones to be used in the regions (2 phones per Branch), but SIM cards are not always available. Volunteers are using their personal sim cards and could request reimbursement with receipt. However, procedures for eligible reimbursement are not clear or recorded.
• Critical numbers saved on all mobile phones including 112 (government emergency services, Head of DM, President, Office number, Finance number).
• NS doesn’t have Emergency Notification Protocol or SOPs. 
• Social media is often used for emergency communications and messaging by staff, as well as volunteers at the branch level. 
• No radio systems, Sat phones are in place. Small generators are purchased and will be distributed to the branches that could be used during distributions or other operational activities to connect telecommunications equipment, heating etc. 
• NS has Wifi connection at HQ, personal phone hotspots are used in the field and branches. 
• Head of DM acts as NS IT focal point.

• MRCS does not have a dedicated function/unit to carry out and coordinate all logistics activities.  
• The only logistics staff is the stockkeeper to manage the NS stock, who has a job description.  There is a Logistics/Procurement officer under recruitment process.
• There is no specific supply chain strategy, and lacking logistics staff and local market context doesn't allow the NS to think about a potential supply chain strategy.

• NS coordinates its stocks use supported by different projects.
• Head of DM is aware of the emergency items catalogue (EIC). However, in general, staff and volunteers lack the knowledge and use of this tool.  EIC is useful for clarifying technical specifications when procuring standard goods.
• There is no document explaining the logistics/supply chain procedure for branch directors and volunteers, but they are aware of the system and know how to request goods to HQ when required.
• International procurement is new for the NS, and it doesn’t have an internal procedure for the importation of goods (depends on the Customs authorities).

• MRCS doesn't have a dedicated function/unit to carry out and coordinate all logistics activities.  Procurement is partially managed by the Head of DM and, more recently, with the support of IFRC logistics staff.
• MRCS doesn't have a documented and approved emergency procurement procedure and  follows IFRC procurement procedures.
• There is no supplier database or supplier registration process.  Whenever goods and services are requested, NS uses previous suppliers with positive evaluations, and looks through the internet for new suppliers.  
• Local suppliers are not strong enough to consider the establishment of Framework Agreements with them.  They have a low level of stocks, and sometimes must import goods to Moldova to complement big orders.

• MRCS doesn’t have a specific manual for fleet management.  All regulations are dictated by Moldovan law, and NS is obliged to apply them (e.g., use of seatbelts, maximum speed, speed limits, and other related measures).
• Vehicles are insured based on the general standards insurance system for the Country.  
• According to the level of activities, the fleet size is adequate.  Branches don't have their vehicles; HQ sends the vehicles to cover field operations whenever there is a need.  Now NS has six operational vehicles.
• When drivers are recruited, they are interviewed and tested. Whenever taking a vehicle, the user fills out a form in the Finance department and provides a copy of the driving license.
• Fleet management is mainly done by the Head of the Finance department.

• MRCS doesn't have a warehouse manual or specific procedures.  During the current Ukraine and impacted countries crisis NS has been implementing IFRC procedures and are supported by IFRC logistics staff.  
• MRCS has one storekeeper now, and another one is under recruitment process.
• MRCS doesn't own a warehouse.  Currently storage capacity is covered by the Emergency Appeal, there is not clarity on how to plan a stock strategy afterwards.
• There is a plan to merge the two operational rented warehouses into one, and both IFRC and NS stocks will be managed with IFRC standards.
• The warehouses currently rented operate only during working hours.  NS communicates with the renting company whenever there is a need to organize access to the goods outside of hours.

component_details.title: Staff and volunteer management
component_details.description: Well-functioning staff and volunteer management systems and practices allow for effective recruitment, supervision, support and encouragement of staff and volunteers.

component_responses.notes:
• MRCS doesn’t have specific ToRs for responders. Role of Branch Director is defined and has a volunteer contract.
• MRCS Strategy on Volunteering (2010) includes some of the elements, but needs to be revised and updated in line with the IFRC Strategy (2019), taking into account the Volunteering Policy of 2022. 
• Multiple training courses have been provided to the volunteers, however, NS doesn't have an established standardized learning paths for responders across all branches. 
• Even though various trainings are conducted for volunteers, it was noted that people trained in various sectors are not consolidated in one place (one volunteer database), so it’s hard to track how many times on what topic each person was trained. 
• Excel table is used as volunteer database. It contains information with volunteers' name, contact information and availability hours. Once volunteers register at the chapters, information is sent to HQ by branch directors and recorded in national table. 
• Some volunteers’ expenses may be reimbursed against receipts.  However, there is no list of approved things that could be reimbursed.  
• Staff and Volunteers must sign the Code of Conduct before, however, not clear whether it’s systematically reinforced.
• Volunteers are briefed on the exciting risks, trainings or briefing sessions are conducted in collaboration with local authorities and partners.
• Volunteers do not have insurance or get per diem during operations.
